“From me he took his sighs and tears, / From thee his Pride and Cruelty; / From me his Languishments and Fears, / And every Killing Dart from thee;”

Analysis
  • Use of pairing reveals two more things that Love took from the speaker and are allusion to her groans and weeping, which reinforces that she is experiencing heartbreak
  • Continues the characterisation of “Love’’ as a parasitic force, which grows in power and strength as it feeds off the speaker’s and the man’s emotions
  • The verb took governs the subsequent phrases in lines 10, 11, and 12 despite not being explicitly repeated each time
  • The implicit repetition reinforces the relentless, one-sided nature of love in the poem
  • How Love continually draws out and takes away sighs, tears, languishments and fears and the beloved Pride, cruelty and killing darts
  • The repetition across both stanzas emphasises the act of conquest, where Love seemingly conquerors and takes over the body of the speaker
  • The anaphoric lines From me… From thee… From me… and the final epistrophe From thee, shows a constant back and forth between thee and me creating the impression that never the twain shall meet (too different to exist together)
  • Constant use of From reinforces the one-sided nature of love too
  • The rhyme scheme composed in alternate rhyme (ABAB not AABB) rather than rhyming couplets evokes the impression of two people remaining at a distance from one another
  • Alongside the subversion of romantic imagery is a subversion of poetic form as Behn defines it as a Song which was often set to music to entertain and to delight courtly listeners with musical rhythms and rhymes yet Love Armed is not a dreamy love song
  • The only song heard is the flourishing of trumpets and beating of drums that accompany the return of a victorious army as it is written in Iambic Tetrameter
  • In a more conventional love poem it might evoke the passionate beating of lovers’ hearts, but here it more readily associates with the iron-shod boots of a marching army, as those hearts are ruthlessly trampled upon
  • Shifts the attention to Persona Two and suggests that they are arrogant and sadistic and it is from them Love got both traits that he is displaying
  • The use of the anaphoric from in the fronted adverbials emphasises the multiple raids that Love engaged in, while her repetition of “took’ emphasises how forcefully he grabbed what he collected, and Love’s insatiable appetite creating a sense of exploitation and imbalance
  • Exposes two additional things that Love stripped from the speaker and are allusions to her weak physical state, sadness, and anxiety through the diction of languishments
  • The imbalance of power between the pair becomes clear as the speaker is debilitated, weak, physically and emotionally drained, overcome with misery and despair, while the man is aloof and unfeeling
  • Shifts the attention to Persona Two and presents them as the only source of the tool from which Love murders people
  • Dart is an allusion to Cupid’s arrow, not as an arrow shot playfully to inspire mutual affection but rather a lethal weapon designed to strike down and cause pain and suffering
  • The killing dart also symbolises a dark twist on the idea of being lovestruck having been physically struck with blood flow[ing] out in a grisly pool
  • The speaker is clearly prone to emotion and suffering from a depth of feel seen through the symbols of emotions “sighs and tears’
  • The softness of the sounds of the diction and long vowel sounds of the ea combination in fears/tears or the breathy onomatopoeia of the word sigh
  • Yet the speaker's beloved displays a certain heartlessness, characterised by words such as Cruelty, Pride, and Fire
  • It is the object of her affection from whom the Tyrant took his Killing Dart, words made of sharp stabbing sounds K/D/T suggesting that this person, is more than capable of inflicting wounds of his own
Effect, style & response
  • This allusion to Cupid is quite obvious In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of love, desire, attraction, and eroticism. Also known as Amor (meaning love) and Eros in Greece, commonly portrayed as a slender winged boy (as above)
  • Always represented and conflated with the cherubim, small, winged angels who interceded between Earth and Heaven, and images of Cupid as a small chubby boy carrying bow and arrow, which are the source of his power to fill others with uncontrollable love and desire, were entering the public consciousness
  • Behn faintly alludes to well-known iconography, by distorting Cupid’s kindly features with malice as he launches yet another Killing Dart at an unsuspecting victim
  • The general semantic field of war armed, Bleeding, pains, power, Tyrannic, hurled, Killing Dart, harmed, and Victor all link to Cupid, drawing out his father’s legacy as the words are not naturally suited to compose a romantic ditty (song)
  • Difficult to judge whether the speaker and this other person have had a past relationship that’s turned sour, or whether this is just a case of spurned affection
  • The diction Cruelty faintly implies the speaker has some experience of the other, and in stanza two, line 13 which is the only line of the poem to feature both thou and I briefly placing the two side by side (more so a conjecture, but interesting!)
13 / 14 / 15 / 16

“Thus thou and I, the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity; / But my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the victor is, and free.”

Analysis
  • Attributes supernatural power to Love and presents it as an instigator (a person that brings about and initiate) that has put weapons in the hands of the speaker and her lover, so that they can fight and harm each other while he watches
  • The speaker and her beloved have both provided Love with the weapons that have enabled him to become a deity and a god
  • How Love is no god by himself, but rather enthroned as a god through others supplying him with the ability to be so
  • Despite both of them being responsible, she is the sole victim
  • The final contrast emphasises the speaker’s suffering and emotional vulnerability as she acknowledged that while they both played a role in empowering Love, only she bears the painful consequences of them both
  • Her heart is wounded and enslaved by the very force they have armed while her beloved remains untouched being the Victor and free
  • This dynamic reinforces the inequity (lack of fairness or justice) in their relationship, where love is not mutual where the speaker is trapped in emotional turmoil, while her beloved escaped unscathed
  • Underscores the parasitic nature of love where one person gives and suffers while the other benefits without sacrifice
  • Enhances the poem’s portrayal of Love in a man’s world, as a cruel and one sided force
  • Turns the focus back on the speaker and is a very direct detail of her claiming to be broken hearted, feeling pity for herself and being wounded
  • Again returns the focus to the speaker’s lover and shows that to her he won and has become unencumbered (Free and not impeded) after their breakup
  • Returning the idea of Dionysian and Apollonian, in contrast, her beloved, cast as the Victor” in this tug-of-war, seems immune to extremes of feeling (possibly his Pride holds him in check, as if he considered himself above such tawdry (showy but poor and cheap) emotions)
  • This major clash between the two is symbolised through the eyes of the speaker and her beloved, and in their brief moment of eye-contact, the fire in the other’s eyes ignited desire in the speaker’s own
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the other six

Comparison hooks (Cambridge anthology pairings)

PoemSharp linking ideaShared technique
'A Different History' (Bhatt)The oppressed co-produce the power that rules them: Behn's lovers 'the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity'; Bhatt's colonised 'unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language'. Both interrogate worship of what wounds — and both hang the scandal on the same adjective, Behn's 'strange Tyrannic power' answering Bhatt's 'strange language'.Personified deity (Cupid enthroned / 'Great Pan… emigrated'); patterned rhetorical repetition (Behn's declarative ledger vs Bhatt's accusing questions).
'The Chimney Sweeper' (Blake)The song form as sugared delivery-system for cruelty: Blake's nursery lilt carries child-labour, Behn's dance-metre carries bleeding hearts — and in both, the powerless are taught to consent to their own harm (Tom's angelic bargain, 'if all do their duty, they need not fear harm'; the lovers' self-made god).Deceptively musical regular metre and rhyme against dark content; dramatic irony at the speaker/singer's expense.
'Where I Come From' (Brewster)Two poems about what beings are made of: Brewster's 'People are made of places' composes selves benignly from their sources; Behn runs the same logic malignly — a god assembled from donated feelings that return as another's weapons. Constitution as belonging vs constitution as expropriation.Anaphoric catalogue as structural spine; accumulation of concrete items building an abstract whole.
'Report to Wordsworth' (Boey Kim Cheng)Humans arm the force that overwhelms them: Boey's 'insatiate man' has ruined Nature until 'God is labouring to utter his last cry' — a deity dying of human agency, where Behn's is empowered by it; both make mankind author of its own cosmic catastrophe.Classical allusion repurposed (Neptune, Triton / Cupid's triumph); personification of a vast power; compressed formal frame (near-sonnet vs song) containing enormity.
'The Cockroach' (Halligan)Both poems stage a spectacle that turns into a mirror: Halligan watches the insect until 'I thought I recognised myself'; Behn watches the triumphant god until line 13 reveals the observers built him. The volta of self-implication — spectator discovered inside the spectacle.Extended conceit sustained then broken by a turn; final-line recognition that redirects the whole poem.
'Lament' (Clarke)Elegy as indictment by litany: Clarke's 'For the…' catalogue of war's casualties parallels Behn's 'From me… From thee…' ledger — repetition as mounting evidence of cost, with the guilty party (war / the beloved) convicted by accumulation. Both also beautify damage ('the cormorant in his funeral silk' / 'Bleeding Hearts… flowed') so that elegance itself feels complicit.Anaphora as structural engine; ironic gap between musical, ceremonial form ('Song', 'Lament') and violent content.
WRITING ABOUT IT

Writing About It

Turning the analysis into paragraphs that score

Writing about it

The poem is on the paper. Nothing below requires memory — only noticing, and the nerve to argue. The differentiator at the top grades is not knowledge but contestability: every paragraph should contain one claim a reasonable reader could dispute, defended from the printed text.

Model paragraph A (form → feeling)

Behn's cruellest rhyme is also her argument. 'Thus thou and I, the God have armed' concludes the poem's long audit with its only compound subject — the lovers united, for a single line, in the act that convicts them — and the rhyme-word returns two lines later with one letter added: 'my poor Heart alone is harmed'. The difference between arming and harming is a single breathed aspirate, an exhalation — almost a sigh — so that cause and consequence are made audible as the same word, once whole and once wounded. The couplet's pathos is sharpened by everything the preceding ledger promised: eight lines of 'From me… From thee' parallelism train the reader to expect symmetrical outcomes, and 'alone' breaks the poem's own contract. The injustice is therefore felt formally before it is understood propositionally — we are cheated of a balance the stanza taught us to want. This is Behn's larger method: the poem does not describe unfairness; it builds fairness into its structure and then withholds it, making the reader briefly suffer the speaker's arithmetic. (≈175 words)

Model paragraph B (language and tone)

The most chilling word in the poem is its lightest. Love takes fire 'From thy Bright Eyes' and throws it 'round about, in sport' — and the comma-isolated phrase sits between the roaming adverbial and the ballistic verb 'hurled' like a shrug between two violences. 'Sport' in Restoration usage covered both game and amorous play, so the pun makes flirtation and cruelty the same gesture: the god's atrocity is recreational, and recreation is how atrocity is done. The register clash — a parlour word inside a siege — defines the poem's tyrant more precisely than 'Tyrannic' does, because caprice is worse than policy: 'Fresh pains he did Create' promises inventiveness, not mere repetition, in the suffering to come. Behn is anatomising a fashionable style of loving, the libertine treatment of desire as a game with points, and her metre colludes ironically: the line dances. The reader, enjoying a song about hurled fire, is caught doing precisely what Love does — taking pleasure, in sport, in someone else's burning. (≈170 words)

Three sentence-patterns that do the most work

  1. The double-function claim: "The [feature] does not merely [obvious function]; it [argumentative function]." — e.g. "The anaphora of 'From me… From thee' does not merely list the lovers' gifts; it trains an expectation of parity that line 15 exists to betray." Forces technique-spotting to become argument.
  2. The placement sentence: "Placed [position], '[quotation]' [claim about what the placement does]." — e.g. "Placed as the poem's final stress, 'free' gives the beloved's liberty the last beat of the music — and its rhyme with 'thee' gives him the last sound." Position is always visible on the printed paper; arguing from it proves close reading without recall.
  3. The concession-turn: "What looks like [X] is also [Y] — and the poem needs both." — e.g. "What looks like helpless complaint is also a forensic case, and the poem needs both: the pain authenticates the analysis, the analysis dignifies the pain." The built-in counter-move that separates Band 1 from Band 2 answers.

Three phrases to avoid

  1. "This shows that love is cruel/powerful." — Restates theme without mechanism; the examiner already knows what the poem is about. Replace with how the specific wording enforces the idea ("the gapped verb makes the theft routine").
  2. "…to engage the reader / make the reader want to read on." — Empty universal effect; true of everything ever written. Name a particular response with its textual trigger ("the broken parallelism makes the reader feel short-changed on the speaker's behalf").
  3. "'X' has connotations of Y." — Harmless only if the connotation is then made to do something; on its own it is a dictionary gesture. Complete the circuit: connotation → why this connotation, here, changes the argument of the line.
EXAM PRACTICE

Exam Practice

Questions, plans, and the marginal gains

Context that earns marks

3.1 The first professional woman writer

  • Behn (baptised, probably, 14 December 1640; died 16 April 1689) is credibly described as one of the first Englishwomen — effectively the first — to earn her living by her pen: some nineteen plays [approximate], poems, translations and prose fictions including Oroonoko (1688).
  • In 1666 she worked as a spy in Antwerp for Charles II's government during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, tasked with turning the exile William Scot; her code name 'Astrea' became her literary name. The debtors'-prison sequel is apocryphal (see 1.2).
  • She was buried in Westminster Abbey's East Cloister under the epitaph 'Here lies a Proof that Wit can never be / Defence enough against Mortality'. Woolf's tribute (exact wording in 1.2) canonised her as the woman who 'earned them the right to speak their minds'.
  • Reception: a woman who published — who sold her words and staged desire — was routinely smeared with the pun on 'public woman'; satirists equated poetess and prostitute. Behn answered in kind: in the preface to The Lucky Chance (1687) she demanded 'the privilege for my masculine part the poet in me' — the right to write with the freedoms allowed male wits. This is the frame for a female-voiced lyric that openly claims 'desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World': the scandal was not the cruelty of Cupid but a woman announcing the scale of her own wanting.

3.2 The Petrarchan tradition inverted — via Petrarch's own Triumph

  • Behn's opening tableau is not a generic Roman parade: it compresses Petrarch's Trionfi, whose first panel, the Triumphus Cupidinis ('Triumph of Love'), shows Cupid as a Roman victor on a fiery chariot leading a procession of captive lovers (Dido, Cleopatra, Caesar; Jupiter chained to the car). Behn's revisions are pointed: the illustrious captives are reduced to anonymous, liquefied 'Bleeding Hearts' (suffering democratised, and de-glamorised); the observing poet is a woman; and where Petrarch's speaker simply joins the procession, Behn's conducts an audit of the triumph's supply chain — where did the conqueror's arms come from? From us.
  • The Petrarchan kit is present but repurposed: the blazon shrinks to a single item ('Bright Eyes') and is instantly weaponised; 'sighs and tears' and 'Languishments' — the badges of the noble suffering lover — are confiscated and redeployed as ordnance. In Petrarchism, suffering ennobles the lover; in Behn, suffering is raw material extracted from the lover. The convention itself is exposed as an economy.

3.3 Ovid's militarised Cupid — and Behn's transformation

  • The conceit descends from Ovid, Amores I.9: 'Militat omnis amans, et habet sua castra Cupido' — 'every lover is a soldier, and Cupid has his own camp'. In the classical militia amoris, the lover is conscripted: he serves in Love's army, besieges doors, keeps night watches.
  • Behn's twist is structural: her lovers are not soldiers but the arsenal. They do not serve Love; they equip him — the beloved supplies ordnance ('every Killing Dart'), the speaker supplies the psychological weapons ('Languishments and Fears'). And note the hidden demotion inside the apotheosis: this Cupid arrives unarmed. The god owns nothing; every power he 'showed' was 'took'. 'Set him up a Deity' is the language of idol-making — the poem quietly says that Love is a god only because two humans built him one, which is as sceptical a claim about deities as a Restoration lyric could hazard. (A modern critical analogy — flag it as analogy, not allusion: Hobbes's Leviathan (1651), where subjects covenant to 'set up' an artificial sovereign person whose power is theirs, yet who stands above them irrevocably.)

3.4 Restoration stage conditions

  • Theatres reopened at the Restoration (1660) with two patent companies and, for the first time, professional actresses; frank stagings of desire — including female desire — were the commercial idiom Behn wrote in. Songs within plays were detachable hits, circulated in miscellanies; this one had a double life (see 3.6).

3.5 How the song works as the opening of Abdelazer — verified against the text

Abdelazer, or The Moor's Revenge (premiered 3 July 1676, Dorset Garden Theatre, Duke's Company; Thomas Betterton in the title role) is Behn's only tragedy, adapted from Lust's Dominion (c. 1600; printed 1657 under Marlowe's name, now usually assigned to Dekker and collaborators). The play's first minutes, from the 1677-based text:

  • Stage direction: 'A rich chamber. A table with lights, Abdelazer sullenly leaning his head on his hands. After a little while, whilst music still plays, SONG.' No singer is specified; the play's first spoken words are the song's.
  • 'After which Abdelazer rouses, and gazes' and snarls: 'On me this music lost? — This sound on me / That hates all softness?' — then, when the Queen enters and bids her musicians 'Play all your sweetest notes', he snaps 'Cease that unwelcome noise'. The play literally opens with a love song being rejected by its addressee — the song's scenario (one who languishes, one who is proud, cruel and free) is performed in the auditorium before it is confirmed in the plot.
  • The serenade is Queen Isabella's gift to Abdelazer, whom she loves obsessively and adulterously; the song is, in effect, her voice: she is the desiring, languishing party, he the 'Pride and Cruelty'. Within the same scene her passion turns lethal — the old King is poisoned at her instigation ('This very hour, the last the king can live') — so the lyric's thesis, desire arms tyranny, is enacted politically before Act I ends.
  • Quote-level continuity (the strongest, least-known evidence for the song's proleptic function): the Queen echoes line 5 — 'Whilst we from eyes — thus — dying, fan the fire'; Abdelazer fuses lines 5 and 12 — 'thousand eyes throw killing looks at me'; and he re-uses the song's key verb of line 13 — 'This many-headed beast your lust has armed'. Behn transfers 'armed' from Cupid to the body politic within one scene: what desire arms in the lyric is a god; in the play, a mob and a usurper.
  • Audience effect: we, unlike Abdelazer, enjoy the song — Restoration audiences came for the music. Behn implicates our pleasure: like Love, we take the lovers' pain 'in sport'.
  • Music caution for candidates: the famous Abdelazer music — Purcell's suite (Z 570), whose Rondeau Britten took as the theme of The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra — belongs to the 1695 revival, six years after Behn's death; Purcell's song for that revival was 'Lucinda is bewitching fair', not this lyric. No composer for the 1676–77 song is securely recorded uncertain. Claiming "Purcell set this song" is a marked error.

3.6 Publication history and textual variants

  • 1677: the play quarto, Abdelazer, or the Moor's Revenge … Written by Mrs. A. Behn (London: J. Magnes and R. Bentley) — the song untitled, simply 'SONG', heading Act I.
  • 1684: reprinted in Behn's Poems upon Several Occasions: with A Voyage to the Island of Love (London: R. and J. Tonson) under the title 'Love Arm'd' — the poem's second life as a free-standing lyric, detached from the play.
  • Variants worth knowing (early printings differ in small ways; check a facsimile before quoting them in print): old-spelling 'Phantastique'; 'about him flow'd' (anthology: 'around him flowed'); the play-text tradition reads plural 'fires … desires' and elides 'Enough t' undo' where the anthology has singular 'fire … desire'; and line 3 has an early reading 'fresh pays' revised to 'pains' [reported variant]. Exam point: quote the anthology text; use the variants only to show the poem existed as both theatre song and printed lyric — evidence of Behn managing her own literary afterlife.

Two exam questions in Cambridge 0475 style

Q1. Explore the ways in which Behn strikingly portrays Love as a tyrant in 'Song: Love Armed'.

  • Thesis: Behn's strike is double — she paints a conventional tyrant-Cupid with shocking vividness, then springs the unconventional accusation that the tyrant is home-made: the portrait of tyranny becomes a portrait of collaboration.
  • Point 1 — The tyrant staged: trochaic seizure of the first stress in 'Love in Fantastic Triumph sat' + the Petrarchan/Roman triumph tableau; 'Bleeding Hearts around him flowed' processes gore to a regular beat — tyranny made ceremonial, atrocity normalised into music.
  • Point 2 — The tyrant's temperament: 'Fresh pains he did Create' (capitalised Create — the tyrant usurps God's verb) and 'in sport he hurled' — the register clash between playful adverbial and ballistic verb defines Behn's tyrant: cruelty performed with insouciance, government by whim ('strange Tyrannic power').
  • Point 3 — The tyrant disarmed by the syntax: the 'From me… From thee' ledger with its gapped verb shows every weapon taken, none owned; 'Thus thou and I, the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity' — investiture and idol-making diction reveal tyranny as a grant from its subjects; armed/harmed rhyme as cause-and-effect in one aspirate.
  • Counter-move: yet the ending deposes Cupid from his own poem — 'Whilst thine the Victor is, and free' restages the opening tableau with the human beloved enthroned; the real tyrant of the last line is not the allegorical god but the person worship has licensed; the 'Fantastic' (fantasy) triumph was our projection all along.
  • Conclusion: the striking thing is the transfer: Behn borrows the oldest picture in love poetry, paints it in blood, then hands the reader the receipt — tyranny in love is manufactured, subsidised and crowned by the lovers themselves, which is far more disquieting than a cruel god.

Q2. How does Behn make the speaker's sense of injustice so moving in 'Song: Love Armed'?

  • Thesis: the injustice moves us because the poem's own form promises fairness — balance, symmetry, equal entries — and then breaks that promise in one word, 'alone'; we feel the verdict as a betrayal of the grammar we have been trained by.
  • Point 1 — The rigged ledger: anaphoric parallelism ('From me his sighs and tears, / From thee his Pride and Cruelty') offers apparent equity of contribution while the content of the entries is already unequal — she donates wounds, he donates weapons ('every Killing Dart from thee'); the pyrrhic sag inside 'Languishments' makes her side audibly weaker.
  • Point 2 — Desire as the greatest gift: the poem's only enjambment, 'desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World', with the period pun on 'undo' (sexual ruin) — her contribution is world-sized and self-endangering, which makes the final distribution of outcomes monstrous rather than merely sad.
  • Point 3 — The two-stage blow: 'Thus thou and I' — the couple's only grammatical union, achieved in shared guilt — raises the expectation of shared consequence; then 'But my poor Heart alone is harmed', where 'alone' detonates against fourteen lines of me-and-thee pairing; the armed/harmed rhyme makes her injury the direct product of her generosity.
  • Counter-move: the speaker is not only pitiable — the forensic control, the epigrammatic close, the covert boast of line 8 give her the dignity of the better rhetorician; Behn moves us with clear-sighted accounting, not tears (the 'sighs and tears' were confiscated in line 9, and the poem sheds none).
  • Conclusion: the pathos is structural: the final couplet's 'Whilst' returns us to line 2 with the speaker now among the bleeding hearts and the beloved's pronoun ('thee… free') owning the very rhyme-sound of the stanza — injustice audible, not just stated, in who gets the last word's music.

Ten 'examiner's edge' facts

  1. Form: two octaves (never "four quatrains"), rhyming ababcdcd efefgfgf — and stanza 2's deviation is the point: the /iː/ of 'thee' captures every even line (Cruelty, thee, Deity, free), so the beloved's sound wins the stanza and the poem's final word, 'free', rhymes with his pronoun.
  2. armed/harmed is a minimal pair: one added aspirate /h/ — a breath, a sigh — converts arming into harming. Cause and consequence are one phoneme apart; quote it as the poem's argument made audible.
  3. Only one enjambment in sixteen lines: 'desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World' — the single overflow in an end-stopped poem, placed on the one commodity that exceeds all measure; unelided, the line even bulges past the tetrameter.
  4. 'Undo' carried the Restoration sense of sexual ruin (a woman 'undone'); 'the Amorous World' can be ruined as a maid is ruined. 'Sport' likewise doubled as a term for amorous play — cruelty and flirtation in one word.
  5. 'Fantastic' = 'of fantasy/imagination' in 1676, not 'wonderful': the triumph is a mental pageant, which primes the ending's revelation that the god was 'set… up' by his own victims. ('Phantastique' in the old spelling.)
  6. 'Thine' in line 16 is elliptical for 'thy heart' (parallel to 'my poor Heart'): the closing contrast is heart against heart, not woman against man — misread it as plain 'you' and the couplet's symmetry is lost. Meanwhile the two 'Whilst' clauses (lines 2 and 16) frame the poem: the ending restages the opening tableau with the beloved in Love's throne.
  7. Intertexts that earn AO3: Ovid, Amores I.9 — 'militat omnis amans' ('every lover is a soldier') — supplies the love-as-war topos; Petrarch's Triumphus Cupidinis (Cupid as Roman victor with captive lovers) supplies the opening tableau. Behn's transformation: her lovers are not Love's soldiers but his armourers — the god arrives unarmed and is equipped by his victims.
  8. Dramatic frame: the song opens Abdelazer (Dorset Garden, July 1676; Behn's only tragedy; Betterton in the title role) before any dialogue; no singer is specified; it is the Queen's serenade to a man who orders it silenced ('On me this music lost?… Cease that unwelcome noise'), and Act I recycles its lexicon — 'killing looks', 'your lust has armed'. Do not credit Purcell: his celebrated Abdelazer music (the Rondeau Britten used) belongs to the 1695 revival.
  9. Two lives in print: untitled 'SONG' in the 1677 play quarto; retitled 'Love Arm'd' in Poems upon Several Occasions (1684) — evidence Behn curated the lyric's afterlife; small variants ('fires/desires', 'about him flow'd') distinguish the traditions, and the anthology text is the exam reference.
  10. Behn precision pack: probably baptised 14 December 1640, died 16 April 1689; spied in Antwerp (1666) under the code name 'Astrea', later her pen name; no evidence she was actually imprisoned for debt (warrant story apocryphal) — say 'threatened with debtors' prison' at most; buried in Westminster Abbey's East Cloister (not Poets' Corner), epitaph 'Here lies a Proof that Wit can never be / Defence enough against Mortality'; Woolf, exactly: 'All women together ought to let flowers fall upon the tomb of Aphra Behn… for it was she who earned them the right to speak their minds.'
EDITORIAL NOTES

Editorial Notes

Text checks and corrections to the source notes

Gaps audit — what the existing notes get wrong, over-claim, or miss

1.1 Contamination: a different (and probably non-existent) poem — EXCLUDE

Lines ~1165–1247 of the notes file describe a poem that is not this text:

  • a four-stanza narrative in AABB couplets in which Love "sneaks in" disguised as a "shepherd boy" / "harmless villager", then attacks;
  • quoted phrases: "For he in Ambuscade did lie, / And out of ambush shot at me", "Bright Scrip", crook turned into a "Bow", weapons of "flame" and "poison", "Bright Bow and Burning Brand", "With all her Silent, Subtle Skill", "fatal wound", "Prisoner", "Then sighing said, 'Ah, welladay!'", "Trust not his seeming simple look".

None of these words or lines occurs in 'Song: Love Armed' (16 lines, two octaves, a tableau plus a ledger — no disguise narrative at all). Searching the quoted lines finds no such poem in Behn's canon or anyone else's; the only revision-site hit carrying these phrases is itself AI-generated. The material is almost certainly a fabricated pastiche (the disguised-Cupid motif resembles the Prologue of Tasso's Aminta, where Love appears in shepherd's dress, but the quoted text matches no identifiable poem). Exclude the whole block, including its "Quick Plot Breakdown", the stanza-by-stanza "flow", the "puppy/T-Rex" analogy, the AABB rhyme claims, and the "Common Mistakes" list built on it. If a genuine companion lyric is wanted, use Behn's real song 'A Thousand Martyrs I have made' — the same love-as-conquest conceit voiced from the victor's side.

1.2 Factual and internal errors in the genuine material

  1. Stanza form contradiction. The "Extended Context" section claims "Four quatrains (4 stanzas of 4 lines each)" and "ABAB throughout"; other sections correctly say two octaves. The 1677 playbook, the 1684 collection and the anthology all print two eight-line stanzas. The quatrain is the underlying rhyming unit, but the printed octave matters (see 2.2).
  2. Three incompatible rhyme schemes are asserted (ABAB throughout; ABABCDCD EFEFGFGF; ABABCDCDEFEFGHGH). Correct: ababcdcd efefgfgf. The erroneous "ghgh" version destroys the poem's best formal fact — the f-rhyme takeover (see 2.2).
  3. "Line 10 is the shortest line in the poem — two words and their article" — false. 'From thee his Pride and Cruelty' is a regular six-word, eight-syllable tetrameter.
  4. "Bleeding" as a Restoration expletive ("sardonic exasperation") — anachronistic; expletive bleeding is nineteenth-century slang. Cut both occurrences.
  5. "Tyrannic had striking political resonance in 1694" — date garble (play 1676; Charles I executed 1649). Related over-reach: implying Behn anticipates the Glorious Revolution (1688) — usable only as reader's hindsight, not authorial intention.
  6. Volta list error: "Line 13 — 'Cruel' reframes tone" — the word does not occur in line 13 ('Cruelty' is line 10). Line 13's actual pivot is 'Thus' (see 2.3), which the notes never analyse.
  7. Enjambment contradiction: "Lack of enjambment shows restriction" vs "the only line with enjambment". The second is right: 7→8 is the poem's only true enjambment; every other line is end-stopped by punctuation.
  8. Epistrophe claim ("'…from thee' ends both lines 10 and 12") — false: line 10 begins 'From thee'; only line 12 ends with it. The real figure is a positional inversion, and it is better than epistrophe (see 2.4).
  9. Biography over-claims. (a) "She stayed in debtor's prison": there is no evidence Behn was ever imprisoned for debt — the story is apocryphal. (b) "Spent time in prison for her political writings": a warrant was issued in 1682 over the epilogue to Romulus and Hersilia (an attack on Monmouth); imprisonment is not evidenced. (c) The marriage to "Johan Behn, Dutch merchant": the husband is a shadowy figure — say "may have married"; some biographers suspect he was invented to supply widow status. (d) "Sung by a Boy singer": unsupported — the 1677-based text gives no singer, only "After a little while, whilst music still plays, SONG".
  10. "'Languishments' is an almost Victorian word" — wrong register: languishment is standard Petrarchan-Restoration diction (the languishing lover was a stock figure). Its strangeness now is not evidence about 1676.
  11. Woolf quotation appears twice with drifting wording. Exact text (A Room of One's Own, 1929): "All women together ought to let flowers fall upon the tomb of Aphra Behn, which is, most scandalously but rather appropriately, in Westminster Abbey, for it was she who earned them the right to speak their minds." Add what the notes omit: she is buried in the Abbey's East Cloister, not Poets' Corner — the "scandalously but rather appropriately" makes sense only with that detail.
  12. Play-plot garble: "Abdelazer … uses Isabella as means to become King by killing her husband and kids." In the text, the Queen procures the old King's poisoning ("This very hour, the last the king can live… I his life betrayed", I.1), urged on by Abdelazer; Abdelazer later has the young King Ferdinand killed; Florella is murdered; Abdelazer has the Queen murdered in turn; he is finally captured and killed and Philip survives to take the throne.
  13. Missing entirely from ~195KB of notes: any scanned line beyond "trochee in line 1"; the armed/harmed rhyme; the f-rhyme takeover; the gapped verb in 10–12; the "Whilst" frame (2↔16); the meaning of 'thine' in line 16; 'undo' as sexual ruin; Ovid's militia amoris; Petrarch's Trionfi; the 1677/1684 publication history; the play-scene echoes of the song's own vocabulary; any queer/ungendered or political reading; comparison hooks; Cambridge-style questions.

1.3 Thin analysis worth sharpening

  • "Iambic tetrameter = relentless march" is asserted repeatedly but no line is ever scanned; the meaningful substitutions (spondees on 'FRESH PAINS' and 'BRIGHT EYES', the pyrrhic sag inside 'Languishments') are unused.
  • "Song-form lightness vs dark content" appears six-plus times as a free-floating irony; it becomes an argument only when tied to the theatre: this was a song, performed as a seduction gift that the onstage listener rejects (see 3.5).
  • "Alternating rhyme = lovers never unified" is decent but unevidenced; the evidence is stanza 2's asymmetric scheme, which the notes mis-transcribe.

Text check

The anthology text (two octaves, sixteen lines, as quoted at the head of the existing notes) is a modernised text of the poem Behn published twice: sung on stage from the premiere of Abdelazer (3 July 1676, Dorset Garden Theatre); first printed 1677 in the play quarto (London: J. Magnes and R. Bentley), where it is untitled — simply 'SONG' heading Act I — and first printed as a free-standing lyric in 1684 in Poems upon Several Occasions: with A Voyage to the Island of Love (London: R. and J. Tonson), retitled 'Love Arm'd'. So "1676" is the performance date, "1677" the first publication; both are defensible in an essay if used precisely.

Line-by-line check against the early witnesses:

LAnthology readingVerification
1Love in Fantastic Triumph sat,Matches the 1677 tradition (old spelling 'Phantastique… sat'). No 'sate' in the verified witnesses.
2Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,Early printings read 'about him flow'd'; 'around' is the modernised reading. Sense unchanged.
3For whom Fresh pains he did Create,An early playbook reading 'fresh pays', revised to 'pains', is reported [reported variant]; the anthology follows 'pains'.
4And strange Tyrannic power he showed;No substantive variant found [as far as verified]. 'Power' is monosyllabic in the metre.
5From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire,The play-text tradition reads plural 'fires'.
6Which round about, in sport he hurled;Medial comma is the anthology's pointing; punctuation varies lightly between printings.
7But 'twas from mine he took desirePlay-text tradition: 'desires'.
8Enough to undo the Amorous World.Play-text elides: 'Enough t' undo th[e] amorous world' — which is what keeps the line a tetrameter.
9–12From me… / From thee… / From me… / And every Killing Dart from thee;No substantive variants found beyond spelling, capitalisation and pointing uncertain.
13–16Thus thou and I… free.As above; the comma after 'I' varies between printings without changing the sense.

As printed in the anthology, each octave is a single sentence (full stops only at lines 8 and 16) — two long breaths, spectacle then verdict; the pointing varies between early printings, but the two-sentence shape is stable.

Exam consequence: the poem is printed on the paper, so none of this needs memorising. The only practical uses of textual knowledge are negative and positive: do not "correct" the paper's wording from a remembered edition (quote exactly what is in front of you); and exploit the printed text for whole-poem noticing moves — counting the three-then-gapped 'took', tracking the two 'Whilst's, re-reading 'Fantastic' after line 14 — which are precisely the moves memorisation-based revision never teaches.

Sujata Bhatt  ·  1988

A culture that treats a book as sacred is asked why its grandchildren now love the language that was used to erase it.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Sujata Bhatt (born 1956)

Sujata Bhatt was born in Ahmedabad, India, and grew up in Pune. She emigrated to the United States in 1968 at age 12, studying creative writing at the University of Iowa (MFA) — the most prestigious creative writing programme in America. She has been writer-in-residence at the University of Victoria, Canada, and has lived in Bremen, Germany since the mid-1980s with her husband, the German writer and radio broadcaster Michael Augustin, and their daughter. Her debut collection Brunizem (1988) won both the Commonwealth Poetry Prize (Asia region) and the Alice Hunt Bartlett Award, establishing her as a major voice in contemporary poetry.

Bhatt writes predominantly in English but has a profound relationship with Gujarati, her mother tongue. She has described Gujarati as the deepest layer of my identity. This bifurcated linguistic identity — English as daily medium, Gujarati as emotional bedrock — is the central subject of much of her work. Her most famous poem Search for My Tongue (not in this syllabus but worth knowing) literally alternates between English and Gujarati script, asking what happens to your mother tongue when you stop using it.

For Bhatt, language is not merely a communicative tool — it is synonymous with identity, memory, and selfhood. She has described her poetic process as translating images, sounds, rhythms and an emotional tone into words. The word translating is significant: she sees herself as always working between languages and cultures, never settled in one.

Historical Context: British Colonialism in India

Britain's involvement in India began with the East India Company in the early 17th century. By the mid-18th century, the Company had expanded to control vast territories. In 1858, following the Indian Rebellion of 1857 (which the British called the Indian Mutiny), the Crown assumed direct rule — creating the British Raj. India was officially ruled as part of the British Empire from 1858 to 1947.

During this period, English was established as the language of administration, law, higher education, and public life. The English Education Act 1835, which followed Thomas Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (2 February 1835), explicitly aimed to create a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect. English was imposed not just as a language but as a culture — and native Indian languages, traditions, and knowledge systems were systematically devalued.

India gained independence in 1947. But the legacy of this linguistic colonialism was — and remains — profound. For educated Indians of Bhatt's generation, English is simultaneously the language of freedom (it gives access to global culture, literature, science) and the language of oppression (it was the coloniser's tongue, used to suppress native identities). A Different History directly engages this paradox.

The Two Stanzas — Two Worlds

The poem's two-stanza structure enacts its central argument. Stanza 1 (lines 1–18) is set in a world of living Hindu and Greek mythology — a syncretic, sacred, warm world. Stanza 2 (lines 19–29) confronts the violence of colonialism and asks the anguished, unanswerable question: how is it that the colonised come to love the coloniser's language? The white space between the stanzas is a border — between worlds, between historical periods, between innocence and knowledge.

Pan and Sarasvati: Mythological Figures

PAN (Greek mythology): god of wild nature, shepherds, flocks, and rustic music. He has the hindquarters, legs, and horns of a goat. Pan was associated with panic (the word panic derives from Pan — the sudden irrational terror that Pan was said to cause). In Christian tradition, The Great God Pan is dead was a legend about the death of paganism with the rise of Christianity. Bhatt denies this: Pan hasn't died; he emigrated to India, where the gods still roam.

SARASVATI (Hindu mythology): the goddess of all learning, arts, music, painting, sculpture, dance, and especially writing and language. She is credited with giving humans the gift of writing so her songs could be preserved. She is the patron of poets and scholars. She rides a white swan or sits on a white lotus. She carries a veena (stringed instrument), a book, and a rosary. Sarasvati is also in tension with Lakshmi (goddess of wealth) — if you pursue wealth, Sarasvati (creativity/wisdom) will desert you.

The coexistence of Pan (Greek) and Sarasvati (Hindu) in the same poem is itself an act of cultural syncretism — a demonstration that diverse mythological traditions can coexist and overlap. This is exactly what colonialism disrupted: the meeting of different traditions as equals. British colonialism did not bring Greek culture and Hindu culture into equal conversation; it imposed one over the other.
