11a sin to slam books down
12hard on a table,
13a sin to toss one carelessly
14across a room.
15You must learn how to turn the pages gently
16without disturbing Sarasvati,
17without offending the tree
18from whose wood the paper was made.
19Which language
20has not been the oppressor's tongue?
21Which language
22truly meant to murder someone?
23And how does it happen
24that after the torture,
25after the soul has been cropped
26with a long scythe swooping out
27of the conqueror's face –
28the unborn grandchildren
29grow to love that strange language.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Line 1
Great Pan is not dead;
Language & devices

ALLUSION to the legend The Great God Pan is dead (supposedly cried out at sea when Christ was born, signalling the death of paganism). Immediate Denial: opens with a flat refutation of this legend. Semicolon: not a full stop — the thought continues, is qualified. Diction: Great — Pan's traditional epithet; also suggests immensity, importance.

Meaning & effect

The opening is quietly subversive: it takes a deeply embedded Western cultural narrative (the death of paganism, the rise of Christianity) and simply refuses it. Pan is not dead. The semicolon performs a grammatical pause that mimics the considering of evidence before delivering the alternative. Tone: matter-of-fact, confident, almost amused. Not angry. The speaker is not arguing — she is informing.

Line 2
he simply emigrated
Language & devices

Adverb: simply — without drama, without announcement. Verb: emigrated — moved from one country to another, specifically for permanent residence. Emigrated not travelled or fled or moved. LOWERCASE he: Pan is not capitalised as a deity — he is treated with familiarity, as an equal.

Meaning & effect

Simply emigrated is a beautifully deflating phrase. The legendary death of Pan — which in Western theology represents the end of the entire pagan world-order — is reframed as an unremarkable act of emigration. He just moved. The choice of emigrated rather than migrated is precise: emigrants leave one country to settle in another, with the intention of staying. Pan has adopted India as his home. Autobiographical: Bhatt herself emigrated — from India to the USA at age 12. There is a quiet self-identification between the poet and the god.

Line 3
to India.
Language & devices

Isolated Line: indented, short, a full stop. The destination is given its own line, its own space — as if the mere act of naming India requires a breath of ceremony. Punctuation: full stop after India — definitive, complete.

Meaning & effect

The visual isolation of to India gives it weight. It is Pan's adopted home, but it is also where Bhatt comes from. The line performs the moment of arrival — the pause before placing yourself in a new world. The indentation visually suggests that India is slightly off-centre, slightly aside from the Western narrative that has been invoked. It is present, but on its own terms.

Line 4
Here, the gods roam freely,
Language & devices

Adverb: Here — India, specifically. Verb: roam — wander without fixed path; animals roam. The gods are not confined to temples or churches but move through the living world. Adverb: freely — unconfined, unconstrained.

Meaning & effect

The shift from Great Pan is not dead to the gods roam freely is from singular to plural — not just Pan but all gods. India is a polytheistic culture with many thousands of deities. The gods roam rather than reside: this is not a religion of fixed institutions (churches, cathedrals) but of a divine presence immanent in the natural world. Freely is a liberating word — the gods here are not imprisoned in buildings or doctrines.

Line 5
disguised as snakes or monkeys;
Language & devices

Cultural Knowledge: in Hindu tradition, the Naga (snake deities) and Hanuman (monkey god) are divine. What Western culture fears (snakes) or dismisses (monkeys) is sacred here. Disguised — the gods choose their forms; these are not their permanent appearances but chosen masks.

Meaning & effect

The word disguised is complex: from a Western perspective, a god disguised as a snake is incomprehensible — gods should look divine. But from a Hindu perspective, this is entirely natural — gods are everywhere and in everything. The word disguised is actually Bhatt gently conceding to a Western reader's likely puzzlement, while insisting on the Hindu truth. The semicolon at the end connects this to the next statement — the sacred pervades all of nature.

Line 6
every tree is sacred
Language & devices

Absolute: every — no exceptions. Not some trees, not special trees — EVERY tree. Diction: sacred — holy, not to be violated. Short Line: the unqualified absoluteness of the statement is enhanced by its brevity.

Meaning & effect

This is a profound statement about the relationship between religion and ecology. In a world where every tree is sacred, deforestation is not merely environmental damage but spiritual transgression. This directly connects to lines 17–18: the tree from whose wood the paper was made is sacred; therefore the book made from that paper inherits the tree's sacredness. The reverential relationship to books is not arbitrary but flows logically from reverence for nature.

Line 7–8
and it is a sin / to be rude to a book.
Language & devices

Anaphora begins: it is a sin. Diction: rude — unexpectedly casual word for a sacred transgression. To be rude to a book is to treat it dismissively, without the respect it deserves. The phrase has the quality of a grandmother's gentle teaching — not a formal religious decree.

Meaning & effect

The introduction of books as sacred objects is the poem's pivot. The logic is: gods inhabit nature → every tree is sacred → paper comes from trees → books inherit the tree's sacredness → Sarasvati (goddess of language/learning) inhabits books → to mistreat a book is to offend both the tree and the goddess. This is a complete, coherent theology. CONTRAST with Western attitude: in Western culture, books are commodities — printed, sold, discarded. In this tradition, each book is a sacred object.

Line 9–11
It is a sin to shove a book aside / with your foot, / a sin to slam books down / hard on a table,
Language & devices

SPECIFIC, Physical Actions: shove aside with your foot (disrespectful dismissal), slam down hard (violent treatment). The specificity is important — these are not abstract prohibitions but precise, recognisable human actions. Indented Continuation: with your foot and hard on a table are indented — they extend and elaborate the preceding line.

Meaning & effect

The granular specificity of the prohibited actions (with your foot) is both comic and serious. With your foot — the most dismissive possible gesture: you don't even use your hands. The foot is lower than the hand, symbolically (the lowest part of the body used for the lowest act). Touching a sacred object with one's foot is a significant cultural violation in many South Asian contexts (you remove shoes before entering a temple). Bhatt is encoding a specific cultural practice into the poem's imagery.

Line 12–14
a sin to toss one carelessly / across a room.
Language & devices

Toss carelessly — the lightness, the indifference. Across a room — not near at hand but thrown at a distance. The carelessness is the sin — not the act itself but the attitude it embodies.

Meaning & effect

The three prohibited actions form an escalating scale of disrespect: shoving with a foot (dismissal), slamming down hard (aggression), tossing carelessly (indifference). Each represents a different failure of reverence: dismissal, violence, and carelessness. Together they define the opposite of the reverence that should accompany books. Contrast: In the second stanza, language (books) will be used to murder people. The contrast between the sacred treatment of books demanded in Stanza 1 and the violent misuse of language in Stanza 2 is stark.

Line 15–18
You must learn how to turn the pages gently / without disturbing Sarasvati, / without offending the tree / from whose wood the paper was made.
Language & devices

Imperative: You must learn. Verbs: disturbing, offending — these are social words, not religious ones. You disturb someone who is present; you offend someone who has feelings. Both verbs treat Sarasvati and the tree as presences with interiority — they can be disturbed and offended.

Meaning & effect

The poem's first half culminates in this beautiful, extended instruction. Turn the pages gently — the simple physical act of reading is given ceremonial weight. The triple levels of reverence: the pages (physical object), Sarasvati (goddess within), the tree (natural origin). Reading is a sacred practice connecting the reader to the divine, the natural, and the linguistic simultaneously. This reading of reading has profound implications for how we understand literature — not as entertainment or information but as a sacred encounter.

Line 19–20
Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?
Language & devices

RHETORICAL QUESTION. LINE BREAK after Which language creates a pause — the question hangs. Diction: 'oppressor's tongue' — the language of the powerful used to dominate. Plural Implication: which language — ALL languages potentially, not just English.

Meaning & effect

The rhetorical question is universal in scope: not 'has English been the oppressor's tongue' (which would be a straightforward anti-colonial statement) but WHICH language has NOT been. This is more subtle and more honest: Latin was used to colonise Europe; Sanskrit was used in caste oppression; Arabic in various imperial contexts. No language is innocent. READING 1 (liberal): All languages have been oppressors; therefore no language is inherently evil. READING 2 (critical): All languages have been oppressors; therefore the problem is power, not language itself. READING 3: The question is unanswerable, and Bhatt knows it — it is a question designed to make us think, not one with a clean answer.

Line 21–22
Which language / truly meant to murder someone?
Language & devices

Repetition of Which language — anaphora. Diction: truly meant — intention is the question. Languages don't have intentions; speakers do. Verb: murder — the strongest possible word for language-killing.

Meaning & effect

Which language truly meant to murder someone? is asking whether language itself can be murderous, or only the people who use it. This is an important philosophical distinction for post-colonial writers: English was used to oppress — but is English itself oppressive? The poem refuses to condemn the language while acknowledging the use. Paradox: Bhatt writes this anti-colonial argument IN English. She is using the oppressor's tongue to question the oppressor's tongue. This is the poem's central paradox embodied in its form.

Line 23–27
And how does it happen / that after the torture, / after the soul has been cropped / with a long scythe swooping out / of the conqueror's face –
Language & devices

The Unanswerable Question: How does it happen — a genuine bewilderment, not rhetorical. Diction: torture, cropped, scythe, 'conqueror's face'. Metaphor: soul has been cropped with a long scythe — the soul is a field of grain, the coloniser is the farmer/reaper. Participle: swooping out — the scythe swoops as a bird of prey swoops. Location: 'out of the conqueror's face' — the violence emerges from the very face/identity/language of the coloniser.

Meaning & effect

The soul has been cropped is one of the most powerful metaphors in modern poetry. Cropped is an agricultural term (to crop = to cut, harvest). The soul is treated like a crop — owned, cut down, processed. This dehumanisation is the essence of colonialism: treating people as natural resources to be harvested. The scythe 'swoops out of the conqueror's face' — violence is not just a policy but is embodied in the conqueror's very appearance, built into their face. The DASH at line 27 creates a dramatic pause before the paradox is delivered.

Line 28–29
the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language.
Language & devices

Temporal Leap: unborn grandchildren — not even conceived yet at the time of colonisation. Verb: grow to love — not sudden love but gradual. Growing suggests organic development over time. Adjective: strange — foreign, uncanny, both alien and wonderful. Absent Question Mark: grammatically this should end with '?' but does not.

Meaning & effect

The poem ends without a question mark on what is structurally a question — transforming the interrogative into a statement of mysterious fact. The grandchildren WILL love that strange language. This is not presented as right or wrong, good or bad — just as what happens. Bhatt herself is one of those grandchildren: she grew to love English, writes in English, wins prizes in English. The word strange is perfectly ambivalent — it holds both alienness (the foreignness of the colonial language) and wonder (the word strange can mean wonderful, magical). The strange language is both the language of the oppressor and the language Bhatt uses to say so.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The poem is usually filed as anti-colonial protest, and its second panel — torture, murder, a scythe out of a conqueror's face — earns the label. But read continuously from first line to last, it is something less comfortable and more valuable: an essay on transmission, on how the sacred and the violent are both taught, written by a poet who is herself the poem's final image.

It opens by correcting Europe's most famous obituary. "Great Pan is not dead" flatly denies the sentence Plutarch's pilot was ordered to proclaim and Christian tradition took as paganism's death-notice; then the denial is deflated further — he "simply emigrated". The joke has a blade in it: what the West recorded as the death of the old gods was only their departure from the West. A "universal" history is exposed as parochial in eleven words. And the direction of travel matters: Pan moves east as Bhatt's family moved west, the god's immigration mirroring the poet's emigration. "Here, the gods roam freely" — that comma'd "Here" is the emigrant's word, a deictic act of repatriation performed from Iowa or Bremen. The poem begins, in other words, by demonstrating that where you stand determines what counts as dead.

The first panel then builds its ethnography of reverence: divinity immanent in despised creatures ("disguised as snakes or monkeys" quietly inverts Western contempt), "every tree is sacred", and the litany — four times "a sin" — that scales holiness down to the hand: how a book is shoved, slammed, tossed, turned. Two things complicate the idyll, and both are load-bearing. First, the moral vocabulary is imported: "sin" is the Christian loanword doing service for pāp, so the stanza describing uncolonised reverence is already conducted in the coloniser's translations — the second panel's problem is present in the first panel's diction. Second, reverence here is discipline: "it is a sin... You must learn". The sacred world also polices, instructs, forbids. The poem needs this severity, because it is establishing that culture travels through teaching — which is exactly the channel conquest will use.

The stanza break is the hinge and the wound; nothing announces the turn. The two questions that open panel two pull in opposite directions, and their grammar must be read precisely. "Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?" convicts every language — not English alone; the "not" universalises guilt. "Which language / truly meant to murder someone?" is routinely misread as its parallel, but it contains no negative and its verb is active: languages do not mean — intend — anything; wielders do. One question finds every language historically guilty; the other finds language intrinsically innocent. Between conviction and acquittal, the true defendant is identified: power, not speech. This is why the poem names no coloniser and no language — Pan, India, Sarasvati are its only proper nouns. The occasion is British India; the grammar is universal.

Then the long unanswerable sentence, in which panel one's pastoral returns as weaponry: the "tongue" of l.20 becomes a scythe "swooping out / of the conqueror's face" — speech literally the blade — and the soul is "cropped": harvested, processed as yield, the metaphor colonial extraction deserves. But "cropped" seeds the ending. What is cut regrows: "the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language." Growth is the crop's own word; the grandchildren are the next planting in cleared ground, and their love is real — gnomic present tense, recurring in every generation, the poet's included. The final deixis answers the first: India was "Here"; English is still "that strange language", loved at arm's length, intimate and foreign in one phrase. And the sentence grammar wants as a question ends with a full stop: bewilderment hardened into fact. The poem refuses to forgive the history and refuses to disown the love. Instead it closes by doing the thing it cannot explain — it is itself a grandchild's act of love performed in the strange language, gently, without disturbing Sarasvati.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Two-stanza structure

The poem is in two stanzas: Stanza 1 (ll.1–18): warm, reverent, sacred world of India. Stanza 2 (ll.19–29): confrontation with colonialism's violence. The white space between them is a visual and emotional gap — a boundary between two histories. The first stanza does not prepare us for the violence of the second, which is precisely the point: the sacred world of Stanza 1 was disrupted and violated by the events Stanza 2 describes.

Free verse

No rhyme scheme, no regular metre. The poem's formal freedom is meaningful: Bhatt writes in English without submitting to its traditional constraints, suggesting that the colonised can inhabit the coloniser's language on their own terms.

Indentation

Short, indented lines ( to India., with your foot,, hard on a table,) create visual hesitations, slow the reader down, and give individual details their own space. The line break before to India (l.3) is particularly powerful — it gives Pan's destination a quiet, understated arrival. Pan just went to India. Simple as that.

Anaphora: a sin

Lines 7–13: it is a sin / … / It is a sin to shove a book aside / … / a sin to slam books down / … / a sin to toss one carelessly. Triple repetition creates a litany — the rhythmic repetition of religious incantation. Books are as sacred as temples; their misuse is genuinely sinful in this cultural framework.

Rhetorical questions

Lines 19–22: 'Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue? / Which language / truly meant to murder someone?' These questions have no single answer — they resist resolution. They challenge the assumption that any particular language is inherently oppressive or innocent. Missing Question Mark: The final lines (ll.23–29) should grammatically conclude the rhetorical question, but the question mark is absent. This transforms what should be a question into a statement of anguished fact. The paradox is so painful it cannot be framed as a question.

Enjambment

Heavy enjambment throughout both stanzas — sentences run across line breaks, creating a flowing, accumulative quality. In Stanza 2, the enjambment accelerates: 'after the soul has been cropped / with a long scythe swooping out / of the conqueror's face –' — the sentence keeps going, like the scythe keeps cutting.

Temporal gap

The poem spans historical time: Stanza 1 is timeless/eternal (the gods always roam freely). Stanza 2 covers the colonial period and its aftermath (unborn grandchildren). The poem moves from the deep past (ancient mythology) through colonial history to the post-colonial present and future.

A diptych of unequal panels

Two free-verse verse-paragraphs: eighteen lines, then eleven. The proportions are an argument. The sacred world is given expansive, unhurried space — a whole panel to establish what reverence looks like down to the fingertips — while the violence arrives late, compressed, and takes up a third less room yet overturns everything. The white space between the panels is the poem's only transition: no conjunction, no "but", no announcement. Cross it and the pronouns, tense and mood have all changed. The gap is border, incision and historical rupture at once — the unwritten middle of the poem is colonisation itself, which happens, as it were, between the stanzas.

The panels are also secretly symmetrical. Panel one traces a chain of material transformation upwards into holiness: tree → wood → paper → pages → book, each stage inheriting sanctity from the last. Panel two traces a chain downwards into harvest: tongue → scythe → cropped soul. One panel consecrates matter; the other processes souls as matter. That mirroring is why the diptych coheres despite the tonal break.

Metre: scansion

Free verse — no metrical contract — but the stresses are managed with great care. (˘ = unstressed, / = stressed)

`` / / ˘ / / Great Pan is not dead; `` Four heavy stresses in five monosyllables: a tolling, spondaic opening that sounds like the funeral sentence it quotes — then the semicolon refuses the toll a full close.

`` ˘ / ˘ / ˘ ˘ ˘ he sim-ply em-i-gra-ted `` After the bell-strokes, a light line that dwindles through unstressed syllables; the grand death deflates into the administrative rhythm of "emigrated". The metre itself shrugs.

`` / ˘ / ˘ / ˘ ev-ery tree is sa-cred `` Trochaic trimeter — a falling, chant-like rhythm; the creed of the first panel in liturgical miniature.

`` ˘ / / / ˘ / ˘ / ˘ / ˘ You must learn how to turn the pa-ges gent-ly `` Eleven syllables, five beats, feminine ending: the closest the poem comes to iambic pentameter — English poetry's home metre — at the exact moment an Indian lesson in reverence is being taught. The form quietly enacts the poem's whole problem: the lesson is already travelling in the coloniser's music. Note too the internal rhyme learn/turn, which makes the instruction memorable as a proverb.

`` / ˘ ˘ / ˘ ˘ / af-ter the soul has been cropped `` Two falling triple rhythms swing and land on the stressed monosyllable "cropped" — swing, swing, cut.

`` ˘ ˘ / / / ˘ / with a long scythe swoop-ing out `` An anapaestic run-up jams into three consecutive stresses ("long scythe swoop-"): the metrical weight is the weight of the blade at the top of its arc.

`` / ˘ / ˘ / / ˘ grow to love that strange lan-guage. `` Heavy monosyllables — grow, love, strange — and then a final falling trochee. The poem ends on an unstressed syllable, a dying fall, exactly where the syntax wants a question's rising lift.

Also worth noting: the isolated interrogative lines are metrical fists — "Which language" is / / ˘, a spondaic attack trailing off — and the two longest lines in the poem (l.9 and l.15, ten and eleven syllables) are both about the handling of books: the verse expands precisely where care, or its violation, is greatest.

Rhyme

No scheme — but structured chimes, and they should be named rather than waved at as "no rhyme":

  • learn / turn (l.15): full internal rhyme; pedagogy made memorable.
  • book / foot (ll.9–10): imperfect rhyme (shared short /ʊ/, mismatched final consonant) binding the sacred object to the offending limb across the line-break — the rhyme commits the sin the sentence forbids.
  • tongue / someone (ll.20, 22): faint assonantal chime on /ʌ/ yoking the two questions together.
  • freely / tree / gently / Sarasvati: a long-/iː/ thread running through the first panel's moments of grace — the serene vowel of the sacred.

The volta

Is the stanza break a volta? Yes — but not the sonnet kind, where argument turns inside continuous discourse. This is a cut: subject-matter continuous (books, language, reverence), but register flipped from indicative and imperative to interrogative, tense flipped from timeless present ("is", "roam") to historical perfect ("has been cropped"), tone flipped from amused tenderness to anguish. A volta of mode hidden inside a continuity of subject — which is the argument in structural form: the same language that is cradled in panel one is the weapon of panel two. There is a second, smaller turn at l.23 ("And how does it happen"), where the paired, almost forensic questions deepen into genuine bewilderment, and the poem's final seven lines become one long suspended sentence.

Syntax and punctuation

Panel one moves from declarative assertion (ll.1–6) into litany — "it is a sin" four times (ll.7, 9, 11, 13), a grammar of commandment — and closes in a double-negative purpose construction ("without disturbing... without offending") hanging from an imperative ("You must learn"). The sacred world's syntax is the syntax of instruction.

Panel two is three questions with a withheld third question mark. The first two are short, parallel, and complete: each isolates "Which language" on its own line — language itself standing in the dock — before the predicate arrives. The third (ll.23–29) is a long periodic sentence: "And how does it happen / that..." followed by two "after..." subordinate clauses, a dash-clause containing the scythe, and only then the delayed main clause — "the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language." The grammar demands a question mark; the poem prints a full stop. Three effects: (i) the question has hardened into fact — the loving happens whether or not it can be explained; (ii) after two properly punctuated questions, the withheld mark enacts the exhaustion of the interrogative mode — history has outrun asking; (iii) the flat stop refuses both protest and absolution, declining to tell the reader how to feel. (Students regularly "correct" the ending to a question mark from memory; the full stop is the reading.)

The dash at l.27 is the poem's second hinge in miniature: it separates the atrocity from its strange consequence, a visual gap between torture and love mirroring the stanza break's gap between reverence and torture.

Lineation, indentation, enjambment

The four indented lines (3, 10, 12, 14) hang like stepped ledges. "to India." gives the destination its own shelf — arrival honoured with white space, and (as the owner's notes sharply put it) a physical image of marginalisation that nonetheless makes "India" the focal point. The three indented completions of the sin-litany — "with your foot," / "hard on a table," / "across a room." — isolate instrument, impact and trajectory, one shelf of shame each.

Enjambment does local mimetic work: "he simply emigrated / to India." crosses its own border in the line-break; "a sin to shove a book aside / with your foot" shoves the completion of the thought down and aside; "and it is a sin / to be rude to a book." delays the object so the solemn word "sin" dangles over what turns out to be an almost comic offence — the swerve into bathos is engineered by the break. In panel two the enjambment accelerates and elongates: "cropped / with a long scythe swooping out / of the conqueror's face –" keeps cutting through three line-endings, the blade emerging in the gap between "out" and "of".

Person and tense

The poem's pronouns trace its history: he (Pan) → the gods → you (the taught child-reader) → the oppressor / someone → the unborn grandchildren. The "you" who must learn to turn pages in panel one is, implicitly, the same person as the grandchild who grows to love English in panel two: both are being formed by teaching. And "grow" is a gnomic present, not a past or future — this keeps happening, generation after generation, the poet's own included.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The first panel builds a soundscape in which the sacred and the transgressive share one hiss. Sibilance carries holiness — "disguised as snakes", "every tree is sacred", "Sarasvati" — but the identical sound carries offence: "a sin to slam", "shove a book aside", "toss one carelessly". The ear is taught early what the argument will state late: sanctity and violation are made of the same material, as love and oppression will turn out to be made of the same language.

Against that hiss, the abuse of books is scored for percussion. "It is a sin to shove a book aside / with your foot, / a sin to slam books down / hard on a table" knocks with terminal stops — book, foot, down, hard — plosive /k/, /t/, /d/ striking like the impacts described, while book and foot thud on the same dulled short vowel. The triad shove / slam / toss is a rising scale of violence in curt monosyllables; the notes' observation of "power of three" is right, but the real effect is that each verb is louder and lighter than the last — from contemptuous push to careless throw, force giving way to indifference, which the poem treats as worse.

Then the consecration passage goes soft. "You must learn how to turn the pages gently / without disturbing Sarasvati, / without offending the tree / from whose wood the paper was made." Fricatives and nasals (w, th, s, n) replace the plosives; the long-e chain (gently, tree, Sarasvati) opens the vowels; and the last line's /w/ alliteration with slow rounded vowels — whose wood... was — lowers the stanza to a near-whisper before its full stop. The panel ends on "made": a made thing, at rest.

Panel two opens with bare, clipped interrogation — "Which language" twice, consonant clusters /tʃ/ and /gw/ with no verb to soften them — and the doubled /p/ of "oppressor's" spits. The scythe passage is the poem's most concentrated sound-effect: "after the soul has been cropped / with a long scythe swooping out". The sibilants — soul, scythe, swooping, then "conqueror's fa*ce*" — make the swish of a blade through air; the long vowels of "long scythe swooping" stretch the backswing; and "cropped" is shut off by the double plosive /pt/, the word amputated as the soul is. It is the rare case where onomatopoeia is doing argumentative work: the sound insists that this violence is physical, bodily, audible — not an abstraction called "cultural loss".

The final line slows into nasals and long vowels — "grow to love that strange language" — and ends on the unstressed second syllable of "language": a dying fall with no click of closure, the audible equivalent of the missing question mark. The poem does not end; it exhales.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motif = recurring element; symbol = element standing for something beyond itself. The poem's motifs accumulate into its symbols.

Motifs

  • The religious register: "sacred", "sin" (four times), "gods", and the devotional-social verbs "disturbing" and "offending". The recurrence does two things: it builds panel one's litany-like texture, and it smuggles in the poem's deepest irony — sin is Christianity's word, standing in for the dharmic concept (pāp). The stanza describing uncolonised reverence is already conducted in translation. The problem of stanza two is present in the diction of stanza one.
  • The material chain of the book: tree → wood → paper → pages → book. It recurs and closes a loop: "every tree is sacred" (l.6) returns as "the tree / from whose wood the paper was made" (ll.17–18). Reverence is not mystical but material — traceable through manufacture.
  • Motion and migration: "emigrated", "roam freely", "shove... aside", "toss... across", "swooping out", "grow". Everything in the poem moves or is moved. Sacred motion is voluntary (roaming, turning pages, emigrating); violent motion is transitive — done to things (shoved, slammed, tossed, cropped). The grammar of motion is the poem's moral grammar.
  • Teaching and learning: "You must learn" → "grow to love". Instruction recurs as the channel through which both reverence and conquest transmit themselves. What is taught with the hands in panel one is absorbed with the soul in panel two.
  • Interrogation: "Which language... Which language... And how does it happen" — a motif of asking that escalates from forensic to anguished and finally collapses into the unpunctuated non-question.

Symbols

  • Pan stands for the supposedly dead older world — pre-Christian Europe, and by extension everything "official" history declares finished — surviving by relocation. He is also a quiet double of the poet: one emigrant crossing eastward as she crossed west.
  • Sarasvati stands for language and knowledge as living presence rather than commodity. Crucially, the book-reverence around her is not a metaphor but lived practice: in many Hindu households books, paper and even money — embodiments of Sarasvati and of vidyā, learning — must not be touched with the foot, and someone who does so by accident touches the object and then their forehead or eyes in apology; at Sarasvati Puja books are placed at the goddess's shrine. Bhatt's litany describes etiquette children are actually taught, which is why its tone is domestic ("rude") as much as theological ("sin").
  • The book is the vessel of culture — the one object in the poem that can be sinned against, and the hinge between panels: cherished object in one, instrument of "the oppressor's tongue" in the other.
  • The scythe is language weaponised. It carries the Grim Reaper's death-shadow, but its precise horror is agricultural: a scythe harvests. Which makes —
  • The crop the poem's darkest symbol: "the soul has been cropped" treats souls as yield, colonialism as extraction industry. And the metaphor is completed, not abandoned, by the ending: the grandchildren "grow to love" — new growth in cleared ground. Love is what comes up after harvest; the tenderness of the last line is planted in the field the scythe made.
  • The tongue and the face: metonyms for language and identity that the poem re-literalises. "The oppressor's tongue" is a dead idiom (as in "mother tongue") until l.26–27 revives it: the scythe comes "swooping out / of the conqueror's face" — out of the mouth. Speech itself is the blade.
THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Colonialism and Linguistic Identity

The poem's central concern. English, imposed through colonisation, becomes part of the identity of colonised peoples' descendants — not through affection but through power, then through familiarity, then (paradoxically) through genuine love. Bhatt traces this trajectory from violence to love without resolving its moral ambiguity.

02

The Sacred in Nature and Language

Stanza 1 presents an entire theology of sacredness: gods in nature, trees as sacred, books as dwelling-places of the divine. This challenges Western secularism and the commodification of language and books.

03

Cultural Syncretism

Pan (Greek/Western) and Sarasvati (Hindu) coexist — different traditions meeting on equal terms. This is the different history of the title: a history in which cultures meet as equals rather than as coloniser and colonised.

04

The Paradox of Love for the Coloniser's Language

The poem's deepest mystery. The grandchildren love the language used to torture their ancestors. Bhatt embodies this paradox by writing the poem itself in English. She neither condemns nor celebrates this love — she holds it open as a question.

05

Title: A Different History

The title is a call to imagine an alternative historical narrative — one that acknowledges violence while insisting on complexity, and one that centres the perspective of the colonised rather than the coloniser. The different history is both a longed-for alternative history (one without colonialism) and the actual history of cultural mixture that colonialism produced.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

The poem is printed on the exam paper, so the marks are not in remembering it but in what can be argued from it — and the highest marks cluster at the points where the text genuinely will not settle. Four such points. In each case the strong move is to show the ambiguity working, not to pick a side and suppress the evidence for the other.

1. The grammar of ll.21–22: does the second question convict or acquit?

The difficulty. "Which language / truly meant to murder someone?" arrives as the visual twin of "Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?" — same anaphora, same two-word line — and the parallelism tempts the reader to carry the first question's "not" into the second. But the negative is not there, and neither is any auxiliary: as printed, the clause is a simple past interrogative — which language ever truly intended murder?

The readings and their evidence. (a) The acquittal — supported by the words on the page: languages do not "mean" (intend) anything; intention lives in wielders; the implied answer is none. The hinge word is "truly", which concedes appearance while denying essence: language has seemed murderous — it has "been the oppressor's tongue" — but never truly meant it. (b) The indictment-by-momentum — supported by the rhetorical parallelism and the stanza's context of "torture": readers complete the pattern as "which language has not truly meant to murder...?", making every language a murder weapon. The grammar forbids this; the design invites it. (c) The instrumental shading — "meant to murder" heard as "[was] meant to murder", the design of users rather than the tongue: ungrammatical strictly, but it is the reading the poem's argument ultimately endorses, since it relocates intention to the hand that swings the scythe.

What a strong answer does. Notices that both questions have the same one-word answer — none — delivering opposite verdicts: no language has not been an oppressor's (universal guilt); no language ever meant murder (universal innocence). The trap is functional: the reader performs the mis-attribution of guilt to language and must catch themselves doing it, which is precisely the confusion — hating English for what was done in English — that the poem is anatomising. Then note "someone", singular: whatever the verdict, the victim is a person, not a population.

2. The ending: bitter, resigned, or reconciled?

The difficulty. "the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language." can be read in at least three tones, and the poem's final punctuation withholds the usual cue.

The readings and their evidence. Bitter: love is the final clause of a sentence governed by "after the torture" — affection as the deepest conquest, the coloniser winning the heart last; "that strange" keeps a cold distance even while "love" is asserted. Resigned: the gnomic present "grow" states a recurring law, not a choice; "And how does it happen" has the flatness of someone no longer expecting an answer; the full stop files the mystery as fact. Reconciled: "love" stands unironised; "grow" is organic, unforced, the opposite of imposition; and the poem's own English — supple, tender, exact — is the love it describes, made audible.

What a strong answer does. Treats the missing question mark as the evidence that the ambivalence is engineered: after two correctly punctuated questions, the poem visibly declines to grade its own feeling. The word built to hold all three tones at once is "strange" — alien and wonderful in one syllable — so the strongest answers argue that the ending is not a tone but a suspension, and that choosing one tone is exactly what the full stop refuses to do.

3. Stanza 1's reverence: ideal or constraint?

The difficulty. Is the first panel a loving portrait of a sacred culture, or does its litany of prohibition carry its own severity — and if both, how do they fit together?

The readings and their evidence. Admirable ideal: the tenderness of "gently", the warmth of "roam freely", the coherent material theology (tree → wood → paper → book) in which respect is logical, not superstitious; the practice is real and lovingly rendered. Constraint: "sin" four times, "must", a code that polices gestures as small as how a page is turned; the accumulating prohibitions can feel like surveillance of the everyday, and a poet who left India at twelve writes this "Here" from a distance that permits ambivalence.

What a strong answer does. Refuses the either/or by finding the structural job the severity performs: the first panel establishes that culture transmits itself through teaching — "You must learn" — and the second panel shows conquest using the very same channel, imposition ripening into "grow to love". Reverence and constraint are one phenomenon seen from before and after; discipline is how both the sacred and the colonial get into a child. Add the lexical complication: the discipline is already voiced in the borrowed word "sin", so the "pure" tradition the idyll-reading wants, and the "native" orthodoxy the constraint-reading wants, are both already translated.

4. "that strange language": estranged, foreign, or wonderful?

The difficulty. Every word of the final noun phrase is contested ground: the distancing demonstrative "that", the triple-valued adjective "strange", and the question of whose perspective the phrase carries.

The readings and their evidence. Merely foreign: "strange" as plain description — a language from elsewhere; the line records a fact of origin, no more. Estranged: the history has made the language uncanny — it might have been merely foreign, but "torture" made it "strange"; the adjective carries damage, and "that" holds the acquired thing at arm's length even inside "love". Wonderful: the older sense of "strange" as marvellous; love's own adjective for what it cannot fully possess.

What a strong answer does. Maps the poem's deictic frame — India is "Here," (l.4), English is "that" (l.29): near and far assigned in two function-words — and then asks the sharper question: to the grandchildren the language is not strange at all; it is their mother tongue. "Strange" must therefore be the ancestors' word, or the poet-speaker's, surviving inside a sentence about the grandchildren's love — two generations' viewpoints compressed into one noun phrase. The phrase is stereoscopic, and the strongest answers say so instead of choosing a single focal point. [The stereoscopic-focalisation claim is an interpretation, not a fact about the text — frame it as argument.]

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation cards

1. "Great Pan is not dead; / he simply emigrated / to India." (ll.1–3)

Techniques: classical allusion; litotes; bathos; caesura (semicolon); indented arrival.

The opening performs a quiet coup: it takes the West's obituary for its own pagan world — Plutarch's "Great Pan is dead", amplified by centuries of Christian retelling — and refuses it in five tolling monosyllables, the litotes "not dead" asserting life by cancelling death. "Simply emigrated" then deflates apocalypse into admin: the death of a world-order becomes a change of address, and the bathos is aimed at Europe's habit of mistaking its local endings for universal ones. The enjambment crosses the border the sentence describes, and the indented "to India." gives the destination its own ledge of white space — marginal on the page, central to the poem. There is a buried self-portrait too: the god emigrates east as the poet's family emigrated west, two carriers of culture crossing mid-ocean.

Intention and effect: Bhatt opens with amused, unarguable authority — the reader is charmed into trusting a voice that will shortly turn and ask them unanswerable questions.

2. "Here, the gods roam freely, / disguised as snakes or monkeys;" (ll.4–5)

Techniques: deixis; plural immanence; connotative inversion; sibilance.

"Here," — comma'd, emphatic — is the emigrant's word: a poet writing from Germany or Iowa plants herself deictically on Indian ground, making belonging a speech-act rather than a location. The plural "gods" widens Pan's welcome into a theology: divinity not housed in institutions but roaming, at large in the living world, and "freely" will retrospectively sharpen once the "oppressor" arrives — freedom of movement is exactly what conquest ends. "Disguised" grants the gods agency over their forms while locating holiness in creatures the West fears or mocks — the snake and the monkey carry Naga-worship and Hanuman within them, so the line quietly inverts a colonial hierarchy of creatures.

Intention and effect: Bhatt renders immanence as ordinary fact, so the reader internalises a world where the divine is ambient — and therefore feels its later harvesting as sacrilege, not merely cruelty.

3. "and it is a sin / to be rude to a book." (ll.7–8)

Techniques: register clash; line-break bathos; anaphora launched; translation-effect.

The solemn theological noun "sin" is made to govern the nursery adjective "rude", and the line-break engineers the swerve: "and it is a sin" dangles gravely, then lands on an offence that sounds domestic, almost quaint. The comedy is a trap — what looks like eccentric etiquette is a complete ethics, in which respect is owed not to abstractions but to objects your hands touch. The deeper irony is lexical: "sin" is Christianity's word, drafted in to translate a dharmic concept, so the coloniser's vocabulary is already inside the poem's most Indian sentence — stanza two's whole argument, compressed into one word-choice.

Intention and effect: Bhatt lets a Western reader smile, then makes the smile feel like the problem — the reflex that finds book-reverence quaint is the reflex the poem is anatomising.

4. "You must learn how to turn the pages gently / without disturbing Sarasvati," (ll.15–16)

Techniques: imperative and direct address; near-pentameter; internal rhyme; anaphora ("without... without"); lived cultural practice.

The gentlest lines in the poem are also commands: "must" converts tenderness into obligation, showing that reverence is not a mood but a discipline transmitted by teaching — the same channel through which, one stanza later, a conquering language is absorbed. The internal rhyme "learn/turn" gives the instruction the memorability of proverb, and the line's eleven syllables fall into the loose shape of iambic pentameter, English verse's home metre carrying an Indian lesson — form enacting entanglement. And the goddess is not figurative: books embody Sarasvati in practice, which is why a book touched with the foot is apologised to; the poem documents etiquette, not whimsy.

Intention and effect: Bhatt makes the reader the addressed child — "you" — so that whoever reads the poem is, for two lines, raised inside the tradition, and cannot afterwards regard it wholly from outside.

5. "Which language / truly meant to murder someone?" (ll.21–22)

Techniques: rhetorical question; isolated two-word line; personification-and-acquittal; grammatical trap; singular diction.

The line-break twice isolates "Which language" — language itself in the dock — but this second question is not the first one repeated, and misreading it flattens the poem. There is no "not" and the verb is active: the question asks whether any language ever intended murder, and the implied answer — none; intention belongs to wielders — acquits the very thing the previous question convicted ("which language has not been the oppressor's tongue?"). Guilt slides off the tongue and onto the hand of power that holds it. "Someone", singular, does its own quiet work: linguistic violence is refused the anaesthetic of scale; murder happens to one person at a time.

Intention and effect: Bhatt builds the trap so the reader enacts the confusion the poem is about — blaming the language, then catching themselves — and so earns the ending's refusal to condemn English.

6. "the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language." (ll.28–29)

Techniques: temporal leap; completed agricultural metaphor; distancing deixis; withheld question mark; feminine ending.

"Unborn" places the grandchildren beyond blame — they were not yet conceived when the torture happened; their love is inheritance, not betrayal. "Grow" completes the harvest metaphor with terrible economy: the soul was "cropped", and what comes up in the cleared field is love — organic, slow, unforced, and therefore impossible to denounce. "That strange language" holds intimacy and estrangement in a single phrase: the demonstrative "that" points from a distance even as "love" closes it, and "strange" means both alien and wonderful. The sentence is grammatically a question, but the full stop prints it as fact — wonder hardened into history — and the final unstressed syllable of "language" lets the poem fall away rather than close.

Intention and effect: Bhatt ends by describing herself without saying so — a grandchild writing in the strange language — so the poem's last effect is reflexive: the reader holds evidence of the paradox in their hands.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Lenses are for generating arguments, not for name-dropping: 0475 rewards the reading, never the theory. Each entry below gives what the lens makes visible in this poem, anchored in quotation, and what it flattens — the second half matters as much as the first, because knowing a lens's blind spot is what stops an essay becoming a template.

Formalist

Makes visible: that the poem's meaning is executed in typography and grammar before it is stated in content. The diptych's unequal panels (eighteen lines against eleven); the punctuation system of two question marks and a withheld third; the ledged indentations ("to India."); the near-pentameter of "You must learn how to turn the pages gently" carrying an Indian lesson in English poetry's home metre; the final unstressed syllable of "language." letting the poem fall rather than close. A formalist could teach this poem from its punctuation alone.

Flattens: everything that requires the world — that book-reverence is lived Hindu practice rather than a conceit; that "sin" is a loanword doing translation; that a real Raj stands behind "the conqueror". Pure form cannot say why the scythe image is earned rather than gothic decoration.

Postcolonial

Makes visible: the poem as an act of what postcolonial criticism calls writing back. "Great Pan is not dead" reverses Europe's obituary for its own gods and provincialises the West — its "universal" history shrinks to a local rumour; the ending — "grow to love that strange language." — is a textbook rendering of colonial ambivalence, attachment and estrangement fused; and the poem's very medium (English of great tenderness and precision) performs the hybridity it describes, Greek god and Hindu goddess cohabiting in a coloniser's tongue.

Flattens — and over-reads: the poem names no coloniser, no Britain, no English; its questions convict every language, including those of the colonised. A strictly anti-imperial reading must suppress ll.19–20's universalising grammar, must read the final "love" as false consciousness against the poem's tone, and tends to cast stanza 1 as pure pre-colonial authenticity when its key moral word, "sin", is already borrowed. The lens finds the poem's occasion and misses its refusal to prosecute.

Ecocritical

Makes visible: a poem in which culture has an ecology. "Every tree is sacred" is not scene-setting but premise: the book's holiness is derived from the felled tree inside it — "without offending the tree / from whose wood the paper was made" is an ethics of use, reverence carrying the acknowledged debt of consumption. And the violence of panel two is agricultural: soul "cropped", a "scythe", love that "grow[s]" — cultural conquest figured as land-clearing, de-forestation and de-culturation made one process.

Flattens: the poem's centre of gravity, which is linguistic. Trees matter here as the origin of books and knowledge; an ecocritical reading that turns the poem into a conservation argument mistakes the vehicle for the tenor.

Feminist

Makes visible: that the custodian of language in this poem is female — "without disturbing Sarasvati" places a goddess, not a god, inside the book — while the violence belongs to a "conqueror" whose iconography (scythe, face, torture) is implicitly male-coded; and that the poem's authority is a teaching voice passing culture down through the intimate, traditionally feminised space of household instruction. A woman poet claims the contested language and its goddess at once.

Flattens: the text's actual reticence — the teacher of "You must learn" is never gendered, nor grammatically is the conqueror; "implicitly male-coded" is inference, not quotation uncertain. Pressed hard, the lens imports a cast the poem declined to specify.

Marxist / materialist

Makes visible: the material base of the grandchildren's love. "The soul has been cropped" frames colonisation as extraction — souls processed as yield, people as resource — and the historical context supplies the mechanism the poem leaves implicit: after the English Education Act 1835, English was the language of administration, law and advancement, so affection for it grew where the economic incentives were planted. Love, in this reading, has a payroll.

Flattens: the poem's spiritual register — Sarasvati, sanctity, sin — which materialism must translate into ideology; and the ending's tenderness, which the lens can only read as mystified interest. The poem audibly does not sneer at the love; a reading that must sneer has left the text.

Reader-response

Makes visible: that the poem constructs its reader and springs traps on them. "You must learn" conscripts whoever reads into the position of the taught child; "rude to a book" invites a Western smile that the stanza then quietly indicts; the parallel questions of ll.19–22 are built so the reader supplies a negative the grammar forbids and catches themselves blaming language. Different readers get different poems — one raised apologising to dropped books reads description where another reads exotic charm — and the poem knows it.

Flattens: the poem's assertions. "Torture" happened whether or not a reader feels implicated; treating everything as reader-effect dissolves the historical claim the poem stakes its anger on. The lens explains the poem's manners, not its wound.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

1. Anti-colonial elegy: the poem mourns a soul-murder and indicts the conqueror

Evidence: the second panel's semantic field — "oppressor's", "murder", "torture", "cropped", "scythe", "conqueror's" — and the graphic central metaphor of harvest, which frames colonisation as extraction of souls.

Weakness: the grammar refuses the indictment's target. "Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?" universalises guilt beyond Britain; no coloniser, country or language is named anywhere; and the ending grants the colonised generation's love of English without irony or rebuke. A pure protest-poem would not acquit the weapon and bless the outcome.

2. Celebration of Indian syncretism: the "different history" is a history of hospitality

Evidence: ll.1–6 — a Greek god welcomed into a Hindu cosmos, "gods roam freely", "every tree is sacred": India as the land where all traditions survive and mingle, against a Europe that lets its gods die.

Weakness: "disguised" hints that survival requires concealment; and the second panel shows what actually happened when cultures met under empire — not hospitality but scythe-work. The reading also flattens the first panel's own severity ("must", "sin" four times): this paradise has rules, and the poem knows it.

3. The acquittal of language: tools are innocent, wielders are guilty

Evidence: the active grammar of l.22 ("truly meant") — languages have no intentions; the poem's own existence in supple, loving English demonstrates that the tongue can be repossessed by the colonised.

Weakness: l.19–20 has just found every language historically complicit — "has not been" is a perfect tense of accumulated fact — and the final line still calls English "that strange language", the distancing demonstrative keeping the acquitted defendant at arm's length. The acquittal is argued for and withheld at once.

4. Reverence as discipline: the first panel is quietly ambivalent about orthodoxy

Evidence: the litany's four prohibitions, the imperative "You must learn", the escalation from theology ("sacred") to policing of trivial gesture — tradition experienced as weight as well as gift; a reading available to a diaspora poet who left at twelve and writes "Here" from abroad.

Weakness: the tone is tender, not satirical — "gently", the loving material chain of tree/wood/paper, the domestic "rude" — and the severity has a structural job (establishing teaching as culture's channel of transmission) rather than a critical one. The panel honours the discipline more than it chafes at it.

5. The ending as reclamation: love wins, and Indian English is the trophy

Evidence: "grow to love" — organic, unforced, gnomic present; Bhatt's own self-description of writing "Indian-English rather than Anglo-Indian poetry"; the poem as living proof that the strange language now serves the grandchildren.

Weakness: the love never stops being aftermath — it arrives only "after the torture", and the withheld question mark preserves bewilderment rather than triumph. Reclamation is what the poem does; it is not what the poem claims, and the gap between the two is deliberate.

CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the other six

Comparison hooks

PoemOne sharp linking ideaShared technique
Love Armed (Aphra Behn)The dominated supply the dominator's power: Behn's lover arms Love with her own sighs and tears as Bhatt's grandchildren sustain the conqueror's tongue with their love — both poems study consent inside subjection.A personified abstract power bearing weapons (Love's darts and fire; language as scythe), driven by antithesis (victor/harmed; love/torture).
The Chimney Sweeper (Blake)Institutions teach the oppressed to bless their oppression: the Angel's promise that duty averts harm does to Tom what imposed English does to the grandchildren — indoctrination experienced as comfort, even love.Religious diction as instrument of control ("sin", "duty", "Angel"); a tender, naive register with irony directed past the speaker at the system.
Where I Come From (Elizabeth Brewster)Identity as deposit: Brewster's people are "made of places" as Bhatt's grandchildren are made of an inherited language — formation you do not choose.Two-part contrastive structure (city/country; sacred India/colonial aftermath); free-verse cataloguing of concrete particulars.
Report to Wordsworth (Boey Kim Cheng)The exact counter-case: Boey's classical sea-gods are dying in the polluted modern West while Bhatt's Pan survives by emigrating east — two verdicts on whether the sacred can outlive modernity and empire.Argument conducted through canonical allusion (Wordsworth's sonnet; Plutarch's legend); gods personified as gauges of cultural health; bleak, unresolved endings.
The Cockroach (Kevin Halligan)The animal as vessel of the self and the sacred: gods "disguised as snakes or monkeys" meet a speaker who suspects a former life in an insect — both poems use Eastern metaphysics of immanence and rebirth to unsettle a Western observer's superiority.Extended animal symbolism turning reflexively on the speaker; an ending that withholds resolution (Halligan's tentative recognition; Bhatt's unpunctuated question).
Lament (Gillian Clarke)The litany as moral accounting: Clarke's "For the..." catalogue of war's victims and Bhatt's "a sin to..." catalogue of violations both count desecrations of a sacred natural order one item at a time.Anaphora structuring an elegiac list; reverence for nature (ocean and creatures; trees and books) set against the machinery of conquest and war.
WRITING ABOUT IT

Writing About It

Turning the analysis into paragraphs that score

Writing about it

The poem is on the exam paper. Nothing below is for memorising: quote in single words and short phrases from the text in front of you, cite punctuation as evidence, and spend the saved effort on argument — the discriminator at the top is contestable interpretation, precisely worded.

Model paragraph 1 — the scythe passage (imagery, sound, structure)

Bhatt's conqueror does not speak; his language leaves his face as a weapon: "after the soul has been cropped / with a long scythe swooping out / of the conqueror's face –". The metaphor literalises the dead idiom of l.20, "the oppressor's tongue": what swings out of a face is the tongue, so speech itself becomes the blade. "Cropped" is the poem's most exact horror — an agricultural verb that treats the soul as yield, colonisation as harvest — and its clipped double plosive cuts the word short just as the soul is cut. The sibilance of "soul... scythe swooping" whistles like the swing, while the enjambment lets the sentence keep slicing across three line-endings, the blade emerging in the gap between "out" and "of". Yet the metaphor is not finished: "the unborn grandchildren / grow to love" — growth is the crop's own word, and love is what comes up in the cleared field. The image thus carries the poem's whole argument: conquest as extraction, and affection as its unforeseeable second harvest.

Model paragraph 2 — the sin-litany (register, anaphora, translation)

The first stanza's holiness is delivered in borrowed words. "and it is a sin / to be rude to a book" suspends the theological noun at the line-break and lands it on a nursery adjective, and the swerve is doing argument: reverence in this world governs gestures as small as manners. The anaphora — "a sin" four times — turns etiquette into liturgy, each clause a bead on a rosary of prohibitions, while the verbs "shove", "slam" and "toss" knock against it in plosive monosyllables, a rising scale of disrespect running from contempt through violence to indifference. But the litany's key word is not native to the world it defends: "sin" is Christianity's term, standing in for the dharmic pāp, so the stanza that describes uncolonised reverence is already speaking in translation. The oppressor's tongue is inside the temple before the conqueror is named. A reader who catches this stops treating the two stanzas as before-and-after and starts seeing the second inside the first — which is where the poem's real disturbance lies.

The three sentence-patterns that do most work

  1. The upgrade — "X does not merely [obvious effect]; it [argumentative effect]." E.g. "'cropped' does not merely sound violent; it files the soul under produce." Forces the essay past description into claim, which is the AO boundary that separates bands.
  2. The tether — "The [word/image] of l.N returns at l.M as [transformed thing]." E.g. "the 'tongue' of l.20 returns at l.26 as the scythe"; "'cropped' returns at l.29 as 'grow'." One sentence proves whole-poem grasp — the thing examiners call "overview" and reward disproportionately.
  3. The both/and holder — "'[word]' holds both [reading A] and [reading B], and the poem needs both because [argument]." E.g. "'strange' holds both alien and wonderful, and the poem needs both because the grandchildren's love is real and the history is unforgiven." Demonstrates contestability without fence-sitting: the ambiguity is asserted and put to work.

The three phrases to avoid

  1. "This makes the reader want to read on." It credits the poem with nothing but momentum and the candidate with nothing at all; no examiner has ever rewarded appetite.
  2. "The poet uses language to convey..." Everything in a poem is language; the phrase is a placeholder where a named device and a quoted word should be. Say which word, what it does.
  3. "This emphasises..." with no object worth emphasising — emphasis is not an effect. State what changes in the meaning when the stress lands: not "the repetition emphasises sin" but "the repetition turns etiquette into liturgy".
EXAM PRACTICE

Exam Practice

Questions, plans, and the marginal gains

Exam practice

Question 1

How does Bhatt strikingly convey the power of language in 'A Different History'?

  • Thesis: language in the poem holds double power — a sacred presence to be handled with the fingertips and a blade that crops souls — and Bhatt makes each power felt through the other, so reverence and violence become two grips on the same instrument.
  • Point 1 — sacred power: the litany "it is a sin... a sin... a sin" plus "without disturbing Sarasvati": anaphora turns etiquette into liturgy; the goddess dwells in the book, so language is a living presence — "rude to a book" makes the page capable of being wronged.
  • Point 2 — murderous power: "the oppressor's tongue" is revived from dead idiom into flesh: the scythe comes "swooping out / of the conqueror's face" — out of the mouth — while sibilance ("soul... scythe swooping") whistles like the swing and "cropped" is cut off by its own plosives.
  • Point 3 — seductive power: "the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language." — the temporal leap and organic verb show language's slowest power, to be absorbed and loved by the descendants of its victims; the full stop where grammar wants a question mark presents this as unarguable fact.
  • Counter-move: yet l.21–22 acquits language itself — "truly meant" has no negative and an active verb; languages do not intend, wielders do — and the poem's own eloquent English proves the weapon can change hands.
  • Conclusion: the poem's final word is "language" followed by a full stop: power lodged, at the last, in the word itself — held up for judgement and deliberately left unjudged.

Question 2

Explore the ways in which Bhatt makes the change of mood in 'A Different History' so disturbing.

  • Thesis: the change disturbs because nothing announces it — the poem crosses from blessing to atrocity through white space alone — and because the second mood is built from the materials of the first, so the reader's comfort is turned against them.
  • Point 1 — the first mood's warmth is earned in detail: wit ("simply emigrated"), tenderness ("turn the pages gently"), chant-like sound (the long-e thread "freely... tree... gently... Sarasvati") — a world rendered so habitable that its loss will register as personal.
  • Point 2 — the cut: no conjunction bridges the stanza break; tense flips from timeless present ("roam", "is") to historical perfect ("has been cropped"), mood from imperative to interrogative — "Which language" twice, a two-word line like a fist — so the rupture is enacted, not described.
  • Point 3 — the second mood weaponises the first: the sacred pastoral returns as harvest — tree/wood/paper becomes soul/scythe/crop — and "torture" and "murder" retro-poison the gentle vocabulary of handling; even "sin", the first panel's word, was the coloniser's loan all along.
  • Counter-move: the moods are not simply opposites — the final lines re-soften into "grow to love", a third mood of bewildered tenderness, and the withheld question mark refuses the consolation of either anger or resolution; the disturbance is that the poem ends loving what it has just called murderous.
  • Conclusion: the diptych's unequal panels (eighteen lines against eleven) mean the violence is briefer than the blessing yet overturns it — Bhatt disturbs by proportion, silence and grammar rather than by raising her voice.

Examiner's edge

  1. Quote across line-breaks with a slash and analyse the break itself: "he simply emigrated / to India." — the crossing happens in the white space; examiners reward candidates who treat lineation as meaning.
  2. Deploy Plutarch in one subordinate clause — the legend that "Great Pan is dead" (told in Plutarch, later read as paganism's obituary) — and move on; a paragraph of Greek background earns nothing.
  3. Name the structure precisely: a diptych of unequal free-verse panels, eighteen lines against eleven, and argue from proportion — expansive blessing, compressed violence.
  4. Get l.22's grammar right: active "meant", no "not" — it acquits language-as-such while l.19–20 convicts every language historically. Reading the two questions as twins is the single commonest analytical error on this poem.
  5. Use the punctuation trio: two question marks, then a full stop where the third should be — bewilderment hardened into fact. Contrast the marks; never "correct" the ending.
  6. Point out that "sin" is a Christian loanword translating dharmic etiquette (pāp): the coloniser's vocabulary is already inside stanza one, so the poem's problem precedes its statement of the problem.
  7. Connect l.20 to ll.26–27: the dead metonym "tongue" is re-literalised as the scythe "swooping out / of the conqueror's face" — out of the mouth. Speech is the weapon; the metaphor is anatomically exact.
  8. Complete the agricultural chain: "cropped" → "grow" — the grandchildren are regrowth in cleared ground; love is the crop that comes up after harvest. Candidates who track a metaphor across a whole poem are marked as top-band.
  9. Note what is absent: no Britain, no English, no Macaulay — only Pan, India, Sarasvati are named. Claims about "the British" belong in context; claims about "the conqueror" belong in analysis. Keeping that boundary clean signals precision.
  10. One biographical clause is worth more than a paragraph: Gujarati-speaking ("the deepest layer of my identity"), Iowa-trained, Bremen-based, writing "Indian-English rather than Anglo-Indian poetry" — Bhatt is one of the unborn grandchildren, and the poem is the love it describes.
EDITORIAL NOTES

Editorial Notes

Text checks and corrections to the source notes

Text check

The full text embedded in the site's own materials is sound: it matches the published poem (verified against The Poetry Archive's text, which carries Bhatt's own recording, and consistent with the Carcanet Brunizem printing used by the Cambridge anthology). The two raw copies pasted at the top of the notes file are corrupted in two places, and the notes' analysis table misquotes a third:

  • l.4 — notes read "Here the gods roam freely,"; the published line is "Here, the gods roam freely,". The comma matters: it isolates the deictic "Here" as a beat of arrival — the emigrant planting a flag — before the claim begins.
  • ll.9–10 — the notes join these into one line ("It is a sin to shove a book aside with your foot,"). The published lineation is "It is a sin to shove a book aside / with your foot,", with "with your foot," indented. The break suspends the act above its instrument, and the join silently shortens stanza 1 to seventeen lines — the true count is eighteen, which the notes' own stanza-numerology depends on.
  • ll.15–16 — the analysis table quotes "You must learn how to turn the pages / gently without disturbing Sarasvati". The published lineation is "You must learn how to turn the pages gently / without disturbing Sarasvati," — "gently" ends l.15, so the two "without" lines open in clean anaphora, and "gently" hangs at the line-edge performing the care it names.

Also confirmed: the semicolon in l.1; the four indented continuation lines (3, 10, 12, 14); a dash, not a comma, after "of the conqueror's face –" (l.27); and the full stop, not a question mark, ending l.29 — see Form and structure.

Corrected lineation for the site display — the affected lines exactly as they should appear:

`` l.4 Here, the gods roam freely, l.9 It is a sin to shove a book aside l.10 with your foot, l.15 You must learn how to turn the pages gently ``

l.10 is printed as an indented continuation line (as are ll.3, 12 and 14). l.15 ends on "gently"; l.16 begins "without disturbing Sarasvati," so that ll.16–17 open with the anaphoric pair "without... / without...".

Gaps and corrections

  1. Roughly a third of the notes describes a poem that does not exist. The "Poem's Journey and Summary" block — barefoot gods, shoes as colonial pollution, a four-stanza structure — and every "quotation" in it ('A different history / perhaps / if they had not worn / shoes', 'a history / of the body', 'You must learn this now', 'the body / is not smart enough') corresponds to nothing in Bhatt's poem. There are no shoes, no barefoot gods, no four stanzas; the block reads like machine-generated confabulation. Delete it and everything built on it (the "shoes vs bare feet theme", "the body remembers", the temple-shoes analogy). Revising from it would sink an exam answer.
  2. East India Company chronology: the Armada was defeated in 1588, not 1598; the Company's royal charter from Elizabeth I is dated 31 December 1600.
  3. Raj dates: "1858 to 1927" should be 1858–1947; the notes' own "89-year period" figure only fits 1947.
  4. "Indian Education Act of 1835" (the error also sits in the site's extended context): the statute is the English Education Act 1835, which followed Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (2 February 1835). The quoted aim — "a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect" — is correctly worded and comes from the Minute. But handle it with care: the poem names no Macaulay, no English, no Britain — its only proper nouns are Pan, India and Sarasvati. Macaulay is context for the poem's world, not an allusion the poem makes.
  5. Biography: born 6 May 1956 in Ahmedabad, Gujarat; grew up in Pune; the family emigrated to the USA in 1968 (the notes' first section says "born in Pune" — wrong; the later section has it right). MFA from the Iowa Writers' Workshop; writer-in-residence at the University of Victoria, Canada; lives in Bremen. Her husband Michael Augustin is a German writer and radio broadcaster, not "a German publisher"; they married in 1988. Brunizem (Carcanet, 1988) won the Commonwealth Poetry Prize (Asia) and the Alice Hunt Bartlett Award — sources conflict on the exact award year, so name the prizes, not a year. Cholmondeley Award, 1991. Her description of Gujarati as "the deepest layer of my identity" is genuine and safe to quote; so is her self-description of writing "Indian-English rather than Anglo-Indian poetry". Drop the "£70 million" Clive figure — popular estimates vary and none is citable; Clive's dates in the notes (arrived 1744, Plassey 1757, left 1767) are right.
  6. "Brunizem" is a missed contextual gift: the title names a dark prairie soil found in Asia, Europe and North America — the three continents of Bhatt's life. A collection named for soil that spans continents frames this poem exactly: a god who emigrates, a language that transplants, grandchildren who grow in cleared ground.
  7. Misquote: "whose woods" → the text is singular, "from whose wood the paper was made".
  8. "Litotes" is pinned to the wrong phrase. Pan's emigration is bathos/understatement; the litotes is l.1 itself — "not dead", life affirmed through negation.
  9. Plutarch, precisely: in De defectu oraculorum, a divine voice orders the Egyptian pilot Thamus to proclaim, as the ship passes Palodes, that "Great Pan is dead" — he is not merely told news, he is made the herald. In Plutarch the story is evidence that daimones can die; the "death of paganism at the rise of Christianity" meaning is the later Christian reinterpretation (Eusebius onwards), fixed in English verse by E. B. Browning's "The Dead Pan" (1844). That layered tradition — pagan anecdote, Christian obituary, Victorian refrain — is what l.1 refuses in five words.
  10. The Pan–Pūṣan claim ("Pan emigrated to India as the Indian counterpart Pushan") is asserted as fact; it is a genuine but contested philological hypothesis (Greek Pan and the Vedic pastoral god Pūṣan traced to a common reconstructed ancestor). Usable only as a flagged curiosity, never as Bhatt's intention. The safer etymological point: a folk etymology as old as the Homeric Hymns connects Pan with Greek pan, "all" — the god of all, finding a home in the land of all gods.
  11. Numerology over-claim: 18 lines = Gita chapters / 11 lines = Rudras is unverifiable intention and reads as padding in an essay. Keep the checkable fact — an eighteen-line panel against an eleven-line panel — and argue from proportion (see Form and structure).
  12. Sound over-claims: not every /s/ is a snake — the same sibilance runs through "sacred" and "Sarasvati". Tie sound-claims to patterns across lines, not single letters (see Sound).
  13. Aotearoa parallels: it is the Māori Language Act 1987 (not "Bill"); the Native Schools Act 1867 established English-medium schooling, and punishment for speaking te reo was practice rather than statute. Rich personal hinterland — but keep it out of a 0475 answer, which rewards engagement with this text.
  14. Spelling: diptych, not "dipytych".
  15. What nothing in the notes or site covers, supplied below: metre and scansion; the grammar of ll.21–22 and its standard misreading; the significance of the unnamed coloniser; "sin" as a translation problem; the deixis of "Here" and "that"; the cropped→grow agricultural chain; the singular "someone".
