CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the other six

Comparison hooks

With 'Love Armed' (Aphra Behn). Linking idea: power assembles itself out of the powerless — Love's tyranny is built from the lover's own contributions ('From me he took his sighs and tears…') exactly as the trinity's heaven is made 'of our misery'; both poems are audits of an extraction. Shared technique: the couplet/quatrain chime used ironically — courtly song carrying harm; personified or institutional power given regal iconography. Genuine difference: Behn's speaker is an adult inside a reciprocal (if rigged) erotic game, and her wound is survivable, even relished as performance; Blake's victim is a child in an economy, and nothing in his poem is a game — where Behn's antithesis balances ('my poor heart… whilst thine…'), Blake's final line refuses balance: heaven on one side, misery on the other, and one is made of the other.

With 'A Different History' (Sujata Bhatt). Linking idea: the oppressor's deepest conquest is pedagogy — Bhatt's 'unborn grandchildren' who 'grow to love that strange language' are the child 'taught… to sing the notes of woe': both poems locate oppression's triumph in what the young are trained to love and perform. Shared technique: the pivotal interrogative (Bhatt's 'Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?' beside 'Where are thy father and mother?'), and religious frames (Sarasvati, the sacredness of books; church, prayer, heaven) tested against actual cruelty. Genuine difference: Bhatt's history has no named culprit — conquest is recursive, every language once the oppressor's, and the poem ends in troubled wonder; Blake names his defendants in a single line and convicts them. Bhatt's is a poem of implication, Blake's of indictment.

With 'Where I Come From' (Elizabeth Brewster). Linking idea: 'People are made of places' is this poem's premise weaponised — the heath-child and the flue-child are different people, and the making is literal: soot is what the city deposits in a person. Shared technique: structuring antithesis of two environments (Brewster's museum-smelling city against berry-picking woods; Blake's heath against street and chimney), with sensory coding — her smells, his black/white. Genuine difference: Brewster's formation is neutral, even tender — nobody chose her chickens and battered schoolhouses for her, and her free verse drifts like memory; Blake's formation is a transitive verb with agents ('They clothed me'), and his nursery metre is a cage someone built. In Brewster place shapes; in Blake people use place — heath taken away, snow left.

With 'Report to Wordsworth' (Boey Kim Cheng). Linking idea: both are reports on a god who no longer functions — Cheng's God 'labouring to utter his last cry', Blake's God privatised by 'his Priest and King'; in both, the machinery of veneration (sonnet-homage, church-going) continues while the thing venerated is destroyed or captured. Shared technique: compressed traditional forms (sonnet; hymn-like quatrains) turned to protest; religious lexis inverted (prayer, heaven, God) so that devotion becomes evidence. Genuine difference: Cheng's culprit is 'man' at large and the damage ecological — grief without a defendant, ending in 'beyond hope'; Blake's culprits are institutions with titles, the damage is one child's body, and the poem ends not in hopelessness but in a verdict — bleaker locally, less resigned globally.

With 'The Cockroach' (Kevin Halligan). Linking idea: a small dark creature, closely watched, turns out to be a mirror — but the mirrors face opposite ways: Halligan projects himself onto the insect ('I thought I recognised myself'), while Blake's 'little black thing' refuses to stay an object of projection and answers back with an analysis of the watcher's world. Shared technique: the observed creature as emblem; tight rhymed form containing unease; the pivot on recognition. Genuine difference: Halligan's poem is private — conscience auditing itself through an insect, no social claim; Blake's is public — the 'thing' is a person made thing-like by named institutions. Halligan ends in a question about himself; Blake's child ends with a conclusion about everyone.

With 'Lament' (Gillian Clarke). Linking idea: the blackened innocent — Clarke's cormorant 'in his funeral silk' is the sweep's 'clothes of death' transposed to war's ecology: in both, a covering (oil, soot) is at once costume, stain and shroud, put onto the innocent by the powerful. Shared technique: liturgical repetition (her anaphoric 'For…' — the cadence of intercessory prayer — beside his biblical polysyndeton); irony of consolation (her 'the boy fusilier who joined for the company', his heaven made of misery). Genuine difference: 'Lament' is a litany — many victims, no speech, the elegist's voice doing all the mourning; Blake gives the whole poem to one victim who does not mourn at all but explains. Clarke's form is grief organised; Blake's is grief analysed — and only his victim gets the last word.

WRITING ABOUT IT

Writing About It

Turning the analysis into paragraphs that score

Writing about it

Model paragraph 1 — sound and the cry (quotation → technique → effect → wider argument):

The poem's second line does its damage phonetically. The child cries ''weep! 'weep!'' — the sweep's street-cry, 'sweep! sweep!', as a mouth too young for its opening cluster actually delivers it: the /s/ drops away, and what remains is, by accident, the truth. The pun is found rather than made — London had heard infants cry 'weep' for decades and chosen to hear 'sweep' — so Blake is not decorating the cry but removing the city's mishearing. Metrically, the two stressed monosyllables form a spondee the nursery lilt cannot absorb: the cry jams the song. And the poem quietly keeps the lost sound for itself — 'snow', 'say', 'smil'd', 'sing' — sibilance everywhere except in the child's mouth, while the trade-word itself never appears outside the title. A society that will not hear grief in its own streets is convicted by a single dropped consonant: the advertisement was always a lament, and only the spelling refused to know it.

Model paragraph 2 — metre as accusation (different aspect, same movement):

Blake's most damning rhetoric is rhythmic. 'And because I am happy and dance and sing' runs on three anapaests — 'and be-CAUSE I am HAP-py and DANCE and SING' — so the line does not describe dancing so much as perform it; the compulsory lightness of the child's trade becomes the reader's own lilt. Two lines later the parents' devotions move to the identical tune: 'And are GONE to praise GOD and his PRIEST and KING'. That metrical rhyme is the accusation: worship and forced performance are one music, a jig the system has everyone dancing. Where a lesser protest poem would break its metre in outrage, Blake lets the prettiness play on, because prettiness is his subject — a society in which everything continues to sound charming while a child freezes. Only the close falters: 'misery' falls away on unstressed syllables, rhymed weakly with 'injury', so the nursery music runs down like a neglected toy exactly as the largest charge — heaven manufactured from misery — is laid.

Three sentence-patterns that do the most work:

  1. Not-merely escalation: '[Quotation] is not merely [the obvious reading]; it [stronger claim] — [wider consequence].' E.g. ''Clothed' is not merely ironic; it converts the tenderest parental act into the transfer of death — the poem's method is to corrupt care itself.'
  2. Mechanism sentence: 'Because [precise formal fact], [the line] [produces effect]: [what that means for the poem].' E.g. 'Because the relative clause tips over the line-end, the objects of praise arrive in the dock: the syntax performs the exposure.'
  3. Held ambiguity: ''[Word]' will not settle between [sense A] and [sense B], and the poem needs both: [what the doubleness achieves].' E.g. ''Make up' will not settle between fabricate and constitute, and the poem needs both: the fiction and the extraction are one act.'

Three phrases to avoid:

  1. 'This shows that…' — the empty hinge. Replace with the mechanism sentence above: name the formal fact, then argue the consequence.
  2. '…has negative connotations' — a way of not saying which connotation. Name it: 'injury' carries the minimising register of the account-book, which is the point.
  3. 'The reader feels pity/sadness' — asserted emotion with no cause shown. Argue the effect from the device: 'the flat full stop makes the sentence sound routine — and the routineness is the horror.'
EXAM PRACTICE

Exam Practice

Questions, plans, and the marginal gains

Exam practice

Question 1. Explore the ways in which Blake makes 'The Chimney Sweeper' so disturbing.

  • Thesis: the disturbance is located not in the suffering but in the normality surrounding it — pretty form, sincere parents, cheerful child — so that comfort itself becomes the crime; the poem disturbs most where it sounds most pleasant.
  • Point 1 — the world's grammar transcribed: 'A little black thing among the snow' / ''weep! 'weep!'' — dehumanising diction is the passer-by's, not Blake's; the cry is the trade-call mangled by an infant mouth into the truth; we begin inside the perception being indicted.
  • Point 2 — care inverted: 'They clothed me in the clothes of death, / And taught me to sing the notes of woe' — polyptoton fuses dressing and shroud; 'taught' makes suffering a curriculum; the two most nurturing verbs in family life (clothe, teach) are the instruments of harm.
  • Point 3 — the alibi machine: 'And because I am happy and dance and sing, / They think they have done me no injury' — the child's real vitality converted into his parents' exoneration; anapaestic metre makes the alibi literally dance; 'think' grants a sincerity worse than lying.
  • Counter-move: concede no real climbing boy analyses ideology in subordinate clauses — then turn it: every adult voice is compromised (parents by belief, questioner by inadequate pity), so lucidity is given to the only speaker with nothing to gain; the implausibility is the accusation.
  • Conclusion: 'Who make up a heaven of our misery' — the lone enjambment arrests the praised; 'our' reveals a class behind the case; the questioner has vanished and the reader is the last adult in the snow, holding a pity the poem has shown to be insufficient.

Question 2. How does Blake powerfully convey his anger at what has been done to the child in 'The Chimney Sweeper'?

  • Thesis: the anger is engineered as understatement — the poem never raises its voice; the indictment travels through grammar, metre and rhyme rather than exclamation, and is the more powerful for arriving calmly.
  • Point 1 — the routine sentence: 'They are both gone up to the church to pray.' — flat declarative with a full stop; 'both' dismantles every mitigating story (no orphan, no crisis — a choice); 'up' begins the vertical irony that ends in 'heaven'.
  • Point 2 — anger as logic: 'Because I was happy… They clothed me…' / 'And because I am happy… They think…' — twice-run causal syntax gives the child the grammar of proof; the scandal ('because', not 'although') is stated as mechanism, and the poem means its preposterous causality.
  • Point 3 — the exposed trinity: 'to praise God and his Priest and King, / Who make up a heaven of our misery' — the possessive chain welds religion to state; the only enjambment tips the venerated into the dock; the weak falling rhyme 'injury/misery' lets the nursery music die as the verdict lands.
  • Counter-move: the opening's tenderness ('little', the grieved exclamation, the kindly question) is not spared — pity is shown to be the wrong size for the problem; Blake's anger includes the well-meaning, which widens rather than weakens it.
  • Conclusion: the child never asks for anything; anger in this poem is not an emotion displayed but an analysis completed — and 'our misery' hands the completed analysis to the reader, who now cannot claim, with the parents, to think no injury has been done.

Examiner's edge

  1. Scan lines 9 and 11 and say they share a tune. Three anapaests each: the child's dance and the parents' worship move to the same rhythm — the poem's accusation made audible. Almost no candidate scans; fewer connect scansion to meaning.
  2. Get the cry's mechanics exact. 'Sweep! sweep!' was the trade's street advertisement; an infant mouth cannot manage the /s/ cluster; the drop leaves a real word — 'weep'. The pun was found in the street, not invented at the desk; the apostrophes are editorial.
  3. Use 'both'. One syllable dismantles orphanhood, accident and crisis: an intact, functioning, churchgoing family chose this. Worse than misfortune, and the poem knows it.
  4. Name the imperfect rhyme. heath/death is the poem's one off-rhyme — final consonants match, vowels refuse — an audibly forced join exactly where free past is bolted to fatal present.
  5. Spot the recycled rhyme. Stanza 2's cross-rhymes reuse stanza 1's snow/woe as rhyme-words: the verse cannot escape its own first sounds — sound as fate.
  6. Point to the poem's only enjambment (11→12): the sentence seems to end on 'King'; the relative clause carries praise over the brink into indictment. Syntax as exposure.
  7. Press 'think'. The parents are sincere, not hypocritical — and sincerity is what institutions manufacture. Locating the evil in belief rather than cruelty is the poem's most modern move.
  8. Refuse to call the happiness fake. The poem needs it real and used: pretext before the harm, alibi after it. Held open, the parents' guilt deepens; resolved, the poem shrinks.
  9. Deploy context as a clause, never a paragraph. 'Written six years after the 1788 Chimney Sweepers Act (minimum age eight) had failed unenforced' or 'a trade whose signature cancer Pott had identified in 1775' — one clause each, attached to a point about the poem's tense of failed reform.
  10. Know what the plate withholds. Blake's engraving has no quotation marks — every voice-boundary is an editor's choice — and its design (a black child crossing the white page beneath a pressing black sky) enacts line 1 visually. One sentence of this signals real scholarship; build arguments on the printed text.
EDITORIAL NOTES

Editorial Notes

Text checks and corrections to the source notes

Text check

The study text is sound as a modernised reading text, and matches the standard anthology version. But it differs from what Blake actually etched, and two of the differences matter analytically. Checked against the illuminated plate itself (Copy F, Yale Center for British Art, colour-printed relief etching, 1794 — the plate is numbered 45 in that copy; plate order varies from copy to copy because Blake bound each copy differently) and the standard edited text:

  • Blake's plate has no quotation marks anywhere. The speech-boundaries in the study text ('Where are thy father and mother?…' / 'They are both gone up…') are editorial decisions, not Blake's. The attribution of lines to voices is an act of interpretation — usable in an essay (see Cruxes).
  • No apostrophes in the cry. The plate reads Crying weep, weep, in notes of woe! The elision-marks in ''weep! 'weep!'' are an editor's signal of the dropped s of 'sweep'. The pun is Blake's; the typography is not.
  • Blake uses ampersands throughout: father & mother, happy, & dance & sing, God & his Priest & King.
  • Plate line 1 ends with a colon (snow:), not a comma; winters snow has no apostrophe; the title is etched THE Chimney Sweeper, with 'THE' in capitals.
  • Line 9 on the plate has a comma after 'happy' (And because I am happy, & dance & sing), which the study text drops — a small loss, since Blake's comma separates the state ('happy') from the actions ('dance & sing').

Dates verified: Songs of Innocence 1789; Songs of Experience 1794; combined that year as Songs of Innocence and of Experience Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul. The first stanza is drafted in Blake's Notebook (British Library Add MS 49460, the 'Rossetti Manuscript'), which he used most intensively 1792–94. The companion poem 'The Chimney Sweeper' ('When my mother died I was very young') is Innocence, 1789.

The plate as object (verified against the Copy F printing): the poem's twelve lines fill the upper two-thirds in Blake's flourished script, on a white ground, with a wavering vine- or flame-like tendril down the right margin and a squiggled flourish under the title and after 'the notes of woe'. Below the text, the design: a small child entirely in black walks towards the viewer up a snowy street between two dark house-walls (a dark shuttered window at left, brickwork at right), both arms raised to grip a bulging soot-sack slung behind his shoulders, his pale face the only light thing on him, turned up and out at us. Above him a heavy black band — storm-cloud and overhanging roofline at once, snow whitening its upper edge — presses down; the snow drives diagonally in streaks. The child is boxed in on three sides by black and walks on the one white surface, which is also the surface the words are printed on. The page enacts the first line: black marks — letters and child alike — among the snow of the paper. In an exam you cannot cite the plate as printed text, but knowing the poem was built as a picture disciplines how you read its black/white system: it is not incidental imagery but the poem's whole visual logic.

Gaps and corrections

  1. The rhyme scheme is wrong in one contributor's section and right in another's. The 'STRUCTURAL & FORMAL ANALYSIS' block claims 'AABB rhyme scheme: … heath/death …' throughout. False: only stanza 1 is couplets (snow/woe, say/pray). Stanzas 2 and 3 are cross-rhymed ABAB (heath/death, snow/woe; sing/King, injury/misery) — heath and death are lines 5 and 7, not adjacent. The later table has this right. Use the correct scheme; an examiner will check.
  2. 'Ballad form' is loose. No alternating four- and three-beat lines, no ABCB. It is a song-like quatrain in rough four-beat lines — the nursery-rhyme/hymn comparison is the defensible one, and it is stronger anyway (see Form).
  3. 'Approximate iambic metre' misses the point. The anapaests are where the meaning lives, above all in lines 9 and 11 (see Form and structure). One contributor knew this ('combination of iambs and anapaests') but never applied it to meaning.
  4. The Purpose/Effect/Feel/Do/Result template is a liability. It asserts reader-feelings as facts ('Feel: Shock… Do: Question… Result: Realise…'), repeats the same conclusions for every line, and buries its handful of sharp ideas under formula. Examiners reward an effect argued from a technique, not a prescribed emotional itinerary. The strongest ideas from that stretch are distilled and credited to you throughout this document; do not reproduce its scaffolding in prose.
  5. 'He could be one of the same boys from the first poem' — no. The Innocence speaker's mother is dead ('When my mother died I was very young') and his father sold him; this child's mother is alive and at church with the father. The relation between the poems is structural — same figure-type, same cry, same title — not narrative continuity. Treating them as the same boy destroys the more interesting point: Experience replaces orphan-misfortune with a functioning two-parent family that chose this.
  6. The apostrophes in ''weep!' are treated as Blake's device. They are editorial (see Text check). The lisp-pun survives without them, but 'Blake's apostrophe shows elision' misattributes the typography. Say instead: the street-cry itself, as young children actually delivered it, was the pun.
  7. The questioner's 'hollow, superficial concern' is over-claimed. Nothing in the text warrants insincerity. The sharper and safer point is the question's inadequacy: it is the wrong question, answered with an analysis it did not ask for.
  8. 'Snow symbolises religious purity' is asserted as fact. It is a reading to be argued, and it must survive line 6, where the same snow is the medium of the child's real, remembered happiness. The snow is not stably 'society's false purity'; its meaning moves (see Motifs).
  9. The original-sin reading (society sees the child as 'besmirched by original sin', his suffering as expiation) is presented as the meaning of black/white. It is one contestable lens — theologically suggestive, textually thin — and should be offered as such.
  10. Missing from ~1,800 lines of notes: the plate as designed object; the grammar of the final 'Who…' clause (whom exactly does the child accuse?); the recycling of the snow/woe rhyme across stanzas 1–2; the specifics of the 1788 Act's failure (minimum age eight; the licensing clause voted down in the Lords; effectively unenforced); and any scansion beyond one line.
  11. The Marx framing flattens Blake. 'Anticipates "religion is the opium of the people" by fifty years' is chronologically fine (1794 → 1844) and worth one sentence, but the notes slide from it into 'religion = lie'. Blake was a Christian visionary. The poem's target is the institution — 'God & his Priest & King' is a possessive chain describing a captured god, not a denial of God. Import Marx's economics, not his atheism.

Where I Come From

Elizabeth Brewster  ·  1977

Identity is not chosen but carried — place gets into the senses and stays there, and the mind keeps its own weather.
