CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Elizabeth Brewster (1922–2012)

Elizabeth Winifred Brewster was born in Chipman, a small logging community in New Brunswick, Canada, on 26 August 1922. She died on 26 December 2012, aged 90. Her publishing career spanned over six decades: her first poetry collection East Coast (1951) established her voice, and her final works continued to appear until her death. She earned four university degrees (BA University of New Brunswick, MA Radcliffe College/Harvard, BLS Toronto, PhD Indiana), yet resisted the grandiosity that often accompanies such credentials — her style remained, as critics noted, plain-spoken, poignant… almost prosaic, concealing great intelligence and a shrewd eye for powerful, if subdued, details.

Brewster spent most of her academic career at the University of Saskatchewan (1972–1990). Her move from rural New Brunswick to academic Saskatchewan, then to writing and teaching, traces the arc of many Canadian lives: the small-community origin, the migration through urban education, the eventual professional world that never quite erases the original landscape from the mind.

Canadian Identity and the Significance of Place

Canada's identity has long been defined by its vast, often harsh natural geography. New Brunswick, where Brewster grew up, is a maritime province dominated by forests, fishing communities, and logging. The Trans-Canada identity is partly an identity of wild nature — of pine forests, of blueberry patches, of hard winters. This is very different from American identity, which is more urban, more myth-driven (frontier, Manifest Destiny). Canadian identity is often quieter, more provisional, more defined by endurance of climate and landscape than by narrative triumph.

Brewster's poem participates in a broader Canadian literary tradition of place poetry — poetry that asserts the formative power of geography. Other Canadian poets (Earle Birney, Al Purdy, Margaret Atwood) similarly anchor identity in specific landscapes. What makes Brewster distinctive is her refusal to romanticise: her New Brunswick is old farmhouses in need of paint, aimlessly clucking hens, burned-out bush.

The Poem's Argument: Place as Identity

The poem's opening thesis — People are made of places — is not a metaphor for Brewster; it is a literal claim about how identity is constituted. She is arguing against more common accounts of identity-formation that emphasise genetics, social class, education, or individual psychology. For Brewster, these factors are subordinate to the question: where did you come from? The places we inhabit in childhood — their smells, textures, seasons, sounds — become part of us so deeply that they constitute (make up) rather than merely influence who we are.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Where I Come From
1People are made of places. They carry with them
2hints of jungles or mountains, a tropic grace
3or the cool eyes of sea-gazers. Atmosphere of cities
4how different drops from them, like the smell of smog
5or the almost-not-smell of tulips in the spring,
6nature tidily plotted in little squares
7with a fountain in the centre; museum smell,
8art also tidily plotted with a guidebook;
9or the smell of work, glue factories maybe,
10chromium-plated offices; smell of subways
11crowded at rush hours.
12Where I come from, people
13carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods;
14blueberry patches in the burned-out bush;
15wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint,
16with yards where hens and chickens circle about,
17clucking aimlessly; battered schoolhouses
18behind which violets grow. Spring and winter
19are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice.
20A door in the mind blows open, and there blows
21a frosty wind from fields of snow.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Line 1
People are made of places. They carry with them
Language & devices

Declarative Thesis: opens with absolute authority. Made of = constituted by, not merely influenced. Verb: carry — active, ongoing, not past-tense. People carry places wherever they go. FULL STOP after places — the thesis is complete before the poem has begun its elaboration.

Meaning & effect

The opening sentence is one of the boldest in contemporary poetry: a flat-out philosophical claim with no qualification or hesitation. The full stop after places isolates the thesis, gives it weight, makes it stand alone. Made of distinguishes this from shaped by or influenced by — people are literally composed of their places, as matter is composed of atoms. The continuation (They carry with them) adds the temporal dimension: this is not just a formative relationship but an ongoing one.

Line 2
hints of jungles or mountains, a tropic grace
Language & devices

Diction: hints — subtle, not obvious. Tropic grace — people from hot countries carry a particular physical quality (grace = elegant ease). Listing begins. jungles or mountains — diverse origins, but all non-urban.

Meaning & effect

Tropic grace is a beautiful but slightly uncomfortable phrase: it associates people from tropical regions with physical elegance, which borders on racial/ethnic stereotyping. Brewster uses this as shorthand for the physical characteristics supposedly produced by hot-country origins. Reading: This is a poem of its time (1950s–60s) — the correlations Brewster draws between climate and character reflect older ideas that are now questioned. This is worth noting for personal response.

Line 3
or the cool eyes of sea-gazers. Atmosphere of cities
Language & devices

Contrast: cool eyes — those from cold or sea-coast origins have a distant, observational quality. The sea-gazer looks outward, contemplatively. Fragmented Syntax: Atmosphere of cities — the sentence seems to break, reflecting the fragmented, disconnected quality of city life itself.

Meaning & effect

Cool eyes of sea gazers contrasts with tropic grace: warm-country people have bodily warmth and movement; sea-coast/cold-country people have mental distance and observation. The syntax fractures at Atmosphere of cities — as if the city has disrupted the smooth flow of Brewster's language. The fragmentation is formally appropriate: cities fragment people from their natural settings.

Line 4–5
how different drops from them, like the smell of smog / or the almost-not-smell of tulips in the spring,
Language & devices

Simile: drops from them like the smell of smog. The city atmosphere clings to people then drops like a smell. Compound Adjective: almost-not-smell — barely perceptible, on the edge of existence. Contrast: smog (ugly, harmful) vs tulips (beautiful, delicate) — both city.

Meaning & effect

Drops from them is a striking verb phrase: the city's atmosphere is something that exudes from city people involuntarily, as a smell emanates from a body. Almost-not-smell of tulips is extraordinary in its precision: city flowers have their natural scent suppressed, reduced to near-absence by the urban environment. The tulip's smell exists in theory (it's a tulip) but barely in practice (city air overwhelms it). This captures how nature survives in cities only partially, inadequately.

Line 6–8
nature tidily plotted in little squares / with a fountain in the centre; museum smell, / art also tidily plotted with a guidebook;
Language & devices

Metaphor: nature plotted (planned on a map or in a garden) — city nature is artificial, managed, mediated. Guidebook — you need instructions to engage with city nature. Adjective: tidily — too ordered, too controlled.

Meaning & effect

City nature is curated and annotated: parks designed by landscape architects, labelled with signs, navigated via maps. This contrasts with the wild nature of Brewster's rural background, where nature is simply there, all around, unlabelled. The word plotted carries a secondary meaning: to plot is to scheme. City nature is a conspiracy — an attempt to convince urbanites that nature is present when really they have tamed it beyond recognition.

Line 9–11
or the smell of work, glue factories maybe, / chromium-plated offices; smell of subways / crowded at rush hours.
Language & devices

Olfactory Listing: glue factories (industrial, acrid), chromium-plated offices (antiseptic, metallic), subways at rush hours (bodily, human sweat). DASH/Semicolon: rapid listing. Crowded at rush hours — the density and pressure of urban commuter life.

Meaning & effect

The three urban smells range from industrial to corporate to bodily — covering all aspects of the urban economy. Glue factories is the rawest: the smell of boiling animal products, acrid and nauseating. Chromium-plated offices gives no smell of its own — it is almost sterile, but not quite (chrome smells metallic). The subway smell is the most human: packed bodies, heat, sweat. All three are unpleasant. Brewster is building a case against the city through its olfactory profile.

Line 12–13
Where I come from, people / carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods;
Language & devices

Pivot: Where I come from — first-person voice enters. Enjambment: people / carry — the line break gives people its own weight before carry specifies what they do. Woods in their minds — extended metaphor continues. Acres of pine woods — specific, real, Canadian.

Meaning & effect

The shift from they (urban dwellers) to where I come from (the poet's community) is a significant move from observer to participant. But Brewster does not say where I come from, I carry — she says people carry. She includes herself in a community. Acres of pine woods introduces a precision of scale: acres, not just woods. The pine woods are imagined in extent as well as type. Pine woods are specifically Canadian/New Brunswick — dark, coniferous, resinous-smelling.

Line 14
blueberry patches in the burned-out bush;
Language & devices

Specific Detail: blueberries grow in burned-out bush — after a forest fire, blueberries colonise the disturbed ground. This is ecologically accurate and symbolically rich. Burned-out bush — damaged, scarred, but generative.

Meaning & effect

The blueberry patches in burned-out bush is an image of resilience — beauty emerging from destruction. But Brewster does not romanticise: the bush is burned-out, damaged. The beauty (blueberries, edible, sweet) is inseparable from the damage (fire, ash). This image refuses easy pastoral comfort. Canadian Context: forest fires are a defining feature of Canadian rural landscape. The burned-out bush is not unusual or catastrophic — it is part of the cycle.

Line 15–17
wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint, / with yards where hens and chickens circle about, / clucking aimlessly; battered schoolhouses
Language & devices

THREE COMMAS around old, in need of paint — create the sense of a house being described and found wanting. Hens and chickens circle about — undirected animal movement. Clucking aimlessly — onomatopoeia and adverb. Battered schoolhouses — worn, endured.

Meaning & effect

Brewster's rural world is genuinely worn and slightly ramshackle: old farmhouses needing paint, aimless hens, battered schools. This is not a pastoral idyll but a working community with real poverty and real age. The word aimlessly is important: it prevents sentimentality. These hens are not romantic symbols of agrarian life; they are confused animals going nowhere. The battered schoolhouse has been used hard and survived.

Line 18–19
behind which violets grow. Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice.
Language & devices

Contrast: behind the battered schoolhouse — violets. Delicacy persisting against neglect. 'Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons' — not all four seasons equally, but two: beginning and end, ice and thaw. Metaphor: ice and the breaking of ice — both physical (literal Canadian winters) and psychological (frozen states and their thawing).

Meaning & effect

Behind which violets grow is a small, perfect image: the wild, delicate violet growing unseen behind the decayed building. This is nature persisting in the margins of human habitation — not cultivated or plotted but self-willed. The spring/winter pairing is the poem's deepest metaphysical statement: the chief seasons of the mind are the extremes — frozen stasis and the violent breaking of that stasis. Summer and autumn (growth and decay) are secondary.

Line 20–21
A door in the mind blows open, and there blows / a frosty wind from fields of snow.
Language & devices

Metaphor: A door in the mind blows open — memory/place-identity erupts involuntarily, without warning. Agent: the wind blows the door; the person has no control. Frosty wind from fields of snow — Canada blows in: cold, empty, white, vast.

Meaning & effect

The poem ends with the involuntary arrival of home — not remembered but experienced again. The door of the mind is not opened deliberately; it blows open, an image of uncontrolled memory. And what enters is not a warm pastoral glow but a frosty wind — cold, harsh, elemental. The ending is deliberately ambiguous: is this landscape cold and unwelcoming, or is it simply the truth of where Brewster comes from, embraced as such? The FROSTY WIND is both threatening and familiar.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

"Where I Come From" opens with the most confident sentence in it — "People are made of places." — and then spends twenty lines appearing to illustrate that thesis while actually revising it. The revision, not the illustration, is the poem. Read as illustration, it is a tidy compare-and-contrast of city and country with a decorative flourish at the end, which is roughly how weak essays treat it. Read as revision, it is an epistemological drama: a poem about two different ways of knowing places and people — acquaintance from outside, constitution from inside — which stages the second overtaking the first, and which ends by discovering that its own opening aphorism was not quite right.

Start with how oddly the thesis is supported. "Made of" is total, passive and finished: manufacture completed at some point in the past. But the evidence offered is instantly hedged — "hints of jungles", "a tropic grace or the cool eyes", "glue factories maybe". The first stanza is written in the epistemology of the observer: someone reading strangers' surfaces in transit, guessing at origins from a posture or a stare, guessing at a city's life from what it smells of. And the guessing is done in the city's own idiom. The stanza's lexicon is the lexicon of curation — "tidily plotted", "guidebook", "museum" — and its speaker is doing to people precisely what the guidebook does to nature: sorting them into little squares. Jungle people are graceful; sea people are cool; city people smell of subways. The typology skirts the postcard and the stereotype, and the poem knows it: that is what "hints" and "maybe" are for. Grammar completes the demonstration. The city sentence sprawls across eight and a half lines with a single finite verb — "drops" — before decaying into verbless inventory ("museum smell"; "smell of subways"): knowledge-about accumulates but cannot predicate, cannot make anything happen. This is not city-hatred. It is a self-demonstration of the poverty of external knowing, performed in the first person plural of all of us who have changed trains somewhere and thought we knew it.

The dropped line at "Where I come from, people" changes the ground of authority, and the economy of that pivot is extraordinary. The first person enters once — a single "I", buried mid-formula, never repeated — and immediately dissolves into "people". The restraint is the argument. A poem claiming that persons are made by places, communally and involuntarily, would refute itself with an insistent lyric "I": whatever an "I" makes of itself is exactly what it was not made of by anywhere. So the speaker claims origin without claiming ownership, testifies for a "people" she belongs to, and lets the certainty of the new catalogue do the self-revealing. And it is certain: no more "maybe". Acres, blueberries, the paint, the hens, the violets behind the schoolhouse — the exactness of memory rather than research, a knowledge that includes what is behind buildings because the knower has stood behind them.

Yet the inventory refuses the reward it seems to promise. Home is peeling, "battered", economically becalmed; its hens go nowhere, "clucking aimlessly"; its bush is "burned-out". The stanza's tenderness is real but it is positioned, not stated — carried by prepositions. Blueberries grow in the burn; violets behind the battered school. Sweetness and delicacy are not compensations placed beside damage; they are located inside it, inseparable from it. This is where the poem's honesty cuts deepest: what home gives is not beauty but constitution, and the constitution includes the damage. Then the epigram names the deepest layer of the endowment: "Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice." Not scenery at all now, but a shape of feeling — a calendar of two extremes, stasis and rupture, with the temperate seasons deleted. No summer: the mind this place makes has no season of ease. What you inherit from such a place is a rhythm — long freeze, violent thaw — and the sentence performs it, two stressed "ice"s flanking a loosened slack of syllables, freeze-melt-freeze.

Everything to this point, however vivid, is willed: catalogues composed by a speaker in full control of her material. And that is exactly why the poem cannot stop there. If places really make people, recitation proves nothing — a tourist can recite. The proof must be something that happens to the speaker, against her will, in the poem's present tense. Hence the couplet: "A door in the mind blows open, and there blows / a frosty wind from fields of snow." Agency has drained out of the human: people carried, hens circled, violets grew — now a door blows open, unlatched from the far side, and weather arrives. The form seals it. The poem's only rhyme and only metrically regular line (a strict iambic tetrameter) close the free verse like a mechanism engaging — or, better, like the mind falling at last into its native measure, the cadence of where it comes from, once it stops steering.

The obvious objection says the poem is rural chauvinism with a canvas tote: city rendered as smells and sterility, country as flowers and growth, with a dash of climatic stereotype ("tropic grace") in the set-up. Concede the tilt; the stanzas are not neutral. But the tilt is epistemic, not moral. The city passage indicts a way of knowing — mediated, curated, olfactory, guessed — and flags its own guesswork while doing so; its human specimens get the poem's most admiring nouns ("grace", "cool eyes"). City-dwellers are inside the opening thesis too: they also carry their place; it is just that what the observer can know of it is residue. Meanwhile the country is given poverty, aimlessness and burn scars, and its climactic gift is a cold draught through the skull. A chauvinist poem ends warm, at the hearth. This one ends "frosty", in an unheatable mind.

The second objection is formal: that the couplet is a bolt-on epiphany — a rhymed, faintly gothic flourish that betrays the catalogue's hard-won specificity (a "door in the mind" could be anyone's; a blueberry patch in a burn is Brewster's). The preparation answers most of this: the mind has been a container since line 13, had a climate by line 19; the long ō of the rhyme is banked three lines early; and the rhyme itself is left imperfect, "blows"/"snow", one consonant short of tidy — the poem declines full closure even while closing. But the generality of the last image should not be argued away, because it is doing the final piece of work: at the moment origin returns as force, it stops being itemisable. Contents can be catalogued; weather cannot. The couplet has no local nouns because possession has reversed — she is no longer holding the place up for inspection; it is moving through her.

So the opening aphorism gets its quiet correction. "Made of places" promised a finished product, identity as material. The poem ends in the present progressive of weather: not made once, but still being made; not composed of a place, but inhabited, visited, blown through by it. Where you come from, on this poem's evidence, is not your substance. It is your climate — and climate does not stay outside.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Stanza logic: 11 / 8 / 2

The three stanzas are a narrowing aperture. Stanza 1 (11 lines) is everyone and everywhere: a typology of humankind sorted by habitat — jungle, mountain, coast, city. Stanza 2 (8 lines) is one community: the speaker's own, inventoried. Stanza 3 (2 lines) is one instant inside one mind. The poem sheds lines as it approaches what it actually cares about, and the shrinking stanzas enact its argument that the vast general claim ("People are made of places") is only verifiable in the smallest possible unit — a single gust through a single head. Alternatively: world, memory, now.

The first stanza break is bridged by a shared line: "crowded at rush hours." occupies the left of one line-slot (5 syllables), and "Where I come from, people" is printed dropped and indented to complete it (6 syllables). Together they make one pentameter-weight line split across the gap. The device does two things at once, and both matter: it separates (new stanza, new grammatical person, new world) and it continues (same line, same argument — the home community is another instance of the opening thesis, not an exception to it). The second break, before the couplet, has no such bridge: the final two lines are cut adrift, because what they describe — the ambush of memory — is discontinuous with the willed cataloguing that precedes it.

Metre: free verse haunted by the pentameter

Full lines run 10–14 syllables, mostly carrying four to six stresses — blank-verse width without blank-verse regularity — until the last line, which is the poem's only strictly regular one. Scansion of ten lines (stressed syllables in capitals):

  • L1 PEOple are MADE of PLAces. || they CARry with THEM — trochaic fall on the poem's subject-word, then three evenly spaced beats landing the aphorism; after the mid-line stop the rhythm turns rising. The poem asserts in falling rhythm and explains in rising: statement, then motion.
  • L3 or the COOL EYES of SEA-GAzers. || ATmosphere of CIties — the spondee "COOL EYES" plus the heavy compound piles five stresses into six syllables: the pace drops to a held stare. Then the new sentence skitters in on a dactylic run ("ATmosphere of") — the city arrives faster and lighter, all surface.
  • L5 or the ALmost-NOT-SMELL of TUlips in the SPRING — the coinage jams adjacent stresses ("NOT-SMELL") so the voice stumbles exactly at the point of perceptual failure, then relaxes into anapaests ("of TUlips in the SPRING") once the non-event is past.
  • L6 NAture TIdily PLOTted in LITtle SQUARES — tidy falling triple rhythm, equal small parcels of sound trotting to a clipped stressed monosyllable: the metre itself is municipal planting, boxed shut at "SQUARES".
  • L11 CROWded at RUSH HOURS. — five syllables, the stanza's shortest line, ending on the spondee "RUSH HOURS": the stanza's longest sentence dies in its most compressed line — maximum humanity per syllable, the verse as crowded as the carriage.
  • L12 WHERE i COME from, || PEOple — scannable as iambic ("where I come FROM"), but sense throws the weight forward onto WHERE, the questioned category; "PEOple" hangs at the enjambment, held over the turn until "carry" catches it.
  • L13 CARry WOODS in their MINDS, || Acres of PINE WOODS — the trochee "CARry" repeats line 1's verb at line-head with the stress now on it; the closing spondee "PINE WOODS" answers "RUSH HOURS" — each world ends a key line on a double-stress, compression against expanse.
  • L17 CLUCKing AIMlessly; || BATtered SCHOOLhouses — wholly falling rhythm, not one rising foot: trochees and dactyls subsiding one after another, movement without direction. Aimlessness performed metrically.
  • L19 are the MIND'S CHIEF SEAsons: || ICE and the BREAKing of ICE — three consecutive stresses ("MIND'S CHIEF SEA-") bear down like the claim itself; after the colon, two stressed ICEs flank a loose anapaestic slack ("and the BREAKing of"): freeze, thaw, re-freeze in rhythm. At 13 syllables this is the poem's widest line — it dilates to hold the epigram.
  • L20–21 a DOOR in the MIND BLOWS Open, || and there BLOWS / a FROSty WIND from FIELDS of SNOW — the mid-line stress-cluster "MIND BLOWS O-" bursts like the door itself; the line ends on an unanchored "BLOWS", the verb hanging in the doorway across the enjambment; and then the final line is perfect iambic tetrameter, the only fully regular line in the poem. After twenty lines of speech-rhythm the poem locks into hymn-measure to close. Two readings of that lock, both usable: the free verse finally "comes home" to the metre that was underneath it all along; or the involuntary memory arrives with a formal authority the willed catalogues never achieved — when the mind stops steering, it falls into measure.

Rhyme

No scheme; one end-rhyme, "blows"/"snow", closing the poem — and it is imperfect: the vowel is exact, but the /z/ of "blows" is unanswered. The poem that mocked the "tidily plotted" ends with a closure one consonant short of tidy. The rhyme is also pre-paid: "grow" (18) and "Open"/"blows" (20) lay down the long ō so the couplet chimes with what the ear already holds. Elsewhere the poem substitutes identical repetition where rhyme would be — "woods … woods" (13), "ice … ice" (19), "blows … blows" (20), "tidily plotted … tidily plotted" (6, 8), "smell" five times — as if this speaker distrusts ornament but cannot stop things recurring; recurrence, not rhyme, is the poem's form of memory. Incidental chimes worth a sentence in an essay: "grace"/"gazers" (2–3) binding the two admiring portraits; "maybe"/"subways" (9–10) letting the shrug echo inside the machinery.

Syntax: six sentences, two of them enormous

#SentenceLinesCharacter
1"People are made of places."1aaphorism
2"They carry … sea-gazers."1b–3athesis instanced
3"Atmosphere of cities … rush hours."3b–11city catalogue, 8½ lines
4"Where I come from … violets grow."12–18ahome catalogue, 6½ lines
5"Spring and winter … breaking of ice."18b–19epigram
6"A door … fields of snow."20–21event

Two facts the site nowhere records, and which repay more pressure than anything else in the poem's grammar:

  • Every full stop inside a stanza falls mid-line (after "places.", "sea-gazers.", "grow."); the only line-final full stops close stanzas (11, 19, 21). Sense-units and verse-units are kept deliberately out of phase inside each stanza — every ending immediately re-opens — and snap into phase only at the stanza edges. The poem therefore reads as continuous carrying: nothing is allowed to rest at a line-end until a whole world has been put down.
  • Sentence 3 contains one finite verb; sentence 4 contains four. The city sentence predicates once — "drops" — and then stops predicating altogether: "nature tidily plotted…" is a hanging absolute, "museum smell" a verbless noun, "smell of subways" an item on a list that has forgotten its grammar. This is anacoluthon doing argument: the sentence about the tidily plotted city is the poem's untidiest, an inventory drifting free of syntax, because guidebook-knowledge accumulates without organising life. The home sentence, exactly as long in spirit, is paratactically clean — "come", "carry", "circle", "grow", each item a well-formed phrase in the same case — and it closes on a finite verb of growth. The city catalogue's last word is "hours" (schedule); the home catalogue's last word is "grow" (life). That is the poem's judgement, delivered entirely by grammar and never stated.

Sentence 3's opening is genuinely broken — "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them" — and the break is functional: see Cruxes 1.

Punctuation

Six semicolons, symmetrically three per catalogue (7, 8, 10; 13, 14, 17): the two worlds are built by the same paratactic machine, which is why the difference between them registers as content, not form. One colon in the poem (19), reserved for the definitional gesture — "chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice" — the syntax of a dictionary entry, the poem's one moment of stating a meaning rather than accumulating instances. The commas of line 15 ("wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint,") postpose the adjectives as afterthoughts — the grammar of a second look, appraisal arriving after recognition, a farmer's eye rather than an estate agent's.

Lineation, caesura, enjambment

  • "They carry with them / hints" (1–2) and "people / carry woods" (12–13): both stanzas launch on the same verb delivered across a line-break — the carried thing arrives after the turn, made to be waited for. The parallel is structural rhyme, and the difference is the payload: city people carry "hints"; home people carry "acres".
  • "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops" (3–4): the atmosphere literally drops down a line.
  • "smell of subways / crowded at rush hours" (10–11): the crowd is pushed below the line, underground.
  • "battered schoolhouses / behind which violets grow" (17–18): the violets are hidden behind the line-break as behind the building — you must go round the line-end to find them.
  • "and there blows / a frosty wind" (20–21): the wind blows through the poem's last line-break; the final gap in the verse is the open door.
  • Caesurae: the three mid-line full stops above, plus the semicolon pauses; line 15's triple-comma stutter is the poem's most halting moment, the voice picking its way across a dilapidated thing.

The turns

Two, of different kinds. Line 12 is a volta of source: third person to first, hearsay to memory, "maybe" to certainty — marked typographically by the dropped line. Line 20 is a volta of mode: catalogue to event, metonymy to metaphor, habitual present ("carry", "grow") to punctual present ("blows open") — marked by the only unbridged white space in the poem. Notice the grammar of agency across the turns: people carry (active), then a door blows open and wind blows in (the mind acted upon). The poem's last discovery is that "where I come from" is not something you hold; it is something that arrives.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The city's signature: sm- and sibilance

Six sm- onsets in seven lines — "smell of smog" (4), "almost-not-smell" (5), "museum smell" (7), "smell of work" (9), "smell of subways" (10) — and then none for the rest of the poem. The cluster /sm/ closes the lips and pushes a small breath through the nose: five repetitions make the reader's face perform a series of little sniffs, the exact gesture of testing city air. And by the fifth occurrence the word has gone semantically numb — repetition wears it featureless, which is the point: the city's identity-marker is a word rubbed smooth by overuse, like its chromium surfaces. Around the sm- spine hisses a wider sibilance — "cities", "spring", "squares", "centre", "museum", "offices", "subways", "rush" — urban static, air that is never quite silent. The vowels of this stanza thud short and flat where the poem's attention is coldest: "smog", "plotted" (twice), "offices" — while the admired coast and tropics got long, opened vowels ("cool", "grace", "gazers"). Vowel-length is this poem's warmth of attention: what the voice lingers on, it values.

Home's signature: plosives and gutturals

The second stanza detonates rather than hisses. "Blueberry patches in the burned-out bush" pops four b/p plosives — small explosions of the lips, buds and berries bursting out of scorched ground; the energy of germination is in the consonants before it is in the image. Then the yard clatters in gutturals: "chickens circle about, / clucking … acres … carry … battered". The onomatopoeia of "clucking" is conventional; what is not conventional is how its consonant spreads into the neighbours — chiCKens, cirCle, cluCKing — so that the whole line clucks, not just the verb. The stanza's binding vowel is the long i: "minds", "pine" (13), "behind", "violets" (18), "ice … ice" (19) — a thin, bright, glassy sound, light off ice. Notice what the first pair does: "minds" and "pine" share their vowel exactly, so the claim "carry woods in their minds" is enacted inside the words — the pine is already lodged in the mind at the level of the phoneme.

The ending's acoustics

The final rhyme is laid down early: "grow" (18), "open" and "blows … blows" (20), "snow" (21) — five long ō sounds converging, with "door" adjacent in vowel-space. The ō is the blown vowel: the lips round into the shape of a draught, and each initial b ("blows") is a plosive released straight into it — a puff. Add the fricatives of "frosty … from … fields" and the w of "wind", and the couplet is not describing wind so much as requiring the mouth to make some: the reader performs the weather that the speaker suffers. Against this, "ice and the breaking of ice" is built of hard glass: two long-i monosyllables at either end, and in the middle the poem's one br- cluster — "breaking" — an audible crack between two panes.

Cadence

The mid-line full stops (after "places.", "sea-gazers.", "grow.") force level, unemphatic closes: the voice cannot rise to a line-end climax inside a stanza, which is how Brewster's famous plainness is enforced, not just chosen. The fastest passage is "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them" — a tumble of light syllables, the city rushing itself; the slowest are the held spondee of "cool eyes" and line 15's comma-hobbled appraisal ("wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint,"), the voice picking its way across a dilapidated thing. "Aimlessly" is a dying fall in the middle of a line — the adverb itself trails off, doing what it says.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

A motif recurs and accumulates; a symbol stands for something beyond itself. This poem works mainly by motif — its method is accretion — and then converts its material into symbol only at the very end, which is one reason the ending feels like a change of key.

Motif 1: smell (and its disappearance)

Smell enters as the very mechanism of place-identity — atmosphere drops from people "like the smell of smog" (4) — then runs the whole register of the city: degraded to near-absence ("almost-not-smell", 5), institutionalised ("museum smell", 7), industrial ("smell of work", 9), and massed ("smell of subways", 10). Then the decisive change: after line 11 the vocabulary of smell is banished. The home stanza names things — pine, blueberry, paint, violets — whose odours are strongly implied (resin, smoke, damp timber) but never claimed. The logic: smell is how you know a place you merely pass through; it is the residue a place leaves on you, the thing that "drops from" you. Home is not sensed from outside but constituted from inside, so it needs no olfactory proof; and when a sense-channel finally returns in the couplet it is touch — "a frosty wind" — the one sense that requires contact. Trajectory: detachable trace → owned contents → felt weather.

Motif 2: carrying and containment

"They carry with them" (1) — carriage as luggage, exterior and portable. "Carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods" (13) — the container is now interior, and impossibly larger inside than out: acres in a skull. "The mind's chief seasons" (19) — the container has its own climate. "A door in the mind" (20) — the container has become a dwelling. And then the reversal that completes the motif: the wind blows in (21). What was carried now arrives under its own power; possession runs backwards. You carry home until home starts carrying itself into you.

Motif 3: the plotted against the unplotted

"Tidily plotted in little squares" (6), a fountain "in the centre" (7), "art also tidily plotted" (8), the "guidebook" (8), "chromium-plated" (10) — a lexicon of imposed finish, and "plotted"/"plated" are near-homophones: mapped surfaces, coated surfaces, the same gesture. Against it the second stanza sets landscapes re-planned by no planner: the "burned-out bush" (14), redesigned by fire; hens that "circle about … aimlessly" (16–17) — motion with no centre, where the city's squares had a fountain at theirs; violets "behind which … grow" (17–18) — growth in unplanned placement, behind rather than on display. The motif accumulates into the poem's structural irony: its own final couplet is the one formally "plotted" object in it (rhymed, metrical) — the unplanned mind turns out to generate pattern of its own, a different order from the municipal kind (and see Cruxes 4 for the reading that finds this a contradiction rather than a triumph).

Motif 4: cold

"The cool eyes of sea-gazers" (3): temperature as temperament, and admired — composure, distance, appraisal. Tulips "in the spring" (5): the city's one season, feeble and curated. Then "Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice" (18–19): cold promoted from style to structure, the mind's actual calendar. Finally "a frosty wind from fields of snow" (21): cold as the substance of the self's origin. The poem begins by admiring coolness in other people and ends by discovering an absolute cold in itself — the motif is a slow homecoming of temperature.

Symbols

  • The door (20) — the threshold between present consciousness and formative past; crucially it is not opened but blown open, from the far side. It stands for the involuntariness of origin: you do not choose to remember where you come from; it lets itself in.
  • The guidebook (8) — a whole epistemology in one object: experience prescribed, routed, and read about rather than had. Everything stanza 1 knows, it knows guidebook-fashion; everything stanza 2 knows, it knows by heart.
  • The violets (18) — unsponsored persistence: delicacy surviving behind an institution that is itself barely surviving. The poem's emblem for what neglect cannot prevent.
  • The fields of snow (21) — the origin as expanse without feature: plenitude or blankness, undecidable (Cruxes 4). What the speaker comes from may be a fullness (fields, space, light) or a white nothing.
  • Ice / the breaking of ice (19) — hovering between motif (literal Maritime climate) and symbol (the psyche's freeze and rupture); the poem's most economical double-exposure.
THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Place as Constitutive of Identity

Brewster's thesis: we are not merely shaped by where we come from — we ARE our places. The places inhabit us as completely as we inhabit them.

02

Urban vs Rural

The poem implicitly critiques urban life (artificial, olfactory unpleasant, nature-denying) while presenting rural life as more authentic — but without romanticising it. Rural life is worn, damaged, aimless — but real.

03

Memory and Involuntary Return

The final image (A door in the mind blows open) presents memory as involuntary and uncontrollable. The landscape returns unbidden, like weather.

04

Canadian Identity

The poem is a meditation on Canadian rural identity: vast, cold, pine-scented, seasonal, honest. It resists the American myth of the frontier-as-triumph and presents instead a landscape of endurance.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them" (3–4): the sentence that will not parse

The difficulty: there is no grammatical reading of this clause that does not require repair. Three candidates. (a) Exclamatory interpolation: "Atmosphere of cities — how different! — drops from them", with the punctuation withheld; supported by the poem's habit of unmarked appositives and by speech-rhythm. (b) Inverted manner adverb: "how different[ly the] atmosphere of cities drops from them"; supported by the logic of the paragraph — the previous sentence described how people carry places, this one describes how differently city people do. (c) Anacoluthon: the sentence genuinely breaks and restarts — grammar failing precisely as the city enters, before decaying into the verbless inventory ("museum smell") it never recovers from. There is a second instability inside the first: "them" should mean city people, but its only grammatical antecedent is the "They" of line 1 — all people. So either city-dwellers shed their atmosphere, or everyone who has passed through a city sheds a little of it. Careless readers silently normalise the line and move on; a strong answer refuses to repair it, notes that the poem about tidiness places its untidiest syntax exactly here, and lets the loose "them" include us all in the city's effect.

2. "a tropic grace / or the cool eyes of sea-gazers" (2–3): is the typology endorsed?

The difficulty: the opening reads character off climate — people sorted by habitat, with a whiff of the colonial postcard in "jungles" and "tropic". Is Brewster asserting this or exhibiting it? Reading A (endorsed): it flows directly from the thesis, the tone is unironic, and the poem never retracts it; a 1950s poem can hold period assumptions about climate and character without embarrassment. Reading B (exhibited): the hedges — "hints", the alternatives strung on "or", the later "maybe" — mark the whole register as guesswork; the stanza's instruments (guidebook, museum) are discredited by the second stanza's insider knowledge; the poem shows what shallow people-reading looks like before performing the deep kind. The evidence is genuinely split, and the date cuts both ways. What a strong answer does: notice that the poem needs the typology to be half-true — people are marked by place (the thesis requires it) — and half-glib — the marks cannot really be read off surfaces by strangers (the structure demonstrates it); and notice that the speaker types her own people identically ("people / carry woods in their minds") — the difference is not procedure but position: testimony instead of tourism.

3. "clucking aimlessly", "in need of paint", "battered" (15–17): what is the tone of the home inventory?

The difficulty: the stanza's nouns are loved but its modifiers are an audit of decline. Three readings. (a) Unsentimental fidelity: love that refuses to prettify; the tenderness lives in prepositions (blueberries in the burn, violets behind the school), not adjectives. (b) Economic elegy: a region running down — outmigration, resource decline — with "aimlessly" the community's condition displaced onto its hens, and the "battered" schoolhouse a public institution wearing out; the drafted-essay question in the notes ("Is the farming industry in decline here?") belongs to this reading. (c) Covert pride: the anti-guidebook — refusing the picturesque is the boast; our place does not need curating to be constitutive. Evidence for each is real, and they cannot be fully reconciled. The strong move: see that "aimlessly" is the exact antonym of "tidily plotted" — the poem's two adverbs are its poles — so the same word carries re-valued freedom (unscheduled, uncentred life; the hens circle where the city's squares have fountains at their centres) and undeniable drift. The hens are liberty and futility at once; an answer that picks one has thrown half the poem away.

4. "A door in the mind blows open…" (20–21): gift or breach — and earned or bolted on?

Three layers of undecidability. (i) Welcome or invasion? The wind as vivid inheritance, identity confirmed at full sensory strength — or as the draught of a mind that cannot be insulated, origin as cold you never chose. The poem's momentum honours where she comes from; but nothing in the couplet is warm, the door is forced from the far side, and winter has already been named the mind's chief season. (ii) "Fields of snow": plenitude or blankness? Space, light, home ground — or a featureless white nothing; what she comes from may be fullness or emptiness, and the line will not say. (iii) Does the poem earn the metaphor? Everything before is metonymy — real adjacent things standing for the place; the ending is sudden full metaphor, mind as house. For "earned": the container-mind is built stepwise ("woods in their minds", 13; "the mind's chief seasons", 19 — contents, then climate, then architecture); the rhyme is banked early ("grow", "open"); and it is left imperfect ("blows"/"snow"), one consonant short of tidy. For "not earned": the couplet's image is generic where the catalogue was owned — a "door in the mind" could be anyone's; a blueberry patch in a burn is hers — and a poem that sneered at the plotted ends in the one plotted form it contains. The strongest answers hold the tension as meaning: at the moment origin returns as force rather than as detail, it stops being itemisable — and being made of a place means your proof of belonging and your exposure to it arrive as the same gust.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

(The famous couplet is deliberately not among the ten — it is worked at length in Form, Sound, Cruxes 4 and the whole-poem essay. These are the moments that repay pressure.)

  1. "People are made of places." — aphorism; passive with suppressed agent; metonymy; earliest possible full stop, mid-line. The passive hides a maker: not "places make people" (process, resistible) but "are made of" (material, done). If a place is your substance rather than your manufacturer, travel cannot subtract it — the claim quietly forecloses escape before the poem begins. The mid-line stop is the poem's first shut door (and its last line will be a door blown open: the frame is exact). It is also the only sentence in the poem stated as law; everything after is instance, hedge or event, so the poem is best read as a twenty-line stress-test of its own first five words. Intention and effect: to win the reader's assent to an absolute before scrutiny arrives, then to spend the poem quietly correcting "made of" into something less finished.
  1. "the cool eyes of sea-gazers" — coined compound; spondee; transferred epithet. "Cool" carries the sea's temperature into the watcher's temperament: metonymy become physiognomy. The coinage names a people not by labour (fishermen, sailors) but by direction of attention — gazers, defined by where they look — so that climate becomes epistemology: cold places make watchers. The spondee ("COOL EYES") slows the line to the pace of the stare it describes. And it opens the poem's thermal thread: the first cold in the poem is admired composure; the last ("frosty wind") is involuntary weather — coolness travels from style to substance across twenty lines. Intention and effect: to establish that place-marks are subtle, bodily and legible only as style — and to plant the temperature the ending will weaponise.
  1. "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them" — anacoluthon; exclamatory interpolation; enjambment. The missing article ("Atmosphere", not "The atmosphere") makes the city's air an abstract substance, and "drops" hands the process to gravity: no one intends it, it simply sheds. The interpolation is the poem's one exclamatory gesture — feeling briefly surfacing — instantly muffled by the grammar going wrong around it. The enjambment performs the verb: the atmosphere drops down a line. Whatever repair you choose (see Cruxes 1), the sensation of disorder arrives before any statement about order — the reader experiences the city before being told about it. Intention and effect: to let syntax fail exactly at the city limits, so that the stanza's later tidiness-vocabulary ("plotted", "guidebook") reads as compensation for a real formlessness.
  1. "the almost-not-smell of tulips in the spring" — hyphenated compound of negation; stress-jam; phenomenological precision. The poem's finest small coinage: a noun built out of a failure to be one. Not "faint smell" — a weak positive — but a presence measured by its distance from nothing, approached from the wrong side. It is exact about a real experience: leaning to municipal tulips, knowing scent should be there, and receiving a trace that may be memory of tulip rather than tulip. The hyphens do municipal work, boxing the vacancy into a tidy compound — language plotting a little square around an absence — so the word enacts the city it diagnoses. Metrically the jammed stresses ("-most-NOT-SMELL") make the voice stumble at the precise point of perceptual failure. Set it against line 18's "Spring", unmodified and "chief": the city's spring is a negative quantity; home's is half the calendar. Intention and effect: to render administered nature as sensory debt — the reader performs a sniff that comes back empty.
  1. "nature tidily plotted in little squares / … art also tidily plotted with a guidebook" — verbatim repetition; "also" as analytic hinge; diminutive; triple pun. "Plotted" holds garden-plot, map-plotting and scheming in one participle — cultivation, cartography, conspiracy — and "tidily" makes neatness itself the accusation. The repetition is the argument: nature and art, the two things a city keeps as proof of soul, are processed by the same verb-phrase, and "also" files them together — a city in which one adverb covers parks and paintings has a single relation to everything, curation. The squares are "little" and have fountains "in the centre": administered space is small, bounded and centred, where home's motion will be aimless circling with no centre at all. The guidebook caps it: experience pre-routed, discovery replaced by confirmation. Intention and effect: to indict mediation, not citizens — and the reader is made to feel the deadness of "also", the most damning flat word in the stanza.
  1. "or the smell of work, glue factories maybe," — metonymy; epistemic adverb; grim materiality. "The smell of work": labour perceived as odour, class known through the nose before the mind. Glue factories boil hide and bone — the city's economy rendering bodies into adhesive — the stanza's ugliest fact, delivered in passing and unprotested. But the load-bearing word is "maybe": the speaker knows the smell, not the world it comes from, and flags her own guesswork in one unstressed shrug. It is the outsider's watermark on the whole stanza — nothing in the home catalogue is hedged, because she knows what grows behind the schoolhouse. Even the syntax (appended, verbless) files work as one more exhibit in a museum she is visiting. Intention and effect: to mark the limit of acquaintance-knowledge; the reader retroactively distrusts the confidence of everything stanza 1 asserted.
  1. "Where I come from, people / carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods;" — dropped line; the poem's only "I"; enjambment echo of lines 1–2; doubling with specification. The first person enters once, buried mid-formula, and dissolves into "people" — origin claimed, ownership declined; a communal thesis kept communal (an insistent lyric "I" would refute the poem's own claim that place, not self-fashioning, makes people). Typographically the phrase completes the city's line while opening its own stanza: continuation and departure at once. "People / carry" re-runs "carry with them / hints" across a line-break — a structural rhyme whose difference is the payload: hints against acres, residue against terrain. And "woods … pine woods" is memory's grammar — category first, then the exact species — while "acres" lays a surveyor's measure over inner space: the impossible arithmetic of a mind bigger inside than out. Intention and effect: authority changes source in six words — from observation to testimony — and the reader hears certainty arrive.
  1. "blueberry patches in the burned-out bush;" — plosive train; fire-succession ecology; idiom double-exposure. The image is fact before symbol — blueberries genuinely colonise burnt ground — and the accuracy licenses the symbolism: sweetness conditional on scorch, renewal that requires damage rather than surviving it. Four b/p plosives pop like buds out of char; the stanza's first colour arrives inside its worst injury. Behind the literal bush hovers the idiom: a burned-out person — the community's exhaustion and its fruitfulness held in one participle. Note what is absent: any causal claim. Just "in" — the preposition carries the whole theology, grace located inside ruin, not compensating beside it. Intention and effect: to found home's beauty on disturbance instead of the picturesque; the reader tastes sweetness and ash in one phrase.
  1. "battered schoolhouses / behind which violets grow." — enjambment as concealment; register-shift; institutional against wild. The building for making futures is the most worn object in the poem. The line-break hides the violets behind the line-end as behind the building: syntax as topography — you must turn the corner of the verse to find them, and readers who miss them have re-enacted the outsider's blindness. "Behind which" is a starchy, taught-grammar relative in a plain-spoken poem: for half a line the syntax puts on its school manners, while the violets ignore the lesson and grow where no plan placed them. They are shade-flowers, unplanted, findable only by those who already know where to look — insider knowledge in botanical form, the exact opposite of the guidebook. The sentence then ends mid-line on "grow": the home catalogue's last word is a verb of life (the city's was "hours"). Intention and effect: home defined as the place whose hidden delicacies need no instructions — and the reader is quietly tested.
  1. "Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice." — colon as definition; epanaleptic fold (A : B-of-A); deliberate exclusion; gerund. The poem's only colon performs its only act of definition — a dictionary entry for a psyche. The fold matters more than the pairing: spring is given no content of its own, defined purely as violence done to winter — renewal exists only as rupture of stasis. What is deleted is as eloquent: no summer (no season of ease), no autumn (no ripeness, no gentle decline) — the temperate middle of feeling edited out of this mind entirely. "Breaking" is a gerund, not a completed event: perpetual process, a calendar of two states and a crack. The rhythm enacts it — two stressed ICEs flanking a loosened slack — freeze, thaw, re-freeze. This, not line 1, is the poem's deepest thesis: what a place installs is not imagery but a rhythm of feeling. Intention and effect: climate converted into psychology in thirteen syllables; the reader inherits the binary in the cadence itself.
CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Ecocritical

Makes visible: the poem literalises bioregional identity — the psyche as ecosystem, people who "carry woods in their minds" and whose emotional calendar is set by the actual freeze-thaw of their latitude ("ice and the breaking of ice"). It also produces one of the sharpest early images of administered nature: "tidily plotted in little squares", scent managed down to an "almost-not-smell" — nature present in the city only as exhibit and deficit. And it is ecologically literate: blueberries genuinely colonise burnt ground; "blueberry patches in the burned-out bush" is fire-succession before it is symbol, which is what licenses the symbol. Flattens: the poem is not conservationist — no protest, no loss-narrative; the burn is a neutral fact of home, not an indictment. An ecocritical reading that turns Brewster into an environmental campaigner has confused her with Boey Kim Cheng.

Postcolonial

Makes visible: the opening's taxonomy — "jungles", "a tropic grace" — is the imperial habit of reading bodies by climate zone, the exhibition-catalogue gaze; and the poem's discredited instruments (museum, guidebook) are the metropole's ways of packaging both nature and culture. Against that centre, a poet from a "battered", unstoried margin writes her periphery into literature without exoticising it — a quietly Canadian assertion that the hinterland is constitutive, not merely scenic. The lens also reads against the poem: this is settler ground — farmhouses, schoolhouses, logging woods — and the Indigenous presence of New Brunswick (Wolastoqiyik and Mi'kmaq land) is nowhere in a poem titled "Where I Come From"; its "people" who carry the woods in their minds are not the people longest made by those woods. The silence is analysable and worth a sentence in any answer on voice. Flattens: the poem's scale is personal and communal, not national-allegorical; pressed into a parable of empire it simply breaks.

Marxist / materialist

Makes visible: the catalogue is class-legible end to end — "the smell of work, glue factories" (rendering plants boiling carcasses to adhesive: industry's rawest conversion of bodies into product), "chromium-plated offices" (white-collar work as surface finish), "subways / crowded at rush hours" (commuting as commodified time — the catalogue's last word is "hours"). Rural poverty is material fact, not mood: private dwellings "in need of paint", public institutions "battered" — underfunded margins of a resource economy whose raw materials leave for the metropole (the owner's drafted note about raw materials and exploitation belongs here, as extension rather than authorial intent). Even leisure is administered consumption: museum plus guidebook. Flattens: the poem stages no antagonism and imagines no change; it converts economic decline into character ("aimlessly") — a materialist would say it aestheticises what it ought to historicise.

Feminist

Makes visible: the poem refuses the heroic frontier register of much North American place-writing — no axe, no conquest, no settlement epic. Its home is the maintained-and-unmaintained communal world historically kept by women: yards, hens, paint, the schoolhouse (rural teaching, a women's profession) with violets behind it. Authority is claimed through attention rather than assertion, and the lyric ego is all but erased — one "I", instantly dissolved into "people" — a counter-model to the proprietorial "I" that plants flags in landscapes. "Grace", the poem's first admiring noun, is a gendered aesthetic reclaimed as environmental inheritance. Flattens: the poem carefully ungenders its "people" — there is not one gendered pronoun in it — and reading it as women's testimony narrows a voice built to be communal.

Psychoanalytic

Makes visible: the final couplet is a textbook return of the repressed — a sealed room in the mind-house breached from the far side, contents arriving as force and cold rather than as narrative; memory not recalled but suffered. "Burned-out" and "battered" double as psychic scar-vocabulary; "ice and the breaking of ice" reads as defence and breach, frozen affect and its violent thaw, a personality organised around containment and rupture with the temperate states deleted. Strangest and most productive: the remembered home contains no people — no parent, no name, only buildings, plants and poultry; attachment has been displaced wholesale onto terrain. Flattens: the climate is also just climate — New Brunswick winters are literal, and a reading that makes all weather symptom loses the documentary ground the poem stands on.

Reader-response

Makes visible: the poem is an engine for self-application. Stanza 1's typology invites every reader to find their own slot among the jungles, mountains, coasts and cities; "Where I come from" is a formula each reader already owns; and the withheld explanations — "maybe", the unglossed final image — delegate completion to us, which is why the poem survives annotation so well. Flattens: treated purely as prompt-material, the poem's actual New Brunswick — its burn ecology, its battered institutions — becomes interchangeable wallpaper, which is precisely the guidebook relation to place the poem despises.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

  1. The loyal-pastoral reading — a tribute to rural origins with the city as foil. Depends on: the structural favouritism (home gets the finite verbs, the flowers, the colours, the closing couplet) and the tender exactness of the inventory. Weakness: it must euphemise "battered", "aimlessly" and "burned-out", and explain away an ending that is cold rather than warm; it also flattens stanza 1's genuine admiration ("grace", "cool eyes") into sneering it does not contain.
  1. The anti-urban satire — an attack on city artifice. Depends on: "tidily plotted" twice, the guidebook, the "almost-not-smell", the numbing sm- repetitions. Weakness: satire needs a verdict, and the poem withholds one — it hedges ("maybe"), admires the marks city people carry, and its opening thesis covers them too. The "disdain" so confidently asserted in the notes is largely imported by readers; the poem's contempt-objects are curation and mediation, never citizens.
  1. The exile reading — spoken from away: a speaker now living in the city, for whom home exists only as memory. Depends on: the intimacy of the city textures (rush hours, museum smell — known, not researched); the emigrant's formula "Where I come from" (you only say it elsewhere); the couplet as memory striking at distance; and the biographical rhyme of Brewster's own decades of migration through cities and campuses. Weakness: the poem never states a present location; the city knowledge could be a visitor's ("maybe" says exactly that); and the reading leans on biography the text deliberately withholds.
  1. The determinist manifesto — the poem straightforwardly asserts that people are products of environment. Depends on: "made of", the opening typology, a mind whose "chief seasons" are set by latitude. Weakness: the hedges corrode the law even as it is stated — "hints", "maybe", "almost" — and the only determinism the poem verifies is first-personal and momentary: one gust through one mind. "Carry" (portable, ongoing) quietly contradicts "made of" (fixed, finished); the poem ends closer to haunting than to manufacture.
  1. The ars poetica — a poem about writing: "art also tidily plotted" as curated, derivative culture; the unplotted catalogue as Brewster's own plain style; "fields of snow" as the blank page from which the real poems blow in. Depends on: the museum/guidebook lines; the self-referential irony of a poem that scorns the plotted and then ends in its one rhymed, metrical couplet. Weakness: nothing in the text names writing; the snow-as-page equation is imported wholesale; and the reading converts a poem about belonging into a poem about poems — clever, unfalsifiable, and thinner than what it replaces.
  1. The mood-cycle reading — a portrait of a psyche given to cyclical shutdown and release: "ice" as depressive freeze, "the breaking of ice" as violent thaw, the couplet as intrusive mood rather than memory (nothing of the farmhouse returns at the end — only cold). Depends on: "the mind's chief seasons" being explicitly psychological; the deletion of the temperate seasons; "aimlessly" as anhedonia displaced onto hens. Weakness: it medicalises a metaphor, and the poem's frame is communal — "people carry", a whole region's inheritance — so the clinical reading keeps collapsing back into what the poem actually says: climate.
REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Structural + General Analysis

Analysis
  • Stanzas of irregular length, the structure is free.
  • Syllable counts vary but turn around 12.
  • Eleven, eight, and two lines (couplet), respectively
  • The indentation in the second stanza is made to follow the first. She wants to show the description of a rural area is in continuation of an urban area, but is still a different idea. The passage from third to first person makes the change more abrupt.
  • The author makes this indentation to show that rural and urban areas depend on each other, need each other mutually. Rural areas give the raw materials and urban areas exploit them to form goods.
  • The change from third to first person is made softer by the fact the word “I” is only used once in the entire poem. The rest of the second stanza is just a description, so the change is really only notable in the first verse of the second stanza.
  • Bold metaphorical statement followed by concrete imagery detailing with contrasting material
  • There is a larger separation with the third stanza as it is not in continuation of the second, as the second is the first. So the third stanza is set apart, it has an entirely different subject, it is not a physical description, we enter the mind of the author, return to childhood.
  • No rhyme scheme, once again a free style of writing, the author does not respect the organisation that she notices in the city, tidily plotted.
  • The three stanzas also present three angles on the poem’s material, as it becomes narrower and more subjective as it goes on
  • First stanza describes people in general, all of whom are made of places
  • The second talks more specifically about people from rural environments, like the one where the speaker grew up
  • The third and shortest stanza presents a particular psychological experience that ties in with stanza two offering a glimpse of what is likely to come from their wintry region, how a frosty wind always seems to blow somewhere in the mind
  • Two lists serving different purposes
  • Catalogues the smells and sensations associated with cities: (Rapid success, busyness, monotony, superficiality overwhelming, chaotic, and fragmented nature of urban life)
  • Repetition of smell revealing how sensory experiences in the city are unappealing, even something as beautiful as tulips are diminished into a not smell reinforcing the idea that City life lacks vibrancy and authenticity
  • Second half shifts to much more descriptive, and nostalgic list of rural images woods, blueberry patches, yards where hens and chickens circle, and violets
  • Evokes a sense of permanence and deep connection, etched into the speaker’s identity
  • Rhythm is slower and more meditative, reflecting the peace and timelessness of rural life. Images are carefully chosen (almost sacred) contrasting with the rushed impersonal tone of the urban section.
  • Juxtaposition of these lists underscores the central theme of the poem, which is that there are fundamental differences between city and rural life
  • Urban life is fleeting, artificial, and disconnected
  • Rural life is enduring, organic, and deeply personal
  • Modulates the rhythm through the use of enjambment and caesura, mirroring the natural ebb and flow of thought
  • Lists of images, all demarcated (limited) by semicolons
  • A layered, cumulative quality
  • As if piecing together impressions to explore the relationship between people and the places they inhabit
  • Reflect and conversational tone
  • Ideas about place and identity seem to unfold organically and naturally
  • Natural rhythm reinforces central idea that identity is shaped by a blend of sensory impression, memories, and connections to place
  • Brewster’s diction is very straightforward to allow for a clear and concise communication
  • Metaphor, Simile, Figurative Language, Sound Patterning are all restrained and understated

Where I Come From

Analysis
  • First line of the second stanza
  • Stress is placed on where expecting the poem and the author to focus on the geographical aspect of her origins
  • Feels as if poem will describe the physical characteristics, landscapes, and details about its location
  • Yet, the stress subtly shifts to where I come from and not others becoming a sense of self, and how her rural upbringing has shaped her personality and worldview
1 / 2 / 3

“ People are made of places. They carry with them / hints of jungles or mountains, a tropic grace / or the cool eyes of sea-gazers.

Analysis
  • Brewster sets out her stall (makes her position very clear) with the metaphor People are made of places, suggests our identities are fashioned by where we grow up, us being the sum of the places we’ve been, not just an incidental part of their history
  • Plosive alliteration “P” subtly suggests the way are inextricably linked, inseparable, while intermingling with one another
  • Short syntax shows the force of this assertion, where she will brook (tolerate) no opposition to her claim
  • The next few lines They carry with them… cool eyes of sea-gazers shows her belief that the connection to place is so deeply ingrained that is physically manifests in people’s demeanour, behaviour and mannerisms
  • Phrase carry with them shows how it's not just memories, but integral, ever-present part of their being, shaping how they move and interact with the world
  • Imagery of tropic grace and cool eyes of sea-gazers shows how these geographical influences are visible in a person’s very essence, making place an inseparable component of identity
  • Positive imagery, linking those who come from the tropics as being elegant, while sea-gazers functions as a metaphor capturing their connection to the sea and the reflective, calm, and expansive qualities that such an environment might instill in them
  • Cool temperature of the sea and sea-breeze changes how coastal people view life, limiting the sunny optimism that warmer places encourage
  • The sea is also paradoxical, always changing yet always the same, thus staring at it gives coastal people a cool, detached wisdom about the nature of existence
  • The relaxed character or way of being in the sunny beautiful outdoors (tropic)
  • The diction hints Brewster imagines this as a subtle expression, not overt, nothing to do with clothing, skin, colour, or any physical feature like that.
  • She’s not suggesting an old sea hand will be a deep person, or a mountain dweller hard, nothing to direct but rather Brewster imagines something ineffable in the way a person might gaze outwards, holding their graceful posture as a sign of their history
  • It asks us to consider the layered complexities of nature which are reflected in people, the qualities of a person felt rather than seen, that one can faintly detect the marks of lived experience
  • The speaker doesn’t tell the reader precisely how such places make people but rather allows the poem to act as an invitation to consider the idea that people are shaped by their surroundings, and asking them to consider how it applies to them and people they know

  • Due to the repetition of the poem’s title, you can almost hear the nostalgia sing from the page
  • The diction woods is repeated twice in the first couple of lines, and a caesura that indents creates a physical partition between urban and rural worlds
  • The indentation in the very first line visually emphasises the shift from the urban to the rural stronger separation between the two worlds

  • Where atmospheres of cities surround, stifle, yet ultimately drop away
  • The shift from the where is placed on the “I” as she draws the distinction between the two types of people, with two main goals:
  • To support and expand on the poem’s opening statement that People are made of places
  • To draw out differences between the city and the countryside
  • Imagery of acres of pine woods; alludes to the area of Chipman, in New Brunswick (where Brewster was born), a logging community, surrounded by forests
  • Acres evokes vast expanses, while implying freedom while pine woods has associations of sweet-smelling freshness, and a sense of freedom
  • The act of carrying woods in their minds shows the omnipresence of nature within their life, thus making a deep impression, while further symbolising the shadowy and secretive regions of the psyche or emotions as it is dense, obscured, leading to city-dwellers, and rural folk to be different
  • The verb carry has connotation of a pride and dignity which are conscious
  • Focus on the minds over the bodies, suggests a sense of intellectual and spiritual superiority
  • The plosive alliteration Blueberry patches in the Burned-out Bush indicating resilience and resourcefulness through the harshness of the conditions
  • Contrasts against the otherwise burned-out and gray landscape offering shocks of blue, to indicate the existence of life, vitality, calmness, and stability even during difficult times
  • The visual imagery of the Blueberry patches offers little explanation causing the reader to question the effect it has on the reader
  • Is it burned out from the sun?
  • It’s sometimes cleared with controlled fires to promote new growth
  • Could also be symbolic of hard-won beauty and survival as it grows out of fire-scarred bush, and thus nature's stubborn attempt and determination to thrive under harsh condition
  • By extension, this is how it shapes the people who live there, forcing them to survive and flourish under difficult circumstance
Effect, style & response
  • The openness of the poem perhaps suggests that People are made of places in idiosyncratic ways, that no two people are alike, even if they come from the same area,
  • Invokes the chaotic yet natural behaviour of nature itself, while also suggesting other factors which shape and form a person

“wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint, / with yards where hens and chickens circle about, / clucking aimlessly; battered schoolhouses/ behind which violets grow.

Analysis
  • The speaker now begins to describe their region in high detail
  • The contrast between the wooden farmhouses and the gleaming chromium-plated buildings, shows a sense of authenticity, timelessness, and simplicity, despite the run down and impoverished nature
  • Also suggests the existence and usages of the farming industry, and multi-generational logging businesses
  • Everyone in the city is always in a rush, yet the rural people just allow life to go on, without any rush
  • Reminds us the beauty that’s left behind despite the dilapidated and rundown nature, reclaiming forgotten niches, and wooden breams showing through decades-old paintwork
  • The subtle alteration to her imagery conveys that the flat, almost-not-smells ceases to exist in this nature
  • Unlike the city life being bustling, busy, and chaotic, rural life reflects with yards where hens and chickens circle about being free, calm, and without rush
  • Life just goes on, with the diction circle about showing a smooth, circular, and non-rigid (like squares) way of life, where everything simply goes
  • Yet it could also symbolises a lack of purpose suggesting perhaps the town and region are adrift due to economic decline
  • This verse causes the crowded trains at rush hour seem lacking movement, as she wrote in a pared down way using as few verbs as possible, so the city felt curiously empty and still
  • The olfactory impressions of fresh pine needles or a hint of lingering woodsmoke from those burnt out bushes
  • Sensory imagery in verse two goes beyond smell; in images of blueberry patches and violets we’re given colour, sweetness, and light
  • Rather than having a square with fountains and regimented row of tulips, it has a harsh condition where buildings are battered (adjective) and weather by wind and snow
  • The delicate violets and by implication the schoolchildren, both take shelter against the elements and thrive despite the bleak environment, showing resilience, and people who survive against the odds
  • Brewster’s language is more kinaesthetic carry, circle, clucking, grow, breaking, blows, open are all words that unlock the stillness of the scene and add a sense of movement
  • This contrast extends to the patterns of sound (alliteration and consonance) whereas the city scene was characterised by thin sibilance, here stronger plosives made with the letters B and P BlueBerry Patches in the Burned out Bush) and guttural C and K “chiCKens cirCle about CluCKing aimlessly
  • Pushes and accentuates the pulse of life that beats at the heart of Brewster’s rural setting
Effect, style & response
  • Again the broadness of in need of paint opens it up to interpretation
  • Is it that the aesthetics in this tight-knit community matter less than they might in a big city?
  • Does it suggest neglect?
  • Is the farming industry in decline here?
  • Is it still loved and used?
  • Or maybe its the fact that urban migration has caused younger generations to abandon rural villages to seek a better, more glamorous life in big cities?
