And the tone will not settle: "due payment" is bookkeeping language, cosmic justice as an invoice, which either deflates the metaphysics into comedy or renders it more sinister — debts fall due whether or not you remember incurring them.

What a strong answer does. Keeps the question double — asked about the roach, meant about the man — and reads "I don't know" as the only honest settlement of it; then presses the syntax: the poem's darkest suggestion, made available but never stated, is that the "former life" is simply the speaker's own earlier life, and the restless present is what it "led to". On that reading line 14 does not change the subject; it answers the question of line 12.

4. "Except I thought I recognised myself." — what, precisely, is being claimed?

The difficulty. The poem's entire payload is delivered through four stacked hedges, and careless readers bulldoze them into "the speaker realises he is the cockroach" — a paraphrase the line was engineered to prevent. Grammatically, the line is not even a sentence of its own: it is a subordinate tail on "I don't know," — the sole exception to a declaration of ignorance.

The hedges, in order. Except: a swerve, conceding one thing rescued from not-knowing — with the bleak consequence that the only certainty on offer is a resemblance to vermin. I thought: past tense and epistemically weak — the writing self reports an impression the present self declines to endorse; by the time we hear of the recognition it is already over, and "I don't know" (present tense) formally outranks it. Recognised: not "saw" or "realised" but a verb of fallible matching — you can recognise wrongly; yet the word also smuggles in intimacy, because recognition presupposes prior acquaintance. You cannot recognise what you have never met: the word hedges the assent while conceding that the face was familiar. Myself, withheld to the final stress: syntax delays the object of recognition to the last possible position, so the poem's whole meaning arrives on its closing beat — where, note, the metre lands its one unhedged commitment.

The competing readings. (i) Full allegorical identification, hedged only for politeness — the reading of most study guides, supported by everything the imagery has built. (ii) A momentary illusion, honestly reported and already disowned — supported by the tense structure and by "Except"'s subordination. (iii) The answer to line 12 — the "former life" was his; the recognition is an admission of guilt, not of kinship. (iv) A deadpan punchline — the mock-solemn form finally tips its hand. What a strong answer does: treats the hedging not as modesty about the claim but as the claim itself — the line asserts exactly as much as this speaker can honestly assert, and its four qualifications are the most precise thing in the poem, not the least. A reading that removes the hedges to get at "the meaning" removes the meaning.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Ten moments chosen because they repay pressure — the famous last line is treated in Cruxes and everywhere else; these are the lines an examiner rarely sees handled well.

1. "Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor." (2) — initial trochee; participle; transferred animation. The metre swerves off the iambic path on "Skirting" exactly as the creature swerves round the obstacle: the first substitution in the poem is mimetic. "Skirting" also carries its social sense — evading, giving a wide berth — planting avoidance in the roach's repertoire twelve lines before the speaker's own avoidances surface. The dust "rode" the floor: passive matter given a jaunty verb of agency, while the genuinely self-propelled creature will end up going nowhere — the poem's first quiet joke about the difference between moving and being moved. The trivially precise detail (a dust ball, observed closely enough to see it drift) is also evidence about the watcher: this is the noticing of a man with nothing else to attend to. Intention and effect: Halligan grounds the allegory-to-come in verifiable small fact, so the reader trusts the eye long before doubting the mind.

2. "At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace" (3) — temporal frame; epistemic hedge; measured adverb. "At first" retrospectively announces a narrative — you only say at first when you know things changed — so deterioration is promised before it begins. "Seemed" is the poem's earliest confession that the creature's inner life is the watcher's construction; "quite" measures the constructed contentment and finds it moderate, faintly disappointing, the adverb of someone grading an experience they do not share. And "he": the third line quietly genders the insect, person-ing it long before line 14 admits why. Satisfaction, in this poem, is the state that exists only in report — never dramatised, only "seemed". Intention and effect: the reader is trained from the outset to read every subsequent mental-state word as speculation, which is what makes the unhedged "looked uncertain" of line 11 so loud.

3. "to trace / A path between the wainscot and the door," (3–4) — enjambment; verb connotation; bounded interval. "Trace" is not "choose" or "make": you trace a line that already exists, following a pre-drawn route — contentment defined at once as obedience to a given track. The enjambment sends the verb over the line-end to find its object, a small performance of path-following. The track runs "between the wainscot and the door": two fixed architectural limits, a life defined by its terminals — and "wainscot" is the traditional lodging of vermin in English domestic writing, an old-literary word that houses the roach in a long tradition of skirting-board lives. The path is real but closed: back and forth inside someone else's architecture. Intention and effect: purpose is introduced already ironised — the reader sees limits where the creature "seemed" to see satisfaction, an irony that will be turned on the speaker himself.

4. "But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings," (5) — conjunction pivot; register drop; oxymoronic geometry. "But" is the poem's first turn — a micro-volta at line 5, well before the form's appointed one, as if the poem cannot wait to start failing. "Jog" is superb comic casting: the leisure-exercise verb, aimless by design (jogging is motion whose destination is its starting point), demoting the creature's crisis to a fitness routine. "Crooked rings" is a geometry that fails twice — a ring returns you to where you began, and these rings are not even true circles. Meanwhile the metre stays perfectly iambic: the line about crookedness scans dead straight, the verse withholding its sympathy — disorder has reached the creature but not yet the poem. Intention and effect: Halligan lets aimlessness arrive in comic dress so that its later escalation ("worsened") catches the reader having laughed at symptoms.

5. "Circling the rusty table leg and back," (6) — initial trochee; synecdoche; floor-level perspective. The trochee makes the line pivot at its head — it starts by turning. The orbit has now shrunk to a single point of reference, and the point is telling: not the table but the "table leg", furniture seen from the floor, the poem's camera lowered to insect height eight lines before the speaker admits to sharing the view. "Rusty" puts corrosion at the centre of the creature's circuit — it orbits decay — and "and back" hangs off the line like the futile return leg it describes, syntax retracing its own steps. Intention and effect: the reader is brought physically down to the roach's scale, so the final identification has been rehearsed by perspective long before it is stated.

6. "And flipping right over to scratch his wings —" (7) — mid-line trochee; colloquial intensifier; suspended dash. The rhythm flips with the creature: "RIGHT O-ver" jams two stresses together and inverts the foot, the poem's one perfectly mimetic substitution. "Right over" is spoken register — the phrase you would use of a toddler or a beetle, affectionate, faintly amused — the watcher's voice warming as his subject loses dignity. The detail everyone forgets: wings. The creature has flight available and spends the poem on its back on the floor, scratching them — capacity unused, escape technically possible and never taken, which is as close as the poem comes to naming the speaker's own situation. The dash then suspends the line mid-air — the roach upended, the syntax withholding interpretation for a beat. Intention and effect: comedy and diagnosis arrive fused; the reader smiles at the tumble and inherits the image of unused wings.

7. "As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness" (8–9) — simile; medical register; bathetic enjambment. "As if" flags the diagnosis as invention even while committing to it — the poem's most honest two words until "I don't know". "Victim" converts behaviour into affliction: the creature no longer acts but suffers, passive before its own movements. "A mild attack / Of—" is engineered suspense: the line-break holds open the grave possibilities (heart, panic, seizure) and pays off with restlessness — bathos that deflates and, in deflating, smuggles the medical frame past the reader's defences. The oxymoronic pressure in "mild attack" (attacks are not mild; mildness does not attack) captures precisely the low-grade, chronic, undramatic quality of the suffering at issue. Intention and effect: Halligan makes the reader laugh at the anticlimax and then discover the laughter has ratified a clinical account of the speaker's own state.

8. "that worsened over time." (9) — prognosis diction; end-stop; double time-scale. Three flat words close the octave with a chart-note: not an event but a course, the tense of chronic illness. The phrase quietly explodes the poem's realism — the vigil has lasted minutes, yet "over time" speaks of a longer duration than any cockroach-watching session contains: two clocks are superimposed, the insect's afternoon and the man's years, and the sentence only makes literal sense on the second clock. This is the poem's first unguarded autobiographical leak, eight lines before "myself". The full stop then seals the octave — the only end-stopped period since line 2 — closing the case-file section of the poem. Intention and effect: the reader registers, perhaps subliminally, that the diagnosis has outgrown its patient, and starts looking for the real one.

9. "After a while, he climbed an open shelf" (10) — initial trochee; vague duration; polysemous adjective. "After a while" is the diction of boredom — unmeasured time, the watcher no longer counting — and its trochee tips the line forward into the poem's final movement. "Climbed" introduces the vertical for the first time: after ten lines of floor-plane wandering, ascent — the allegory's career move, aspiration itself. But the summit is "an open shelf": open as in exposed (no cover, a predator's sightline), open as in available (nothing yet stored), open as in empty. The reward for the poem's one upward effort is a bare board. Every meaning of "open" converges on vacancy. Intention and effect: the reader receives the poem's bleakest structural irony — that climbing changes the view but not the condition — one line before it is enacted in "And stopped."

10. "A former life had led to? I don't know," (13) — mid-line interrogative; tense shift; refused full stop. The question mark falls inside the line, mid-stride, second of the sestet's two syntactic stumbles — and what follows is the poem's only present-tense main verb. Everything else is narrated from afterwards; "I don't know" is spoken now, the single thing the writing self will assert in its own moment, and it is a disclaimer. The causality of the question deserves pressure: the life "had led to" the crime — living itself as the road to the offence, guilt accumulated by trajectory rather than act. And the admission is not even granted a full stop: a comma, and the sentence leans into "Except" — ignorance immediately qualified, the poem's entire self-knowledge suspended from a confession of not-knowing. Intention and effect: the reader experiences the collapse of the poem's one metaphysical structure in real time, and is handed the question the speaker drops.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist. The lens under which the poem gives most, because its deepest ironies are structural: the couplet that never arrives after an octave that promised one; the sestet whose second tercet comes back out of order (EGF); the pentameter that ticks undisturbed through "And stopped."; the all-full rhymes polishing the surface of a breakdown; the seven-line sentence enjambing across the form's main seam at "attack / Of restlessness". Formalism sees the poem's true drama — a mind keeping perfect table manners while getting lost — enacted in verse-machinery rather than stated. What it flattens: the "I". Formalism can describe the hedges of line 14 as devices but has nothing to say about why a person hedges; it also brackets the karmic material, which is doing real work, as mere "content".

Psychoanalytic. Makes visible that the poem is a study in projection and displacement: the speaker deposits his own interior into a creature ("seemed quite satisfied", "looked uncertain") and then is ambushed by it — "Except I thought I recognised myself" is a textbook return of the repressed, the disowned self met as an other, and uncanny precisely because half-familiar ("recognised"). The choice of host matters: vermin, the culturally abject, the thing flinched from — self-disgust selects the one creature the self can safely despise, and the recognition therefore carries a charge of shame no neutral animal could deliver. What it flattens: the comedy, which it must read as defence; and the poem's epistemological scruple, which it converts into symptom — "I don't know" becomes resistance rather than honesty, and the reading starts diagnosing the patient instead of the poem.

Ecocritical. Makes visible what every other reading uses without noticing: the actual insect. What the speaker pathologises as "restlessness" is ordinary cockroach behaviour — exploration, grooming, edge-following; the disorder exists in the watching mind, not the watched body, and the poem half-knows it ("As if"). Ecocriticism catches the anthropomorphic machinery in the act — "he" from line 3, human verbs throughout — and names the poem's method for what it is: a colonisation of animal life by human meaning, in which the creature is never itself, only a mirror. Yet the lens also credits the poem's countercurrent: "giant" grants scale, "he" grants person-hood, and the final line levels the hierarchy — the human does not stoop to the insect but finds himself already there. What it flattens: the poem's actual interest, which is unashamedly the human; an ecocritical reading done stubbornly ends up reviewing the poem for a moral failure it openly performs and confesses.

Marxist / materialist. Makes visible the material preconditions nobody in the poem mentions: a man with time to watch an insect at length is a man released from labour — the vigil presupposes leisure, or unemployment, or expatriate vacancy, and the shabby interior ("dust", "rusty") is a material environment being read as a metaphysical one. Sharpest of all, the lens notices that when the speaker reaches for cosmic justice he can only imagine it as an economy — "due payment", a debt falling due — and that the roach "jogs", the leisure-exercise verb of the comfortable classes pasted onto subsistence movement. Even this poem's transcendence is denominated in money. What it flattens: the interiority; a strictly materialist account has to treat the epistemic drama — "seemed", "I don't know", "thought" — as superstructure, and so misses that the poem's subject is consciousness, whatever its economic base.

Reader-response. Makes visible that the poem's ending is completed in the reader or not at all. "I don't know" hands the metaphysical question across the page; the four hedges of line 14 leave a gap exactly reader-shaped — the poem never says and so are you, but the definite-article title's fable-promise, the universalising sonnet form and the pointed smallness of the occasion all pressure the reader into extending "myself" to themselves. The reader's own flinch at cockroaches is the poem's imported energy: revulsion converting to recognition happens in us, unstated. What it flattens: the historical and biographical specificity of the one speaker the poem actually has; and it licenses precisely the inflation ("this is all of us, the human condition") that the poem's deadpan holds at arm's length.

Postcolonial / historicist. Makes visible the direction of borrowing: a Western observer, reportedly in Buddhist Southeast Asia, reaches for karmic categories — "due payment", "A former life" — as a passing hypothesis for a private malaise, tries the doctrine on and shrugs it off within two lines ("I don't know"). The lens asks who gets to use whose metaphysics as metaphor, and notices that the poem's single room, with no street, no city, no named country, is legible as the expatriate's insulated bubble — the "outside" world present only as a system of ideas to be sampled. In the Cambodian frame the notes supply, "some vicious crime" and undischarged guilt acquire a historical shadow. But the caveat is structural: the poem names none of this. No place, no religion, no history appears in the text; the entire postcolonial reading rides on thinly documented paratext, and an exam answer must present it as context brought to the poem, not found in it. What it flattens: the possibility that the karmic question is doing exactly what it appears to do — expressing, in borrowed but seriously entertained terms, a guilt that has no local address.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

  1. The existential allegory (the standard reading). The roach's trajectory — purpose, restlessness, arrest — maps human aimlessness; the poem universalises through smallness. Evidence: the geometry's collapse (path → rings → stop); "uncertain where to go"; the fable-promising title. Weakness: it flattens the hedges — the poem says "myself", once, four qualifications deep, and never "ourselves"; read as universal statement it becomes the grand, solemn poem its deadpan was built to avoid.
  1. The clinical reading. The poem describes a psychological condition — anxiety or depression — in deliberate medical language: pacing, agitation ("a mild attack"), chronicity ("worsened over time"), psychomotor arrest ("And stopped."), anhedonia at the summit. Evidence: the sustained prognosis lexis; the double time-scale of line 9; the vigil itself as symptom. Weakness: the whole diagnosis sits inside "As if" — a simile, flagged as the watcher's invention; and the karmic question belongs to a different explanatory world the clinical frame cannot absorb.
  1. The karmic confession. The metaphysics is meant: the speaker half-believes his condition is "due payment", and line 14 answers line 12 — the "former life" is his own past, the recognition an admission of guilt. Evidence: "due payment", "vicious crime", the reversed causality of "had led to"; "I don't know" (not no); "Except" grammatically rescuing one certainty from the ignorance. Weakness: the tone will not hold still — "due payment" is bookkeeping comedy as much as doctrine; and the poem's only stated belief is unbelief ("I don't know").
  1. The mock-heroic comedy. The poem is a sustained joke: the grandest lyric form handed to vermin, "giant" inflation, the bathos of "a mild attack / Of restlessness", a punchline curtain-line. Evidence: the engineered anticlimax of the 8–9 enjambment; "jog"; the deadpan timing of 14. Weakness: it cannot account for the poem's residue — why "worsened over time" and "And stopped." are not funny, and why the last line, if a punchline, fails to release its tension rather than doubling it.
  1. The life-course allegory. The poem compresses a biography: the given track of youth ("trace / A path" between fixed limits), the crooked circling of the middle years, the climb, the summit that turns out bare, the arrest. Evidence: the sequenced time-markers ("At first", "soon", "over time", "After a while") — a lifetime's connectives spent in minutes; "climbed" as aspiration. Weakness: point-for-point mapping is mechanical and unfalsifiable (what is the dust? the table leg?); the poem offers a trajectory-shape, not a key, and readings that allegorise every noun end up writing their own poem.
  1. The meta-poem. The true subject is interpretation itself: a mind watching itself plant meaning in a neutral creature, with "trace" as the writer's own line-making and the sonnet failing to conclude as the essay-of-the-self fails to conclude. Evidence: the epistemic verb-chain ("watched, seemed, As if, looked, don't know, thought, recognised"); the dropped hedge at line 11; the confession that recognition, not observation, was the vigil's product. Weakness: nothing in the lexis names writing or reading; pushed hard, the reading turns a poem of felt unease into a seminar on epistemology — precisely the coldness the deadpan voice never has.
REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

1

”I watched a giant cockroach start to pace,”

Analysis
  • Line opens with first person pronoun “I”
  • Immediate and direct, places the speaker in the moment, lack of distancing suggests a connection between the cockroach and the speaker.
  • The speaker watched [watching] the cockroach implies sustained and deliberate attention rather than glancing, inviting the reader to question why the speaker chooses to watch a cockroach.
  • The intentionalness of this could hint towards the speaker’s boredom, drawing him towards a conventionally unattractive creature, showcasing the pointlessness of his life.
  • Hyperbolisation of the cockroach being giant captures the reader's attention, its size grants it a presence and allows it to be the centre of attention in a poem discussing its actions.
  • Otherwise, the hyperbolisation suggests the speaker’s unreliability, suggesting an unstable period of time.
  • Beginning to pace, the poet hints towards the cockroach's anxious restlessness, hinting towards its inevitable restlessness.
  • Subtly anthropomorphic as pacing is inherently a human quality, drawing a connection between humans and the insect.
2

”Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor.”

Analysis
  • Diction in skirting suggests agility and movement, almost in a lively manner. Continuation from previous line + enjambment suggests how the cockroach’s movement cannot be contained.
  • Skirting also connotes avoidance, possibly of tasks till it snowballs at the end of the poem where the speaker is forced to confront what they avoid.
  • Personification of dust riding the floor as if it is drifting like it’s alive. As the dust moves, it suggests purpose as if it has a place to be, giving it a direction the cockroach doesn’t possess.
  • The dust cumulates on the floor, suggesting the unkempt state of the room, contrasting the even and tidy form of a sonnet.
  • Neglected room establishes atmosphere and the speaker’s inner state
3 / 4

”At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace” / A path between the wainscot and the door,

Analysis
  • Temporal: At first, introduces a narrative progression of the cockroach's journey.
  • The cockroach begins with a purpose, a defined path between two fixed points. As the poem progresses, the purpose deteriorates, the temporal verb indicates the baseline of where the cockroach begins.
  • The verb seemed introduces an uncertainty of the speaker not being able to identify the cockroach’s internal state, both reflecting his own uncertainty and permits the reader to recognise that a person will likely not fully understand another’s thoughts.
  • Introduces doubt from the start, the satisfaction may not be real, only apparent.
  • Tracing feels mechanical, as if the cockroach has a path designated to it from the beginning, paralleling the idea of humans having a set purpose by their peers or parents, further undermining the satisfaction the cockroach experiences. It also indicates the mindless motions the cockroach experiences rather than living.
  • At first, the cockroach has a defined path between the wainscot and the door, suggesting defined limits, representing the safe parameters of early adulthood as people chase goals they’ve set.
  • The intentions of the cockroach is evident, contrasting the restlessness and uncertainty further on
  • Wainscot: A usually paneled wooden lining of an interior wall
5 / 6

”But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings,” / Circling the rusty table leg and back,

Analysis
  • But indicates a flaw or a hiccup in a journey, suggesting a change between the previous certainty and the restlessness creeping into the cockroach’s motions.
  • Diction of crooked indicates a lapse in judgement and wobbliness, as if the cockroach is uncertain of which path to continue upon. The path is no longer laid out right in front of him, paralleling the experience of adults as they struggle to grasp the complexities of life.
  • Rings connote a circular path, indicating purposeless movement. The straight line satisfaction in early life dissolves into aimless circling, paralleling a midlife crisis.
  • Circling a table leg suggests how the cockroach is wound about a point rather than travelling in large circles to expand its knowledge. He refuses to leave a spot where safety is guaranteed, illustrating his own entrapment with no progress.
  • Circularness of the path seems to mimic a spiral, hinting towards the mental degradation of the speaker.
  • The rusty table leg implies the world the cockroach inhabits is degraded and neglected, also underlining the passing of time.
7

”And flipping right over to scratch his wings —“

Analysis
  • The physical action of the cockroach rolling onto its back suggests a momentary loss of control and vulnerability, paralleling a human’s willingness to sacrifice for momentary pleasure.
  • On the contrary, the cockroach flipping indicates a total loss of footing and ending up on its back captures his directionless journey.
  • Loss of composure seems undignified with em dash suspending the moment before explanation arrives.
  • Rhythm mirrors stumbles as Halligan inserts a trochee (right o-ver) that breaks the iambic pattern, allowing the line to lurch forward and mimic the action of the cockroach.
  • Dash permits pause before interpretation in the following line.
8 / 9

”As if the victim of a mild attack” / Of restlessness that worsened over time.

Analysis
  • Simile comparing the cockroach to a victim of its own behaviour. He’s passive rather than an active agent of harm and suffering beyond something beyond its control.
  • The cockroach falls prey into life’s pointless wander, unable to comprehend and therefore panicking till restlessness makes it worse.
  • Halligan captures the psychological impact of aimless wandering, suggesting a person’s panic from a lack of work done escalates from their urge to complete a task and reach a goal.
  • Use of victim suggests the cockroach is not choosing to behave erratically but rather suffering. This hints towards the speaker’s own emotions, being involuntarily consumed by existential crisis.
  • Enjambment from line 8 continues the idea, running over the stanza boundary between octave and sestet while ignoring the traditional volta, disrupting the rigid structure of a sonnet.
  • His condition worsened over time, a clinical and ordered interpretation towards a disorderly state. This implies restlessness is a condition deteriorating the cockroach where the passage of time exacerbates rather than heals.
10 / 11

”After a while, he climbed an open shelf” / And stopped. he looked uncertain where to go

Analysis
  • After a while indicates the passing of time and the cockroach aging
  • Cockroach has achieved something, reaching the metaphorical peak (top of the shelf) where the achievement brings not satisfaction but bewilderment.
  • Full stop indicates finality of previous movement, almost anticlimactic in the sense that the cockroach is still uncertain
  • The open shelf suggests possibility and exposure simultaneously where the cockroach decides his own path and there are no walls to guide him. Him and the speaker are confronted with freedom and find it paralysing.
  • The caesura after stopped pauses the reader and allows the reader to feel the silence, similar to the lack of direction the speaker feels. It formally enacts the epiphany of emptiness.
12 / 13

”Was this due payment for some vicious crime” / A former life had led to? I don’t know,

Analysis
  • Alludes to karma + reincarnation where the speaker ponders upon philosophical questions reaching beyond the cockroach. The speaker grasps at unrealistic strings to explain his confusion, implying the total degradation of his mentality.
  • Vicious crime introduces guilt where the speaker wonders if their own purposelessness is a punishment where all other answers have run dry, leading to self blame.
  • The answer of I don’t know brings the poem out of detached observation and serves as a direct link between the cockroach and the speaker.
  • The flat, simple and immediate answer suggests the speaker has been pondering for an extended period of time and reached the same conclusion and how the grand question deserves no grand answer. The speaker refuses to pretend to certainty he doesn’t possess.
14

”Except I thought I recognised myself.”

Analysis
  • The volta is situated at the end of the poem where the speaker realises he is the cockroach and the allegory completes itself. Despite his newfound self awareness, the speaker remains cautious and uncertain with thought rather than knew.
  • The final line is the poem’s entire point where the speaker recognises his own restless and aimless journey, realising his life trajectory took the same directionless path as a cockroach. The reader is invited to extend this further as a part of their lives. The poem universalises this concept through a cockroach, diminishing the reader’s ego.
  • The word recognised implies the speaker affirming a suspicion or like the self was meant to be found there.
  • The final line transforms the detached observation of the speaker into a confession of his own aimlessness ending with honesty rather than resolution.
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the other six

Comparison hooks

With "Love Armed" (Aphra Behn). Link: both poems give an inner state a body and watch it act — Behn enthrones desire as an armed tyrant, Halligan lodges restlessness in a roach — and both use immaculate formal poise to contain disorderly feeling. Shared technique: emblem-making (title as label for a staged figure) and the vocabulary of victimhood — each speaker casts himself as the injured party of his own emotion. Difference: Behn's harm has agents and a politics — the beloved's eyes arm the god, and the speaker's griefs are conscripted — so blame flows outward; Halligan's harm has no perpetrator at all, and the poem ends by suspecting the victim.

With "A Different History" (Sujata Bhatt). Link: both reach for South and Southeast Asian religious frames — transmigrating gods and sacred books in Bhatt, karmic debt and rebirth in Halligan — and both end without settling the questions those frames raise. Shared technique: the structural question — each poem's climax is interrogative, and the refusal to answer is the meaning. Difference: Bhatt's karma is collective and historical, asking how a people's tongue comes to love the conqueror's language; Halligan's is rigorously private, one man's afternoon — her unanswered question indicts history, his indicts (perhaps) himself.

With "The Chimney Sweeper" (Blake). Link: a small blackened creature moving through domestic architecture becomes legible as a condition its own perspective cannot name — the sweep inside the chimneys and coffin-dream, the roach on its wainscot track — and both poems run on the gap between what the figure knows and what the reader sees. Shared technique: dramatic irony from a limited viewpoint, plus confinement imagery doing symbolic work. Difference: Blake's irony indicts institutions — Church, parents, the trade in children — and demands the reader's outrage; Halligan's irony has no culprit to indict but the self, and asks for nothing louder than a wince.

With "Where I Come From" (Elizabeth Brewster). Link: both poems read interiors as minds — Brewster's claim that people are composed of their places, Halligan's dusty, rusting room externalising its watcher's state before he admits to having one. Shared technique: the inventory of particulars (her smells and door-yards; his dust-ball, wainscot, table leg, shelf) trusted to do the psychological work unstated. Difference: Brewster affirms formation — place composes a self that can be traced home; Halligan's room is placeless and anonymous, and the self it discloses arrives only as a hedged glimpse: her poem believes in origins, his doubts even recognition.

With "Report to Wordsworth" (Boey Kim Cheng). Link: the set's two subverted sonnets — Boey files an environmental elegy through the machinery of the Romantic sonnet of address; Halligan hands the love-lyric's form to vermin — both turning an inherited structure against its own tradition of consolation. Shared technique: sonnet subversion with a suppressed turn — in both, the sestet deepens rather than resolves the octave's trouble, and the close is diminuendo, not couplet-confidence. Difference: Boey's poem is public and apostrophic, petitioning a dead poet about a dying planet; Halligan's has no addressee at all — the largest possible audience versus a man talking himself into one admission.

With "Lament" (Gillian Clarke). Link: animals bearing human meaning — but pointed in opposite directions: Clarke's oil-choked, war-ruined creatures are real casualties of human action, mourned outward in a litany; Halligan's roach is perfectly fine — the suffering is projected onto it by the only casualty in the room. Shared technique: creaturely imagery carried by ritual registers — Clarke's elegiac dedications, Halligan's karmic audit of payment and crime. Difference: in "Lament" the grief is certain and the guilt collective; in "The Cockroach" both are hedged and private — Clarke writes the animal as victim of us, Halligan the animal as mirror of me, and the ethical weather of the two poems differs accordingly: mourning versus misgiving.

WRITING ABOUT IT

Writing About It

Turning the analysis into paragraphs that score

Writing about it

Model paragraph 1 — on the withheld couplet. Halligan's quietest structural decision is to promise a couplet and then withhold it. Two cross-rhymed quatrains ("pace/trace", "floor/door") set the English sonnet's template, so the ear expects the poem to close with a clinching pair; instead the sestet turns Italian and ends E-G-F, so that the final line, "Except I thought I recognised myself", must reach four lines back to "an open shelf" for its rhyme. The couplet is the English sonnet's gesture of confidence — two lines snapping shut on a summarising truth — and confidence is what this speaker cannot honestly perform. Closure therefore arrives at the edge of audibility: technically present, practically lost, the acoustic equivalent of "I thought I recognised". The pairing is also semantic: "myself" chimes with "shelf", binding the self to the bare ledge where movement stopped. A poem about a creature "uncertain where to go" closes in a form that cannot quite find its own way home — structure failing in precise sympathy with its subject.

Model paragraph 2 — on the diagnosis. The poem's central account of its creature arrives as a joke that turns clinical. The line-break in "As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness" is engineered for bathos: "a mild attack" raises the grave medical possibilities, and the enjambment suspends the reader for a beat before paying off with mere restlessness. But the comedy carries serious cargo. "Victim" renders the creature passive, suffering a condition rather than choosing behaviour; "mild… worsened over time" is the tense of prognosis, chronic illness established under the laughter — and the duration it implies belongs to the watcher's years, not the insect's afternoon. Crucially, the whole diagnosis is governed by "As if": the speaker flags his reading as invention even while committing to it, so the medicalised despair belongs, on the poem's own evidence, to the watcher rather than the watched. The sentence meanwhile pours across the octave–sestet seam, momentum overriding the form's appointed pause: restlessness has become not the poem's subject but its syntax.

Three sentence-patterns that do the most work:

  1. The truer-verb pattern: "The [device] does not [expected effect] so much as [truer effect]…" — e.g. "The final rhyme does not resolve the poem so much as file it away, 'myself' reaching four lines back to 'shelf'." Forces analysis past the first idea.
  2. The split-level concession: "Although the [one layer] stays regular, the [other layer] breaks…" — e.g. "Although the pentameter ticks straight through 'And stopped.', the syntax halts dead." This poem's signature effects all live in the gap between orderly and disorderly layers; this sentence-shape finds them.
  3. The precision-of-degree claim: "The claim is not that…, only that…" — e.g. "The claim is not that the speaker is the cockroach, only that he 'thought' he 'recognised' himself — and the distance between those verbs is the poem's subject." Protects you from over-reading while still asserting.

Three phrases to avoid:

  1. "This shows that…" — connective without content; replace with a verb that does the work: concedes, withholds, defers, plants, smuggles, ratifies.
  2. "…to engage the reader" / "makes the reader want to read on" — empty circuitry that would be equally true of any competent line; state instead what the device does to expectation, voice or pace.
  3. "The cockroach symbolises all humans" — bulldozes the poem's four hedges and its singular "myself"; write about the speaker's hedged recognition and let the universal remain the reader's inference — which is where the poem deliberately left it.
EXAM PRACTICE

Exam Practice

Questions, plans, and the marginal gains

Exam practice

Question 1. How does Halligan vividly convey the speaker's state of mind through his description of the cockroach?

  • Thesis: the poem never describes the speaker directly; his state of mind leaks entirely through how he watches — what he notices, what he plants, and what his sentences do — so the "description" is a self-portrait executed in insect.
  • Point 1 — the planting verbs: "seemed quite satisfied", "As if the victim", "looked uncertain": mental states are all the watcher's constructions, and the hedges thin as the poem proceeds until an insect's interior is stated as fact — projection completing itself in grammar.
  • Point 2 — the collapsing geometry: "trace / A path" → "crooked rings" → "Circling" → "And stopped.": the movement degrades from line to orbit to point, while the octave's single seven-line sentence enacts the restlessness and the sestet's fractured syntax enacts the arrest.
  • Point 3 — the leak of scale: "a mild attack / Of restlessness that worsened over time" — bathetic enjambment and clinical prognosis whose time-span ("over time", "After a while") outgrows any insect vigil: two clocks superimposed, the diagnosis visibly transferring to the diagnostician before "I thought I recognised myself".
  • Counter-move: concede the comic register ("jog", "flipping right over") and argue it is load-bearing — deadpan is the only voice in which this speaker could confess without self-pity, so the humour is evidence of the state of mind, not relief from it.
  • Conclusion: the vividness is cumulative and structural: by the final line the reader has inhabited the watcher's mind for thirteen lines without being told a single fact about him — which is why the four-times-hedged recognition lands as certainty.

Question 2. Explore the ways in which Halligan makes the ending of "The Cockroach" (lines 10–14) so quietly unsettling.

  • Thesis: the ending unsettles by withholding — the couplet, the answer, the assertion — so that the poem closes on technically resolved form and completely unresolved meaning.
  • Point 1 — the hinge: "an open shelf / And stopped.": enjambment tips the climb over the line-end onto the poem's only mid-line full stop; the pentameter ticks straight through the arrest, the world's pulse indifferent to the creature's paralysis; "He looked uncertain where to go" then reads a mind into the insect without any hedge at all.
  • Point 2 — the metaphysics raised and dropped: "Was this due payment for some vicious crime / A former life had led to?" — karma phrased as bookkeeping, the line-break falling between crime and life like the gap between incarnations; answered by the poem's only present-tense verb, "I don't know", which is not even granted a full stop.
  • Point 3 — the four-hedged disclosure: "Except I thought I recognised myself" — subordinate to the ignorance it excepts itself from, past-tense, fallible verb, object withheld to the final stress; the rhyme reaching four lines back to "shelf", closure at the edge of audibility.
  • Counter-move: address the punchline reading — the line has deadpan comic timing — and fold it in: the joke-shape without a released laugh is precisely what unsettles; the tension the couplet would have discharged is left in the room.
  • Conclusion: the ending's power is its refusal of scale: the largest recognition in the poem is made in the smallest available voice, and the reader is left holding the enlargement the speaker declined to perform.

Examiner's edge

  1. Name the withheld couplet, not just the scheme. ABAB CDCD EFGEGF is the fact; the top-band move is what it means: two Shakespearean quatrains promise EFEF GG, and the couplet — the form's gesture of confident summary — never comes.
  2. Get line 11 right. It does not break the metre; it is five clean iambs around the poem's only mid-line full stop. Distinguishing caesura (syntactic break) from substitution (metrical break) — and noticing the pentameter ticking through the arrest — separates you from every answer repeating "iambic pentameter except line 11".
  3. "I don't know" is the poem's only present-tense main verb. Everything else, including the recognition, is narrated from afterwards; the one thing the speaker asserts in his own now is ignorance. Cheap to deploy, devastating in effect.
  4. The poem is one unbroken stanza. Octave and sestet exist in the rhymes, not on the page — never write "in the second stanza"; write "at the form's buried seam, which the syntax pours straight across".
  5. Every rhyme is full. No pararhyme anywhere: disorder never reaches the poem's local finish, only its large structures — outward polish over structural lostness, which is also the speaker.
  6. Use the rhyme-distances. Quatrain partners sit two lines apart; the sestet's drift to three, two and four — with "myself" waiting longest, and pairing with "shelf", the site of arrest, while "time" pairs with "crime" — is precise, quotable architecture.
  7. Quote "As if" whenever you claim the roach suffers. The diagnosis is the watcher's simile, flagged as such; answers that write "the cockroach is anxious" as fact have missed the poem's grammar of projection.
  8. Track the pronouns. "He", not "it", from line 3 — personification begins eleven lines before recognition; first word "I", last word "myself"; the "I" brackets the poem and finally absorbs the "he".
  9. Date and biography discipline. First collected in Utopia (2009); already in print by 2005 (Songs of Ourselves); born 1964. Do not write "published 1999" (that is Blossom Street, a different book) or "written in Cambodia in 2009" (impossible given 2005). Cambodia, the Cambodia Daily and Buddhist study are reported but thinly documented — frame them as context, cautiously.
  10. Keep Kafka, Camus and Cambodia outside the text. The karmic lexis ("due payment", "A former life") is in the poem; Kafka, archy and mehitabel, absurdism and the genocide are frames brought to it. Saying which is which — and arguing from the poem's smallness and deadpan rather than inflating it — is the single clearest marker of a first-rate answer.
EDITORIAL NOTES

Editorial Notes

Text checks and corrections to the source notes

Text check

The fourteen-line text used by the site and the notes is sound: it matches the text as printed in the Cambridge anthology Songs of Ourselves Volume 1, and every line checked against independent sources agrees ("rode the floor", "wainscot", "jog in crooked rings", "mild attack", "due payment", "vicious crime", "recognised" with British spelling). One transcription slip inside the notes' line-by-line table: line 11 is quoted there as "And stopped. he looked uncertain where to go" — lowercase "he", missing final full stop. The correct reading is "And stopped. He looked uncertain where to go." The dash ending line 7 appears variously as en and em dash across the notes; the anthology prints a dash, and nothing hangs on its width.

The date is not sound, and the chapter cover is wrong. The site prints "date": "1999" (in src/content/06-the-cockroach.json). No source dates this poem to 1999. What is documented: Halligan's individual poems appeared in the Times Literary Supplement between 1998 and 2006; the poem was in print by 2005 at the latest, because it is in Songs of Ourselves Volume 1 (the Cambridge anthology, published 2005 — the very book this syllabus sets); and it was first collected in Halligan's volume Utopia (2009). The "1999" circulating in study notes is the publication year of Blossom Street, Halligan's first collection — a different book, with no evidence this poem was in it. The cover should read 2009 (first collected in Utopia; in print by 2005), or simply "2009" if one date is required. Note also that the widely repeated claim that Halligan "wrote the poem in 2009 in Cambodia" cannot be right either: a poem anthologised in 2005 was not written in 2009. Composition date is undocumented; "before 2005" is all that can be said.

Biography, verified: Kevin Halligan, born 1964, Canadian poet and writer — that much is solid. Birth in Toronto, long periods living in England, and a period in Asia (usually given as Cambodia, sometimes specifically Phnom Penh) during which the poem is said to have been written are consistently reported across study sources but thinly documented; Wikipedia's stub records only the birth year, the TLS publications and the association with Utopia. The claims that he worked for the Cambodia Daily and studied Buddhist theology there circulate in teaching materials with no traceable primary source — treat both as uncertain. Collections: Blossom Street (1999), The Belfast of the North (2005), Utopia (2009).

Gaps and corrections

  1. The date is wrong on the cover and contradicted inside the site's own context panel. The cover says 1999; the context paragraph says he "was living in Cambodia when this poem was published in 2009". Both cannot be true, and neither is quite right (see Text check). Fix the cover to 2009; fix the context sentence to "first collected in Utopia (2009); already in print by 2005".
  2. The notes give three incompatible rhyme schemes, and all three are wrong. The letters pencilled against the poem text read ABAB CDCD EFGEFG; the structure notes say the sestet is "Italian influenced EFGEFG"; the drafted essay says "ABAB CDC EFEF GG" (thirteen letters, and a phantom couplet). The actual scheme, worked line by line below, is ABAB CDCD EFGEGF — there is no couplet, and the sestet's second tercet inverts. The essay's phrase "the closing couple[t], 'Except I thought I recognised myself'" applies couplet-language to a single unrhymed-with-its-neighbour line.
  3. "Iambic pentameter with the exception of line 11" is false. Line 11 — "And stopped. He looked uncertain where to go." — is one of the most metrically regular lines in the poem: five clean iambs. What breaks in line 11 is syntax (the poem's only mid-line full stop, after two syllables), not metre. The genuine metrical substitutions are elsewhere: initial trochees in lines 2, 6 and 10, a mid-line trochee in line 7, pyrrhic feet in 8 and 9, spondaic pressure in 12. Conflating caesura with metrical disruption is the single most common error in circulating guides on this poem (some also call it "a Petrarchan sonnet", which the cross-rhymed ABAB CDCD octave rules out).
  4. "Smooth enjambment" in lines 1–4 overstates. Lines 1 and 2 are end-stopped (comma, full stop). The only enjambment in the first quatrain is "to trace / A path" (3–4). The octave's real fluency comes from having no internal punctuation at all, not from run-on lines.
  5. The dust contrast is backwards. The notes say the drifting dust has "a direction the cockroach doesn't possess". At line 2 the cockroach still has direction (it is tracing a path); what the dust lacks is agency — it "rode the floor", passively carried, while the roach propels itself. The contrast the poem sets up is self-propulsion versus drift, and its irony is that the self-propelled creature ends up no better directed than the dust.
  6. "Giant" as evidence of an unreliable narrator is an overclaim. If the Asian setting is real, "giant" is close to reportage — tropical cockroaches are genuinely large. The word does mock-heroic work (magnifying the creature to sonnet-worthy scale) without needing the machinery of narrative unreliability.
  7. The volta claims are scattered rather than argued. Different parts of the notes place the turn at 8–9 ("traditional"), at 12 ("a clear volta"), and at the final word ("displaced volta"). These need adjudicating, not accumulating; the adjudication is in Cruxes below.
  8. The Cambodia context panel over-reaches. "By 2009, Cambodia was a functioning democracy" is at best contestable (Hun Sen's Cambodia is standardly described as electoral authoritarianism), and "Halligan was confronted daily with questions about guilt, fate, suffering" is invented interiority. More importantly, the poem itself names no country, no war, no religion: the post-genocide frame is context around the poem, not evidence in it, and an answer that treats it as textual will lose marks for imported material.
  9. Kafka and Marquis are presented as things the poem "references". There is no verbal echo of either. The karmic language ("due payment", "A former life") is in the text; Kafka and archy and mehitabel are frames readers bring. The distinction matters and gets its own treatment under Critical lenses and Alternative readings.
  10. The "post-Cold War directionlessness" claim is padding — unevidenced, undated, and connected to nothing in the text. Drop it.
  11. The life-course mapping is applied too mechanically. Wainscot-and-door as "the safe parameters of early adulthood", the shelf as career "peak", the circling as "midlife crisis": the trajectory-shape is genuinely in the poem, but point-for-point allegorisation collapses under its own questions (what is the dust? the table leg?). The poem offers a felt correspondence, not a key.
  12. What the notes get right and the site should keep: the trochee analysis of line 7 ("right o-ver"); the reading of "seemed" as meaning constructed rather than discovered; the enjambment across the octave–sestet seam as momentum where the form demands pause; "I don't know" as the refusal of a grand answer. These are rescued and developed below.

Lament

Gillian Clarke  ·  1991

A prayer with no god in it: twenty-one lines of "for", mourning a war’s casualties without ranking them.

Lines
21
Form

Date
1991
Analysed

07Lament
ContextThe PoemThe Whole PoemForm & StructureSoundMotifs & SymbolsThemesDifficult MomentsClose AnalysisCritical LensesOther ReadingsRevision NotesConnectionsWriting About ItExam PracticeEditorial Notes
CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The First Gulf War (1990–1991): The Environmental Catastrophe

Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. A US-led coalition of 35 nations launched Operation Desert Storm on 17 January 1991, following a UN deadline. The air campaign was followed by a 100-hour ground offensive that drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait. Before retreating, Iraqi forces committed an act of calculated eco-terrorism: they opened the valves of the Sea Island Terminal and dumped approximately 400–800 million gallons of crude oil into the Persian Gulf — the largest deliberate oil spill in history. They also set fire to over 700 Kuwaiti oil wells. The fires burned for months (some for years). The smoke plume stretched over 800 miles. An estimated 111 million barrels of oil spilled into the sea, creating a slick 60 miles long and 13 miles wide. The ecological damage was catastrophic: seabirds, marine mammals, sea turtles, fish, and coastal ecosystems were devastated.

Clarke was watching television reports and reading newspaper photographs of this disaster when she began writing Lament. She has stated: 'All the details in the poem came from reports in the media. There were newspaper photographs of cormorants covered with oil — in his funeral silk.' The photograph of the soldier in his uniform of fire was a real image of a soldier burned when his tank was bombed. The boy fusilier who joined for the company and 'the farmer's sons, in it for the music' came from radio interviews with the mothers of soldiers.

The Lament as Genre

A lament is one of the oldest poetic forms: a song of grief for someone or something lost. The genre appears in Ancient Sumerian literature (the Lament for the Destruction of Ur, c.2000 BCE), in the Hebrew Bible (Lamentations, the psalms), in Celtic bardic tradition, and in the military tradition (The Last Post, the most famous English-language lament, played on a bugle at funerals and Remembrance Day ceremonies). Clarke explains: A lament is an elegy, an expression of grief. It can be a sad, military tune played on a bugle. The poem's structure — the word Lament as the opening, then For preceding each item — is a list of all that is lamented.

Metonymy as Poetic Strategy

Clarke's key technique is metonymy — using a part to represent the whole. One green turtle stands for all endangered sea turtles. One cormorant stands for all oil-soaked seabirds. Ahmed at the closed border stands for all civilian refugees. This technique makes the incomprehensible scale of the disaster (hundreds of thousands of individual animals, thousands of human lives) emotionally accessible by focusing on individual, imaginable cases.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Lament
1For the green turtle with her pulsing burden,
2in search of the breeding ground.
3For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness.
4For the cormorant in his funeral silk,
5the veil of iridescence on the sand,
6the shadow on the sea.
7For the ocean's lap with its mortal stain.
8For Ahmed at the closed border.
9For the soldier with his uniform of fire.
10For the gunsmith and the armourer,
11the boy fusilier who joined for the company,
12the farmer's sons, in it for the music.
13For the hook-beaked turtles,
14the dugong and the dolphin,
15the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder.
16For the tern, the gull and the restless wader,
17the long migrations and the slow dying,
18the veiled sun and the stink of anger.
19For the burnt earth and the sun put out,
20the scalded ocean and the blazing well.
21For vengeance, and the ashes of language.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Line 1
For the green turtle with her pulsing burden,
Language & devices

Preposition: For — this is the lament. Green turtle = specifically the endangered green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas). Adjective: green — colour, life, nature, hope. Personification: her — female, maternal. Pulsing burden — the eggs she carries, living, heartbeating.

Meaning & effect

The poem opens with one of its most powerful metonymies: a single green turtle, pregnant, searching for her breeding ground. The word pulsing gives the eggs a heartbeat — they are already living, already vulnerable. The turtle's burden is both physical (the weight of eggs) and emotional (the weight of responsibility — she must find safe ground). The Gulf oil spill made the breeding beaches of the Persian Gulf toxic — this turtle cannot do what millions of years of evolution have prepared her to do.

Line 2
in search of the breeding ground.
Language & devices

Continuous Action: the turtle is searching — she has not found it. The breeding ground is her annual destination, encoded in her biology over millennia. The absence of punctuation connecting this to line 1 creates flow — the turtle's journey continues unbroken.

Meaning & effect

The tragedy of this line is temporal: sea turtles return to the exact beach where they were born, every breeding season. The oil spill has fouled these beaches — the very places encoded in the turtle's deepest instincts. There is nowhere else to go. The turtle's search is futile; the breeding ground is gone.

Line 3
For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness.
Language & devices

Oxymoron: nest of sickness — a nest should be a sanctuary; here it is a bed of contamination. Possessive: her eggs — the turtle's maternal investment is complete; she has laid them in the only ground available, which is toxic.

Meaning & effect

This is one of the poem's most heartbreaking images: the most vulnerable moment in the turtle's reproductive cycle (when she has laid her eggs in the ground) coincides with maximum contamination. The eggs will die. The nest — which should be the safest place in the world for these lives — has been made lethal by human action. Sickness is both literally accurate (contaminated sand) and metaphorically resonant: the environment itself is sick.

Line 4–6
For the cormorant in his funeral silk, / the veil of iridescence on the sand, / the shadow on the sea.
Language & devices

Funeral silk — oil-soaked black feathers = mourning clothes. Metaphor: veil of iridescence — the oil film on the sand is rainbow-coloured (iridescent), described as a veil. Both beautiful and funereal. Shadow on the sea — the oil slick as darkness spreading across water.

Meaning & effect

Funeral silk is Gillian Clarke's most celebrated image in this poem. The cormorant is already wearing its own funeral clothes: the oil has dressed it for death. Iridescence creates a disturbing aesthetic effect — the oil slick IS beautiful, its rainbow sheen is real. Clarke forces us to acknowledge that environmental destruction can be visually stunning even as it kills. The three images (funeral silk / iridescence / shadow) form a triptych of death: animal, beach, sea.

Line 7
For the ocean's lap with its mortal stain.
Language & devices

Lap — the gentle, rhythmic movement of waves against a beach (personified, like a cat's tongue lapping). Adjective: mortal — both fatal (deadly) and human (mortal = of the earth, of death). Noun: stain — indelible mark of guilt and pollution.

Meaning & effect

Mortal stain is a perfect phrase carrying three meanings: (1) the oil physically stains the ocean; (2) mortal = deadly — the stain kills; (3) moral stain — the pollution is also a guilt, a mark of human shame. The ocean's lap — its most gentle, intimate gesture — is contaminated. Even the softest action of the sea is now lethal.

Line 8
For Ahmed at the closed border.
Language & devices

Human Individual: the only named person in the poem. Ahmed — an Arabic name, specifically from the Arabic-speaking world (the Gulf region). Situation: at the closed border — a civilian unable to enter or leave his country during the war.

Meaning & effect

Ahmed is the poem's human metonymy — one person, but thousands like him. Borders were closed during and after the Gulf War: Kuwaiti refugees, Palestinian workers (many of whom were expelled from Kuwait), Iraqis — all found themselves at closed borders. Ahmed has a name (unlike the animals); he is a specific individual. The brevity of his line is devastating: he gets one line in the poem, one line in history.

Line 9
For the soldier with his uniform of fire.
Language & devices

Real Image: Clarke saw a newspaper photograph of a soldier burned alive in his tank. Metaphor: uniform of fire — his soldier's uniform replaced or consumed by fire. Ambiguity: this soldier could be on either side — coalition or Iraqi.

Meaning & effect

Uniform of fire is one of the most striking metaphors in modern war poetry. A uniform identifies and protects; fire destroys identity and identity along with it. The soldier has become his own burning. Clarke deliberately does not specify which army he belongs to — the image transcends political allegiance to describe pure human suffering. This is Clarke's evenhandedness: soldiers from both sides die horribly in war.

Line 10–12
For the gunsmith and the armourer, / the boy fusilier who joined for the company, / the farmer's sons, in it for the music.
Language & devices

Escalation: from makers of weapons (gunsmith, armourer) to users of weapons. Boy fusilier — young, barely adult. Joined for the company — seeking friendship, belonging, not heroism. 'Farmer's sons, in it for the music' — drawn by the adventure, the bands, the communal spirit of an army.

Meaning & effect

This tercet humanises soldiers by revealing their completely human, unmartial motivations: friendship (the company), music and adventure (the music). These are not warriors who chose their profession but boys who enlisted for social reasons, who are now casualties. Clarke learned these details from radio interviews with soldiers' mothers — which means these are real people, real reasons. The lament for them is the more painful for this.

Line 13–15
For the hook-beaked turtles, / the dugong and the dolphin, / the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder.
Language & devices

Listing of marine mammals. Hook-beaked turtles — specific species. Dugong: large, gentle marine herbivore, often called a sea cow, endangered. Struck dumb — silenced. 'By the missile's thunder' — the sonic blast of a missile detonating underwater.

Meaning & effect

'Struck dumb by the missile's thunder' is the poem's most compressed argument against war: the whale — whose song can travel hundreds of miles through the ocean — has been silenced by human weapon noise. Whales use sound to navigate, communicate, and find mates. The military use of the ocean with sonar and explosions genuinely deafens cetaceans. The whale is struck dumb as effectively as the speaker might be struck dumb by grief. The comparison between whale song and human speech (language, which the poem's final line mourns) is implicit.

Line 16–18
For the tern, the gull and the restless wader, / the long migrations and the slow dying, / the veiled sun and the stink of anger.
Language & devices

SEABIRDS listed. Restless wader — shore birds that cannot rest because their habitat is destroyed. Long migrations and the slow dying — birds that migrate thousands of miles only to die at the end of their journey. Veiled sun — smoke from the oil fires blocking sunlight. Stink of anger — synesthesia: anger has a smell.

Meaning & effect

Long migrations and the slow dying is the poem's most elegant pairing: the epic biological achievement of long-distance migration (some waders fly from the Arctic to Antarctica) made futile by the dying that awaits at the destination. The stink of anger is one of Clarke's most arresting synesthetic images: the burning oil produced an actual stench that pervaded hundreds of miles of the Gulf. Clarke identifies this smell as the smell of human rage — as if war itself has a body odour.

Line 19–20
For the burnt earth and the sun put out, / the scalded ocean and the blazing well.
Language & devices

Apocalyptic Scale: these final images are total — not individual animals but whole elements. Burnt earth — the scorched Kuwaiti desert. Sun put out — the smoke from the wells blocking sunlight (this actually happened). Scalded ocean — the heated, oil-covered sea. Blazing well — 700 oil wells on fire.

Meaning & effect

The poem moves from the individual (one turtle, one cormorant, Ahmed) to the total (earth, sun, ocean, all oil wells). The scale expands to planetary in this stanza. Clarke is describing not a local disaster but an assault on the fundamental elements: earth, fire, water (air is already poisoned by veiled sun). The four classical elements are all damaged. Scalded is an extraordinary word for the ocean: scalding is what you do to skin with boiling water — the ocean has been scalded by burning oil.

Line 21
For vengeance, and the ashes of language.
Language & devices

Abstract Nouns: vengeance and ashes of language. The poem moves beyond physical damage to psychological and semiotic damage. Ashes of language — words reduced to ash, truth incinerated in war.

Meaning & effect

The final line is the most philosophically rich in the poem. Clarke ends not with a physical image but with two abstractions. Vengeance names the emotional motor of war — wars are fought for revenge as much as for strategy or resources. The ashes of language is Clarke's most self-referential moment: as a poet, she mourns the destruction of language — the death of honest communication — in war. Multiple Readings: (1) Language is used to lie during wartime (propaganda, disinformation — the ashes of truth). (2) The languages and voices of the dead are ashes — their capacity to speak is gone. (3) Clarke's own language struggles to represent the inexpressible scale of destruction — poetry itself may not be adequate. The poem ends on its deepest grief.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Lament' is usually described as a sad catalogue: a list of the Gulf War's victims, human and animal, delivered with mounting grief. That description is accurate about the contents and wrong about the poem, because it misses what the poem withholds. The argument here: 'Lament' is built on a double refusal — it refuses to assert, and it refuses to accuse — and its power comes from performing, in grammar and ceremony, the only kind of speech it believes survives a war: naming without saying. The poem does not describe the death of honest language; it writes as if from inside it, and the form is the demonstration.

Start with what reading the poem actually feels like, line 1 to line 21. The title gives a genre-noun and stops. Then "For the green turtle" — and the ear understands at once that the title has not ended: Lament for. Every subsequent sentence re-attaches to that governing word, which means the reader is made to re-say "Lament" silently eleven times — the poem conscripts its reader into performing the rite, not observing it. This is the first sense in which the anaphora is the poem: it is not emphasis, it is liturgy, the structure of a litany of intercession — "For the sick… for the dying…" — in which a congregation offers up names. And a litany implies a hearer. The poem never names one. Prayers are said, in perfect order, into what may be an empty sky: that suspension — rite intact, addressee gone — is the poem's religious temperature, and one measure of what the war has burnt.

The sequence of the named is exact and means something. Two stanzas of sea-life first — turtle, eggs, cormorant, sand, sea — so that when the humans arrive in stanza 3 they arrive into a world already dying, not the other way round. Human suffering is not the context for environmental damage; environmental damage is the context for human suffering. Stanza 3 sets ocean, refugee and soldier as three grammatically identical, one-line, full-stopped sentences — the poem's strongest formal statement of its flattest claim: there is no hierarchy of grief here, a sea and a man take the same syntax. Ahmed, the only named being in the poem, stands at its threshold moment: the first human is not a combatant but a man stopped at a line someone drew. Then stanza 4, the poem's centre, does the hardest thing in it: it mourns the war's makers — gunsmith, armourer, fusilier, farmer's sons — in the same breath as its victims, because by the poem's logic they are its victims. After that the circle widens back out through species (stanza 5), flyways and atmosphere (stanza 6), to the elements themselves (stanza 7): earth, light, water, fire — creation's inventory, each item cancelled — and last of all the medium in which inventories are made: language.

Now the obvious objection, which any strong reading must meet head-on: a poem that ends by declaring language ash is self-refuting. Here is a poem — shapely, eloquent, anthologised, taught — whose final claim its own existence appears to disprove. If language were really ashes, 'Lament' could not have been written. The objection dissolves once you look at which language the poem has renounced. Go through all twenty-one lines looking for a statement — a main clause, something asserted of something — and you will not find one. The poem is eleven sentences with no predication in them: it never says the war is wrong, never says the turtle died, never says who set the fires. It has given up the assertive functions of language — the functions that reportage, propaganda, communiqués and euphemism share, the grammar in which a bombardment can be called a "surgical strike" — because in war those functions are the first corrupted. Clarke's own gloss is exact: "the ashes of language are the death of truth during war." What survives the fire is smaller and older: the capacity to name, and to set a name inside the dative of care — for. The poem is not self-refuting; it is self-exemplifying. It ends by mourning the language of saying in the only language left, the language of dedication.

The same withholding governs agency, and this is where the poem is most contestable. Its single finite verb is "joined"; its single agent is a boy; every act of destruction arrives as an agentless participle — laid, closed, struck, veiled, burnt, put out, scalded. Nobody in 'Lament' does anything except enlist. One reading calls this the poem's deepest evenhandedness: grief refuses to become prosecution; at a funeral you do not read out the charge sheet. The other reading calls it evasion: the Gulf oil spill was not weather — it was a deliberate act, ordered by identifiable men, and a poem that mourns "the blazing well" without an arsonist converts a war crime into something like climate, to be grieved rather than judged. The defence, and it is a strong one, is that the poem does name the motive even as it withholds the men: "For vengeance". The last line files the accusation in the only grammar the poem allows itself — vengeance is not said to have caused anything (no clause could say so); it is simply set on the list, mourned-and-indicted in one word, the human faculty whose exercise fills the previous twenty lines. The charge is there; it has been folded into the rite.

And the rite itself is the answer to the poem's other great pressure: scale. A war's damage is uncountable, and the poem knows it — you can watch it running out of room, two griefs per stanza at the start, seven crammed into stanza 6, the singulars giving way to plurals — and a lesser poem would have answered scale with excess: piled adjectives, raised voice. Clarke answers it with ceremony and with terrible smallness of speech: "who joined for the company", "in it for the music" — the recruits' own idiom, or their mothers', lifted from radio interviews and left unimproved. The poem's tonal control is nowhere more severe: it will not translate a mother's flat phrase into poetry, because the flatness is the truth of it, and any eloquence added would be the first step back towards the language that ends in ashes. This is why calling the poem "sad" misses it. Sadness is an emotion the poem induces; the poem itself is doing something harder — holding grief, accusation, and a working ritual in a single unbroken posture, twenty-one lines at attention.

So the movement first line to last is best described not as a list but as a widening and a turning-inward at once: the circle of the mourned expands from one turtle to the four elements, while the poem's attention closes in on its own medium, until the two arrive together at the final line — the largest circle (everything, even abstraction) and the innermost point (the words this is written in). "For vengeance, and the ashes of language." — with the poem's one comma-before-"and", the drawn breath before the last name at a memorial, and then the full stop the owner's notes read exactly rightly: "no more words to be said proceeding last line". The lament ends because its medium has joined its subjects. What remains standing is the shape of the rite itself — seven equal stanzas, eleven dedications, order held all the way down — which is the poem's real, unstated claim: when truth has burnt, form is how grief keeps faith.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

The site has no other form section for this poem; this one is self-contained.

The governing grammar: a title with no sentence attached

The title is not a label but the poem's grammatical head. Every stanza — and in fact every sentence — completes the phrase "Lament / For…": Lament for the green turtle. Lament for Ahmed. Lament for vengeance. This is the oldest naming convention of the genre ("Lament for the Makaris", the Welsh marwnad or death-song tradition Clarke inherits, Lorca's Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías), broken open: Clarke snaps the conventional title after its first word so that the poem's whole body becomes the title's unfinished second half. Twenty-one lines try to complete the phrase "Lament for—" and none of them closes it.

The consequence is stark and almost never noticed: the poem contains no main clause. It is eleven sentences long, and every sentence is a prepositional phrase — a dedication, not a statement. Count the full stops: eleven (after lines 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 15, 18, 20, 21), and each of the eleven sentences they close begins with "For". Nothing in the poem is asserted; nothing is predicated of anything. The poem cannot say "war destroys" or "grief is unbearable", because saying — assertion, the grammar of reportage and propaganda alike — is precisely what the last line declares burnt. What survives of language is the dative gesture: pointing grief at its objects, one by one.

Within this clause-less grammar there is exactly one finite verb: "the boy fusilier who joined for the company" (line 11). Every other verb-form is a participle with its agent deleted — laid, closed, struck, veiled, burnt, put out, scalded: things done to the world by no named doer. No Saddam, no Bush, no army performs an action anywhere in the poem; even the missile appears only as a possessive ("the missile's thunder"). The single completed action in 'Lament', and the single grammatical agent, is a boy joining up in innocence. That is the poem's ethics compressed into syntax: agency belongs to the naive, damage arrives agentless — either a profound evenhandedness or a deliberate refusal to prosecute, and the tension between those two readings runs through the whole analysis below.

The anaphora, mapped exactly

Eleven of the twenty-one lines begin "For" — Clarke's own count. The distribution is not even, and the unevenness is the argument:

StanzaLinesLines beginning "For"Pattern
11–31, 3two of three
24–64opening line only
37–97, 8, 9all three
410–1210opening line only
513–1513opening line only
616–1816opening line only
719–2119, 21two of three — incl. the poem's last line

So the shape is 2 – 1 – 3 – 1 – 1 – 1 – 2. Three observations, each worth exam space:

  • Every stanza restarts from the title. Whatever else varies, each tercet's first word re-sounds "Lament for—", so the reader silently supplies the title eleven times. The anaphora is not "repetition for emphasis"; it is the mechanism by which a one-word title governs a twenty-one-line poem.
  • The density peaks at stanza 3 — the pivot from nature to people. Ocean, refugee, soldier: the only stanza in which every line begins "For" is also the only stanza in which every line ends with a full stop (the owner's notes spotted this and it is the best single observation in them). Three self-contained, walled sentences: For the ocean's lap with its mortal stain. For Ahmed at the closed border. For the soldier with his uniform of fire. The stanza about a closed border is built of closed lines — each victim sealed in a grammatical cell, unable to reach the next line. Form performs border.
  • The frame: stanzas 1 and 7 have the same sentence-architecture. Each is a two-line "For" sentence followed by a one-line "For" sentence (lines 1–2 + 3; lines 19–20 + 21). The poem ends with the syntactic shape it began with — ritual returning to its opening posture — except that the opening's one-line sentence held eggs in a nest, and the closing's holds vengeance and ash. And line 21 is the only final line of any stanza to begin "For": after six stanzas in which the formula launches grief and lower-case lines absorb it, the last word-of-dedication arrives where a stanza should be subsiding. The lament refuses to end anywhere but on its own first word.

Where the anaphora does not hold, the exceptions are pointed. Nine lines begin with "the" — continuations, each victim still definite, still known. One line in the poem begins with neither: "in search of the breeding ground." (line 2). The line about searching is the only line that escapes the formula — syntax slipping off-pattern exactly where the turtle slips off her map.

Finally, the two lowercase "for"s. "Joined for the company"; "in it for the music". The same word that consecrates each victim reappears, small, inside the small print of motive — for meaning "in exchange for", "for the sake of". The elegy's word of dedication and the recruit's word of transaction are one word. That collision detonates in the last line, where "For vengeance" can be read with either grammar — dedication or motive — and the poem needs both (see Cruxes).

Metre: scansion and what the substitutions do

Free verse, but with strong local shapes; lines run from 6 to 12 syllables, mostly carrying 3–5 stresses. Stressed syllables are marked in bold; the notation beneath is x (unstressed) / (stressed).

Line 1 — "For the green turtle with her pulsing burden," x x / / x x x / x / x — an anapaestic lift into a spondee ("green tur-"): the line rises to its subject, then falls through two trochees, "pulsing burden", a dying fall on a feminine ending. The rhythm enacts dedication then weight: lift the creature up, feel what she carries.

Line 2 — "in search of the breeding ground." x / x x / x / — the poem's shortest early line, three stresses, ending on a stressed monosyllable plus full stop. After line 1's swell, the clipped masculine close is the search hitting its wall.

Line 3 — "For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness." x x / / x x / x / x — the spondee "eggs laid": two adjacent stresses where the line's weight is set down, as the eggs are.
