CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the other six

Comparison hooks

  • Love Armed (Behn). Link: both poems anatomise who pays for a grand abstraction — Behn's Love "in fantastic triumph sat" while only one heart bleeds; Clarke's "vengeance" sits unnamed at the head of a casualty list it never joins. Both are structured on unequal ledgers (thy joys / my pains; the mourned / the never-blamed). Shared technique: patterned repetition building a rhetorical case (Behn's balanced antitheses; Clarke's anaphora). Difference: Behn's suffering is performed within courtly wit — symmetrical, musical, self-delighting even in pain; Clarke's register is documentary restraint, and her asymmetry (eleven dedications, no verdict) refuses the closure Behn's final couplet snaps shut.
  • A Different History (Bhatt). Link: both end at the same wound — language after violence. Bhatt asks "which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?" and marvels that the descendants love it; Clarke ends with the tongue itself in ashes. Conquest corrupts language from within; war burns it down. Shared technique: the pivot from concrete scene to abstract linguistic close; sacred framing (Sarasvati and book-reverence; litany and rite). Difference: Bhatt's poem holds a future — "the unborn grandchildren" will speak, strangely, lovingly, something; Clarke's ends in residue with no generation to follow (the eggs of line 3 were already doomed). Bhatt's is a history; Clarke's is a terminus.
  • The Chimney Sweeper (Blake). Link: children recruited by warm words — the sweep consoled with an angel's promise, the fusilier with "the company", the farmer's sons with "the music"; in both, the institution's language of comfort is the mechanism of exploitation. Shared technique: devastating use of the victims' own naive idiom, left uncorrected so the reader must do the condemning (Blake's "So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm"; Clarke's "in it for the music"). Difference: Blake gives his children voices and a consoling (ironised) theology; Clarke's recruits never speak and no heaven is on offer — her irony is quieter and her frame is planetary, where Blake's is a single city's economy of soot.
  • Where I Come From (Brewster). Link: both are catalogue-poems in which a list builds a world — Brewster's "People are made of places", itemising woods, farms, chromium-plated offices; Clarke's litany itemises a world being unmade. The catalogue as memory versus the catalogue as obituary. Shared technique: asyndetic listing; the definite, plain noun-phrase as unit of meaning. Difference: Brewster's list is generative and ends on an opening — "a door in the mind blows open" to spring and frogs; Clarke's ends on a full stop and ash. One poem trusts accumulated detail to preserve; the other uses the same device to count losses that accumulation cannot restore.
  • Report to Wordsworth (Boey Kim Cheng). Link: the closest pairing in the set — both are eco-elegies that end by doubting their own medium as the sky itself fails: Boey's "sky slowing like a dying clock", where "poetry and piety have begun to fail" and God labours "to utter his last cry"; Clarke's "sun put out" and "ashes of language". Both mourn nature and the tradition of mourning nature. Shared technique: inherited elegiac machinery under strain — Boey crams his report into a sonnet addressed to a dead poet; Clarke strips the lament to its ritual skeleton. Difference: Boey's poem is thick with literary ancestry (Wordsworth, Milton, Neptune, Proteus) and speaks to someone; Clarke's has no addressee and almost no allusion — Boey laments that the tradition cannot help; Clarke writes as if it is already ash and only the bare rite remains.
  • The Cockroach (Halligan). Link: both use an animal to dissolve the human/animal boundary — but in opposite directions: Halligan scrutinises one insect until it mirrors himself ("I thought I recognised myself"); Clarke mourns many creatures as fellow victims who mirror no one and matter in themselves. Introspection versus intercession. Shared technique: minute animal observation carrying moral weight; a closing turn that reframes the whole poem (Halligan's unanswered question, Clarke's abstract final line). Difference: Halligan's is allegory — the animal exists to read the self, in a private room; Clarke's animals refuse allegory — the turtle is not a symbol of humanity but a casualty alongside it, on the scale of a biosphere. One poem ends in a question about the self; the other in a full stop over everything.
WRITING ABOUT IT

Writing About It

Turning the analysis into paragraphs that score

Writing about it

Model paragraph 1 — the anaphora and its breaks (form → argument):

Clarke's anaphora is usually described as repetition for emphasis, but its real work is grammatical: every sentence in the poem — eleven of them — begins "For", completing the title, so that the whole text is one extended dedication with no main clause anywhere. Nothing is asserted; victims are named, never narrated. The pattern's local variations then carry the argument. In the third stanza, uniquely, every line both opens with "For" and closes with a full stop — "For Ahmed at the closed border." — three sealed, one-line sentences in the stanza that mourns a sealed frontier, so that the refugee is confined by syntax before he is confined by politics. By contrast, the crowded sixth stanza lets one "For" govern seven griefs, commas rushing them together, as if the rite were running out of room. A form this controlled cannot mean chaos; it means ceremony — the poem meets a war's disorder with liturgical order, and holds it to the last full stop. (166 words)

Model paragraph 2 — tonal restraint in stanza 4 (register → effect):

The most shocking lines in 'Lament' are its least dramatic. The boy fusilier "joined for the company"; the farmer's sons are "in it for the music" — idiom you would use of a Saturday football team, applied to the war dead. Clarke took these phrases from radio interviews with the soldiers' mothers and left them unimproved: no "brave", no "tragic", no elegiac upgrade. The metre matches the diction — "in it for the" runs four unstressed syllables, the flattest stretch in the poem — so the verse itself declines to mourn aloud. The restraint is the meaning. Eloquence about these boys would repeat the trick that recruited them, since "the music" — the band, the parade — was itself war's advertising; and "the company" splits as we read it, companionship hardening into military unit. By refusing to raise its voice, the poem transfers the work of grief to the reader, which is why the lines wound more than any lament the poet could have performed. (159 words)

Three sentence-patterns that do the most work:

  1. Concession-then-turn: "It would be easy to read X as …, but the [word/form] insists on …" — the pattern that shows an examiner you have seen the naive reading and gone past it.
  2. Double-meaning held open: "X hovers between … and …, and the line needs both, because …" — for "burden", "company", "mortal", "For"; never resolve a productive ambiguity, spend it.
  3. Form-as-agent: "The [stanza/sentence/stress-pattern] performs what the line describes: …" — the move that links technique to meaning without the word "effect" ever appearing.

Three phrases to ban:

  1. "This shows that…" — the formula that replaces analysis with assertion; go straight to the claim.
  2. "Creates a sense of sadness / makes the reader feel sad" — 'Lament' is precisely not busy being sad; name the actual effect (unease, implication, suppressed accusation, enforced slowness).
  3. "The poem flows" / "lacks structure because it is free verse" — this is the most rigidly structured free verse on the syllabus; both clichés are disprovable from the text in front of you.
EXAM PRACTICE

Exam Practice

Questions, plans, and the marginal gains

Exam practice

Q1. Explore the ways in which Clarke movingly conveys grief for the victims of war in 'Lament'.

  • Thesis: the poem moves the reader not by expressing grief but by enacting it — a funeral rite in language, whose ceremonial control is more affecting than any outcry; the grief is in the form.
  • Point 1 — the litany: every sentence a dedication completing the title ("For the green turtle…"); the reader made to perform the rite, silently re-supplying "Lament" eleven times; asyndeton like names read at a memorial.
  • Point 2 — dignity distributed equally: identical grammar for ocean, refugee, soldier (stanza 3's three sealed sentences); personal pronouns for animals ("his funeral silk"); one name, "Ahmed", where the world sees a category.
  • Point 3 — the borrowed flatness: "joined for the company", "in it for the music" — the mothers' own idiom left unimproved; the pun in "company"; restraint as the register that cannot lie, transferring grief's work to the reader.
  • Counter-move: concede the poem never says it grieves — no "alas", no first person, no addressee — then turn: that absence is the mechanism; a stated grief could be argued with, a performed rite cannot.
  • Conclusion: the final line mourns the medium itself ("the ashes of language"), so the poem's last act of grief is for the possibility of poems like this one — and the full stop after "language" is the rite completed with nothing left over.

Q2. In what ways does Clarke make you vividly aware of the destructiveness of war in 'Lament'?

  • Thesis: destruction is made vivid by scale-work — one poisoned nest to an extinguished sun in twenty-one lines — while the destroyers are grammatically deleted, so the reader confronts pure consequence.
  • Point 1 — intimate scale first: "her pulsing burden… her eggs laid in their nest of sickness" — war experienced as the corruption of birth; the paradox of "nest of sickness" establishing that safety itself is what war destroys.
  • Point 2 — the beautiful poison: "the veil of iridescence", "funeral silk" — destruction that shimmers; the reader implicated in finding it lovely; oil never named though present in every image.
  • Point 3 — cosmic scale last: stanza 7's elemental inventory — "burnt earth", "the sun put out", "scalded ocean" — hyperbole made literal by the well-fires; Genesis run backwards, ending at language itself.
  • Counter-move: concede there is no violence shown in progress — no battle, no blood, one finite verb in the whole poem — then turn: agentless participles ("struck", "burnt", "closed") present a world where damage simply arrives, which is how war is experienced by everything in the poem's list.
  • Conclusion: the most destructive image is the quietest — "the ashes of language" — because it destroys the means of knowing all the others; war's last casualty is the truth about war.

Examiner's edge

  1. Quote the grammar, not just the images. The strongest available fact: eleven sentences, every one beginning "For", none containing a main clause — the poem asserts nothing, dedicates everything. Few candidates will say anything about syntax; this alone separates an answer.
  2. One finite verb. "Joined" (l.11) is the only completed action and the boy the only grammatical agent in the poem: agency belongs to the innocent, damage arrives agentless. Two sentences on this outweigh two paragraphs of image-spotting.
  3. Stanza 3 is unique twice over — all three lines begin "For" and end with full stops: the closed-border stanza built of closed lines. Say "form performs the border", then move on.
  4. Frame the frame: stanzas 1 and 7 share the same sentence-architecture (two-line sentence + one-line sentence), so the rite ends in its opening posture — eggs at one end, ashes at the other.
  5. The two lowercase "for"s ("for the company", "for the music") set up the last line's double grammar: dedication or motive, tribute or cause — "For vengeance" needs both. This is the subtlest point in the poem; deploy it at the essay's climax, not in passing.
  6. The unique ", and" — "For vengeance, and the ashes of language" contains the poem's only comma-before-"and": the drawn breath before the final name at a memorial reading. A punctuation-level observation, and examiners reward nothing more reliably than punctuation read closely.
  7. Never say "free verse = chaos". The reflex claim is disprovable in one glance: seven equal tercets, total end-stopping, a single repeated formula. Argue ritual order containing chaos, and you are ahead of most of the room.
  8. Use the arithmetic of crowding: griefs per stanza run roughly 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 7, 6 — the lament audibly running out of room — and singulars give way to plurals ("sons", "turtles", "migrations", "ashes"). Numbers, used once, read as rigour.
  9. Oil is never named. Every image is oil unnamed — silk, veil, iridescence, shadow, stain, scald, blaze, smoke — the war's cause, weapon and shroud kept as a structuring absence. One sentence of context (deliberate spill, 600+ well-fires, 1991) is enough; the poem is printed on the paper, so spend your time on its words, not its war.
  10. End where the poem ends. Whatever the question, the strongest final paragraph in the exam is about "the ashes of language": an elegy whose last casualty is its own medium, ending in the only language it still trusts — naming — and then in silence. The full stop is the poem's last technique; read it.
EDITORIAL NOTES

Editorial Notes

Text checks and corrections to the source notes

Text check

The 21-line, seven-tercet text supplied in the notes is sound, with four points to fix or flag:

  1. Line 9 exists in two published forms. The Cambridge anthology text and most study editions print "For the soldier with his uniform of fire"; Clarke's own website notes on the poem, and some teaching sources that follow her, quote "the soldier in his uniform of fire" (gillianclarke.co.uk; poetryprof.com prints "in"; LitCharts prints "with"). The owner's notes contain both, unremarked. In the exam, quote whichever the printed paper gives — it will be the anthology's "with". The variant is worth ten seconds of thought, not exam time: "in" dresses the soldier in flame (fire as clothing worn); "with" issues fire to him like kit (fire as equipment carried). Both keep the terrible logic that what should protect him is what burns him.
  2. Capitalisation. Two of the three transcripts in the notes capitalise "The" at the start of lines 17, 18 and 20 ("The long migrations…"). The published text uses lowercase "the" — Clarke does not capitalise line-openings. This matters because the eleven capital "For"s are then the only capitals inside the poem apart from "Ahmed": the anaphora is typographically marked, and the name stands out even on the page.
  3. The final full stop. One transcript in the notes ends "…the ashes of language" without a stop. The published line ends with a full stop — and the analysis below leans on it, so get it right.
  4. Loose quotation in the notes. "the scalded ocean and the burning wells", "a shadow on the sea", "put out the sun" all appear as quotations in the notes; the poem has "the blazing well" (singular), "the shadow on the sea", "the sun put out". Also "farmer's sons" is a singular possessive — one farmer, several sons; one family, multiplied loss — not "farmers' sons".

Date and publication. The notes' bare "1991" is a composition date, not a publication fact, and stated that way it is half-wrong. Verified position: Clarke (b. Cardiff, 1937; National Poet of Wales 2008–16) wrote the poem in response to the Gulf War of 1990–91, drawing every detail, by her own account, "from reports in the media" — newspaper photographs of oil-covered cormorants, a photograph of a soldier burnt "when his tank was bombed", radio interviews with soldiers' mothers, and a Friends of the Earth list of creatures at risk from the oil. Its verifiable collected publication is her Collected Poems (Carcanet, 1997); Poetry Prof states it was "published in 1997 but had been several years in the writing, its inception going back to 1990/91". No authoritative source was found confirming an earlier appearance in The King of Britain's Daughter (1993), so do not assert one. Clarke's site also confirms the structural fact the analysis below builds on: "every verse, and 11 lines, begin with 'for'", and glosses the ending — "The ashes of language are the death of truth during war."

Gaps and corrections

  1. A whole contributor section in the notes analyses a poem that does not exist. The block headed "1. Understanding the Context and the Title (AO2)… 2. Structure and Form (AO3)" claims the poem has "six stanzas… long stanzas… irregular line lengths" and quotes, as Clarke's, the lines "the ocean's injured back", "the wasted journey of the whale", "For the fly-pasts, the flashes", "For the woman in the veil", "mother's milk", "For the unborn", "the dead hands, the dead men, the dead weapons", "the wastes of history", "a slick of crude that has clung to the bellies of gulls", and a closing image of a mother "scanning the horizon for the mother-of-pearl of the moon". None of these lines is in 'Lament'. The section is confabulated (machine-generated or conflated with another text) and must be discarded wholesale — including its stanza count, its "M.O.T." mnemonic, and its final-stanza reading. Any essay built on it would be quoting a phantom poem.
  2. The oil-spill numbers in the notes are internally contradictory and partly wrong. One paragraph says "approximately 400–800 million gallons" and, two sentences later, "an estimated 111 million barrels" — which would be ~4.7 billion gallons, out by an order of magnitude. Credible estimates for the deliberate 1991 Gulf spill run from about 4 million to about 11 million barrels (roughly 170–460 million gallons); it remains the largest oil spill in history. "400 million gallons" is defensible as a mid-to-high figure; "111 million barrels" is not. For the fires: retreating Iraqi forces ignited over 600 Kuwaiti oil wells (commonly "600–700"); the last was capped in November 1991, months after the ceasefire — the burning outlived the war, which matters for a poem written "at the time".
  3. The Kenneth Jarecke identification is overstated. The notes assert as fact that "the soldier with his uniform of fire" "alludes to photograph (Kenneth Jarecke) of Iraqi soldier burned to death… Photo: Highway of Death, 1991". Clarke's own account says only that she saw "a horrific photograph of a soldier burnt when his tank was bombed" — she names no photographer, and Jarecke's famous image shows an incinerated man in a truck, not a tank. The connection is plausible (Jarecke's was the most notorious such photograph, taken on the Basra road in the war's final hours and largely refused by Anglo-American media) but it is conjecture, not fact — and the media's refusal to print it actually serves the "ashes of language" argument better as context than the attribution does. The long unattributed description quoted in the notes ("The Iraqi soldier died attempting to pull himself up over the dashboard of his truck…") is the opening of Torie Rose DeGhett's 2014 Atlantic essay "The War Photo No One Would Publish" — never quote it as anonymous reportage.
  4. "Absence of rhyme indicates lack of resolution + chaos in war" — the reflex reading, and wrong for this poem. 'Lament' is one of the most ordered free-verse poems in the anthology: seven equal tercets, every line end-stopped, eleven sentences every one of which begins with the same word. Nothing here is chaotic. The absence of rhyme removes chime and consolation — rhyme's little promise that sounds come home — but the right claim is the reverse of the notes': the poem meets chaos with ceremony. Ritual order is what people reach for when events exceed sense; the form is a funeral rite, not a mimicry of disorder.
  5. The anaphora count in the notes is muddled. "The anaphora and repetition of 'For' of a total of Eleven times (In the beginning) and 4 times (in the body of the poem)" is not a coherent count. Correct figures: eleven line-initial capital "For"s (lines 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 19, 21 — confirmed by Clarke herself), plus two lowercase mid-line "for"s ("joined for the company", "in it for the music") — thirteen in all, and the gap between the two kinds is the poem's centre of gravity (see Form, Cruxes).
  6. "Polysyndeton" is the wrong term. The notes repeatedly credit the poem's momentum to polysyndeton, but there is no conjunction-chaining anywhere: no "and X and Y and Z". What the poem actually does is the opposite at sentence level — asyndeton: the eleven "For" sentences follow one another with no connectives at all, like names read from a list. Within lines, single "and"s hinge balanced pairs ("the dugong and the dolphin"). The one exceptional conjunction is in the last line — "For vengeance, and the ashes of language" — the only "and" in the poem preceded by a comma: a drawn breath before the final item, the pause before the last name at a memorial reading.
  7. "First four stanzas: one item per line" is imprecise. Line 10 already carries two ("the gunsmith and the armourer"). The real pattern is an acceleration in griefs per stanza: roughly 2 (S1), 3 (S2), 3 (S3), 4 (S4), 4 (S5), 7 (S6), 6 (S7). The owner's inference — "as if Clarke doesn't have enough time // space to lament all affected" — is exactly right and worth keeping; it just needs the corrected arithmetic under it. Add the parallel drift from singular to plural: every victim in stanzas 1–3 is singular; plurals enter with "the farmer's sons" and spread ("turtles", "migrations", "ashes") as individuation loses ground to multitude.
  8. The numerology of seven ("No. 7 associated w/ completeness") is over-reading as stated — but rescuable. As a bare symbol-code claim ("seven means completeness, therefore total grief") it is unfalsifiable and would earn nothing. It becomes defensible only by the textual route: stanza 7 systematically reverses Genesis — earth burnt, light extinguished ("the sun put out"), the waters scalded, and finally the word itself in ashes, in a creation story where the world is spoken into being. Seven stanzas as seven days of un-creation is arguable from the imagery; seven as a magic number is not. Argue the imagery, not the arithmetic.
  9. "Personification" via "her" and "his" is loosely claimed. A female turtle is "her"; a male cormorant is "his" — the grammar is biologically accurate, so this is not personification in the strict sense. The precise point is the refusal of "it": Clarke extends to animals the pronouns of persons, which is a dignifying choice rather than a figurative device. Name it as that and the analysis sharpens.
  10. What the notes miss entirely (developed below): that the poem contains no main clause and only one finite verb; that stanza 3 is the only stanza whose every line both begins "For" and ends with a full stop; that stanzas 1 and 7 share an identical sentence-architecture (a two-line sentence, then a one-line sentence) and so frame the poem; that "burden" is also the technical word for a song's refrain; and that oil — the poem's actual subject — is never once named.
Synthesis

All seven at once

A comparison question rewards a thread that runs through several poems, not a list of similarities between two. Seven threads first, then the poem-by-poem table — read down a row, not across a column.

01

Power, and who pays for it

Each of these poems locates a beneficiary and a bill, and refuses to let them be the same person. The interesting move is always the accounting: who is enriched, who is spent, and whether the poem says so outright.

Song: Love Armedthe lover is spent; the beloved goes free The Chimney Sweeperthe parents rise to church on the child's labour A Different Historythe conqueror's tongue is paid for in soul Lamentthe war's bill is presented in turtles and boys
02

Language as an instrument

Four of the seven treat language itself as the thing under examination — a weapon, an inheritance, a failing organ, or a ledger.

A Different Historythe oppressor's tongue, loved by the grandchildren Lamentgrief ends at the ashes of language Report to WordsworthPoetry and piety have begun to fail Song: Love Armedthe poem is an audit written in balanced clauses
03

Nature under pressure

Nature is never scenery here. It is either a casualty, a witness, or the thing that formed the speaker — and often it is being measured for loss.

Report to Wordsworththe sea-gods entombed in what we dump Lamentthe scalded ocean and the blazing well Where I Come Fromthe mind keeps the weather of its landscape A Different Historythe tree the paper came from must not be offended
04

Identity as inheritance, not choice

The speakers do not decide who they are. Place, language and history have already decided, and the poem is the discovery of that.

Where I Come FromPeople are made of places A Different Historythe grandchildren inherit the language, and love it The Cockroachthe self recognised in something it did not choose The Chimney Sweeperthe child inherits the clothes of death
05

Institutions and their alibis

Church, state, empire and war all appear with an explanation ready. The poems are interested in the gap between the explanation and the damage.

The Chimney SweeperGod and his Priest and King A Different Historycolonial education as cultural cropping Lamentthe gunsmith, the armourer, and the company Song: Love ArmedLove set up a Deity by mutual agreement
06

Form turned against itself

The strongest single comparison in the set: four poems adopt a form with an established emotional promise, then break the promise deliberately.

The Cockroacha sonnet that refuses its own resolution Report to Wordsworththe sonnet as a casualty report The Chimney Sweepera nursery rhyme used as an indictment Song: Love Armeda stage song whose lilt delivers a verdict
07

Watching, and being implicated

Several poems open with a speaker at a safe distance and close with that distance gone. Track the pronouns and you can date the collapse exactly.

The CockroachI watched becomes I recognised myself Report to Wordsworththe waste / we dump — the poet is inside the we Song: Love ArmedThus thou and I, the God have armed The Chimney Sweeperthe observer's question hands the poem to the child
